caseno: CIVIL PETITION FOR LEAVE TO APPEAL NO. 448 OF 2001
lawyer:
For the petitioner : 
Mr. Mahbubey Alam Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record. 
For respondent No. 1 
Mr. Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record. 
Respondents : Not represented.
parties:
Principal, Daka Medical College, Dhaka & another
  ------  Petitioner.
Versus
Dr. Manzoor Rasheed  Chowdhury and another ------  Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammed Fazlul Karim , J.: The petitioner moved this petition for leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 8.5.2000 passed in Writ Petition No. 5038 of 1999 making the Rule absolute with direction that respondent No. 1 (writ-petitioner) should be allowed to pursuit his higher study in M.S. Course (Urology) without admission test and he should be admitted in the said Course forthwith even by increasing one seat by the petitioners (writ-respondents).

2. Fact relevant for disposal of this petition, in short, is that the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University issued a notification Memo No. BSMMU/CE/Jan/2000/ 3705 dated 28.9.1999 published in the daily newspaper Janakantha on 30.9.1999 inviting application from the candidates including the candidates who are in Government service specifying the age limit for 40 years for the year 1999-2000. Subsequently the University published an amended notification dated 4.11.1999 in the newspaper on 5.11.1999 increasing the age limit of Government candidates form 40 to 45 years for this year only. The Medical Education Division, the Ministry of Health and family Welfare, Government Bangladesh in its recent policy circulated by the Memo dated 3.2.1998 for Post Graduate Education of the BCS (Health) Cadres has also fixed the age limit up to 45 years. The other affiliated colleges including Non-Government excepting Dhaka Medical College issued notice inviting application for admission in the Post Graduate Course fixing the age limit for the Government candidate up to 45 years complying with the aforesaid Government policy. Dhaka Medical college, however, published notice dated 7.10.1999 inviting application for admission in various courses including M.S. Course Urology fixing 40 years limit for the Government candidate vide notification dated 28.9.1999 On publication of notification dated 5.11.1999 By Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University dated 5.11.1999 the petitioner in order to avail last change of obtaining degree of MS. (Urology) obtained the admission form on payment of requisite fees and submitted it after filing up with required documents on 14.11.1999 and was expecting issuance of admit card for appearing at the admission test on 21.11.1999. The petitioner without getting the admit card on 21.11.1999, the date of admission test made an enquiry at the office of Principal, Dhaka Medical College came to learn that Professor Dr. S. A. M. Golam Kibria, Head of the Department of Urology made an endorsement in the admission form "over age not eligible" and as such his form was not process for issuance of admit card. The petitioner was 42 years 4 months 25 days on 31.12.1999 and was quite eligible for admission according to the amended notification issued by the University and the Government policy mentioned above. But the petitioner herein illegally did not process his admission form with malafide intention although the opportunity of Post Graduate Course at 45 years was given by the University only for this year only. Respondent approached the petitioners praying for making an arrangement for his admission in to Post Graduate MS Course (Urology) as it was last chance for him but without any result. Respondent filed application on 29.11.1999 to the Vice-Chancellor of the University praying for making an arrangement for his admission into the M.S. Course (Urology) but with no result. Thereafter respondent was constrained to move High Court Division and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division upon hearing made the Rule absolute as aforesaid.

3. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioners, has strenuously argued that the respondent No. 1 not having appeared at the admission test and not being qualified in any written test for admission. The High Court Division wrong in directing the petitioner to be admitted at the Dhaka Medical College for MS Course (Urology) without any admission test inasmuch as the petitioner advertised the age limit for admission being 40 years and that having not been challenged at any point of time, the writ-petitioner being over aged could not be eligible to be issued with admit card as admittedly the respondent No. 1 was over aged.

4. The Medical Education Division, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of Bangladesh in its recently adopted policy circulated by the Memo dated 3.2.1998 for Post Graduate Education of the BCS (Health) Cadres fixed the age limit upto 45 years. Bangabandhu Sheilh Mujib Medical University issued a notification dated 28.9.1999 published in the newspaper dated 30.9.1999 inviting applications from the candidates including the candidates who were in Government Service for post graduate courses, inter alia, of M.S. Urology fixing the age limit at 40 years as on 31.12.1999 and subsequently issued amended notification dated 4.11.1999 in the newspaper published on 5.11.1999 increasing the age limit of the Government candidate form 40 to 45 years for the years 1999 to 2000.

<u>5. Meanwhile on 7.10.1999 Dhaka Medical College an affiliated college with Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujub Medical University published notice inviting application for admission in various courses including MS Urology fixing 40 years for the Government candidate following the notification of the University dated 28.9.1999 notifying that the date of admission test would be at 10.00 A.M. on 21.11.1999 and the admit card would be distributed on 17.11.1999 and 18.11.1999. Meanwhile the University published an amended notification on 4.11.1999 published in daily Janakantha on 5.11.1999 increasing the age limit of (Government candidate from the 40 to 45 years for the year 1999-2000 only After publication of the said notification the respondent No. 1 obtained the requisite form on 14.11.1999 and submitted on the same date with the hope that this was the last chance for him for appearing the test for availing the course. The petitioner not being supplied with the admit card, on the date of admission test made enquiry at the office of the Principal and the Department and learnt that petitioner No.2 did not process the application making an illegal endorsement "over age not eligible" in the admission from. Petitioners, the college authority in their affidavit-in —opposition have stated that they published notice dated 7.10.1999 on the basis of the notification dated 28.9.1999 published by the Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujib Medical University and admitted that the amended notice dated 4.11.1999 published by the University on 5.11.1999 escaped the notice of the college authority. It further appeared from the affidavit-in-opposition of the college authority that Dr. Syed Amjad Ali, a candidate for the Department of Pediatrics who are also over aged were given chance to appear at the admission test by issuing of admit cards. It is to the noted here that Dhaka medical College being an affiliated college like other medical colleges under Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujub medical University had been admitting the students to M.S. Course including Urology on the basis of the notification dated 28.9.1999 and 4.11.1999 are bound by those notifications so far the admission of the students pursuant to notice dated 7.10.1999 issued by Dhaka Medical College. In view of the amended notification which according to petitioners escaped their notice the respondent No. 1 was eligible to be issued with the admit card which the petitioner deliberately, discriminatorily and intentionally did not issue to the detriment of the respondent No. 1. Herein High Court Division as well found that the endorsement as to age limit being over age has been done without lawful authority and resorting to discrimination. In view of the above, for the fault of the petitioners, the respondent No. 1 should not suffer as he had only last chance to be admitted into M.S. Course (Urology) pursuant to the notification dated 4.11.1999 which was for one year only and accordingly allowing to pursuit him higher education in M.S. Course (Urology) on being admitted in the said Course even by increasing one seat if necessary by the authority as mentioned in the impugned order do not suffer from any illegality but the same is also warranted in the facts and circumstances of the case, in order to secure the ends of justice.</u>

6. The petitioner is accordingly dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 1789 of 2013
lawyer:
Mr. Md. Abdur Razzak Miah, Advocate, instructed by Mr. Zahirul Islam, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Petitioner. 
Mr. Munsur Habib, Advocate, instructed by Mr. Gias Uddin Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record ------- For Respondent Nos.1-23. 
For Respondent Nos.24-50:------- Not represented.
parties:
Md. Amir Hossain
Vs.
Baby Bewa And Others
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali, J:-This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgement and order dated 13.05.2012 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.542 of 2010 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts, relevant for disposal of the instant civil petition for leave to appeal, are that Abdul Jalil Baki respondent No.24 herein as plaintiff instituted Other Suit No.138 of 2008 in the Court of Joint District Judge, First Court, Bogra, for setting aside the preliminary decree dated 24.08.2006 and final decree dated 24.11.2007 passed in Partition Suit No. 2 of 2004. He stated, inter alia, that Mst. Rezia and Motiar Rahman defendant Nos.48 and 49 respectively mortgaged the suit property to Rupali Bank, and since they failed to repay the loan, Rupali Bank filed Artha Rin Case No.129 of 2000 and the suit was decreed and, thereafter, Money Execution Case No.233 of 2007 was filed and in that execution case the property was auction sold and the plaintiff purchased 1.27 acres of land out of 1.53 acres of Plot No.28 and got possession of the case land through Court. The further case of the plaintiff is that Amir Hossain defendant No. 1 by manufacturing some false papers claimed that he purchased land of Plot No.28 from Azizur Rahman (defendant No. 47) his predecessor and, thereafter, claiming as a co-sharer he filed Partition Suit No.2 of 2004, and by showing false service got an ex parte decree on 24.8.2006 and on the basis of such false decree obtained final decree on 28.10.2007. When the defendant went to take possession, the plaintiff learnt about the partition decree and then filed the instant suit.

3. The petitioner herein as defendant contested the suit by filing written statement and denied the claim of the plaintiff. He contended, inter alia, that the suit property belonged to Mrs. Hameda Mohammad Ali, wife of late Mohammad Ali, Ex-Prime Minister of Pakistan and after her death her son Hatem Ali Chowdhury got the property through a family arrangement and sold the same to the petitioner. The petitioner after purchasing the suit property took possession of the land through Court and established a Madrasha, which is known as Abdul Jabbar Madrasha with a Hostel built therein for the students lie also planted 250 saplings. When the petitioner learnt about the Partition Suit No.55 of 2000 in respect of the suit property, he got himself added as a defendant and filed written statement. Thereafter, the plaintiff did not proceed with the suit and the same was dismissed for default. Then the petitioner fi led Partition Suit No.2 of 2004 to demarcate his purchased land, but as the defendant did not contest the suit, the said suit was decreed ex parte and the final decree was passed on 28.11.2007. He filed Partition Execution Case No.6 of 2008 and by an order of the Court dated 30.08.2008 an Advocate Commissioner was appointed. When they went to the suit land the plaintiff did not allow them to enter into the land, so the Advocate Commissioner with the help of police gave possession of the suit land to the petitioner. Thereafter, the petitioner and Abdul Jalil Baki in order to resolve the dispute about their interest in the suit land filed a compromise petition. The Joint District Judge allowed the compromise petition and the suit was disposed of as per terms of the solenama.

4. The petitioner claimed that opposite party Nos. 1-23 in the civil revision before the High Court Division (respondent Nos. 1-23 herein) were defendant Nos. 23-45 in the said suit, but did not contest the suit nor filed any written statement. The compromise petition between the petitioner and opposite party No.24 Abdul Jalil Baki related to Plot No.28, which comprised 1.53 acres of land and the petitioner claimed 78 decimals out of it and the respondents claimed rest of the land in Plot No.28. He stated that respondent Nos.1-23 had no interest in that plot. They have not been affected by the compromise and, if they are aggrieved, they could file a partition suit to state their claim, if' there is any, in the suit land.

5. Respondent Nos.1-23 by filing counter affidavit before the High Court Division stated that the compromise petition filed by Mohammad Amir Hussain, the petitioner with Md. Abdul Jalil Baki, opposite party No. 24 in the civil revision, (respondent No. 24 herein) was illegal and could not be entertained. The joint District Judge, Court, Bogra committed an error of law in accepting the compromise petition overlooking the nature of the suit and declaring the final decree dated 24.08.2006 in Partition Suit No.02 of 2004, which was collusive, null and void and not acted upon and, therefore, confers no title and interest upon the suit land and prayed for setting aside the said decree dated 24.08.2006 passed in Partition Suit No.02 of 2004.

6. Respondent Nos. 1-23 (defendant Nos.23-45 of the Partition Suit No.02 of 2004), claimed that they did not receive any notice of the Partition Suit No.02 of 2004, in the Court of Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Bogra and the decree was obtained by the plaintiff by practicing fraud upon the Court, and as such, Other Suit No.138 of 2008 is required to be proceeded up to its finality to look into the matter whether the ex-parte decree passed in Partition Suit No.02 of 2004 was correct. They claimed to have right, title, interest and possession in the suit land and they are seriously prejudiced by the ex-parte decree passed on 24.08.2006 and had they been aware of the filing of Partition Suit No.02 of 2004 they would have contested the suit claiming their saham. They further claimed that the judgement dated 20.01.2010 passed in Other Class Appeal No. 147 of 2009 allowing the appeal was correct in setting aside the order dated 24.05.2009 in Other Class Suit No. 138 of 2008, however, the appellate Court in Other Class Appeal No. 147 of 2009 failed to notice the nature of the suit and the prayer of Other Class Suit No. 138 of 2008, wherein the Court decreed the suit in terms of the final decree dated 24.08.2006 in Partition Suit No. 02 of 2004, which was illegal, collusive and null and void and bore no right, title and interest for Abdul Jalil Baki in schedule Nos. 1 and 2 of the plaint. After hearing the parties and considering the evidence and materials on record, the Joint District Judge, First Court, Bogra, allowed the compromise petition and the suit was thus disposed of as per terms of the solenama by the judgement and decree dated 24.05.2009.

7. Being aggrieved, the defendant Nos.1- 23 preferred Title Appeal No.147 of 2009 before the District Judge, Bogra and the same was heard by the Additional District Judge, Bogra, who by his judgement and decree dated 20.01.2010 allowed the appeal. Then the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No.542 of 2010 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing the parties was discharged. Hence, the plaintiff is now before us having filed the civil petition for leave to appeal.

8. Mr. Md. Abdur Rezzaque Miah, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that the High Court Division did not apply its mind in evaluating the facts and materials on record since there is proof available in the record of the case that the defendants of Other Class Suit No. 138 of 2008 received notice of the suit in time, but they did not contest and claim their saham in the suit land. He also submitted that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 138 of 2008 has been validly executed by the petitioner and respondent No. 24 to settle the dispute in respect of land of plot no. 28 where present respondent Nos. 1 to 23 had no interest and the Joint District Judge, First Court, Bogra, rightly determined the suit based on the solenama and declaring the terms of the solenama as part of the decree and hence, the impugned judgement is liable to be set aside. He further submitted that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that admittedly defendant Nos. 48 and 49 of the original suit mortgaged the suit property with Rupali Bank and when they failed to repay the loan, the bank filed Artha Rin Case No. 129 of 2000 and the suit was decreed. Thereafter, the bank filed Money Execution Case No. 233 of 2007 and in due course the property was sold in auction and respondent No. 24 purchased 75 decimals of land of plot No. 28 and got possession thereof through Court, it has been clearly described in the solenama, and hence, the High Court Division erred in discharging the Rule on the ground that 23 co-sharers of the property were left out of the solenama.

9. Mr. Munsur Habib, learned Advocate appearing for respondent Nos.1-23 made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division.

<u>10. We find from the judgement of the appellate Court, being the last court of fact that out of the 7.24 acres of land detailed in the schedule, there was no apportionment of the property in respect of 51 defendants and that the plaint and written statement did not resolve the controversy between the parties entirely the solenama was signed by the plaintiff Md. Abdul Wit Baki and Md. Amir 1-lossain on behalf of the defendants. These two persons are not the sole owners of the property in the jote. It was observed by the appellate Court that the 23 appellants, who are defendants in the suit, were not party to the solenama.</u>

11. The High Court Division observed that the petitioner and opposite party No. 24 (Md. Abdul Jalil Baki) through entering solenama divided some portion of the suit land amongst themselves in an ex parte decree wherein 23 other co-sharers of the property were left out. The High Court Division observed that the appellate Court rightly pointed out that the 23 appellants had been deprived of their legal right to get the property partitioned in accordance with law.

<u>12. When any number of parties to a suit reach a compromise in the absence of other parties, clearly those, who are excluded from the compromise, are deprived of their opportunity to put forward any claim that they may have in the suit land.</u>

13. In the facts and circumstances discussed above, we are of the view that the impugned judgement does not suffer from any illegality or impropriety and does not call for any interference by this Division.

14. Accordingly, the civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali with Ms. Nasima K. Hakim and Mr. M. Ashraful Islam, Advocates ------ For the petitioners. 
Mr. Tanjibul Alam with Mr. Kazi Ershadul Alam, Advocates ------ For the respondent’s No. 9. 
Mr. Md. Motaher Hossain Sazu, DAG with Ms. Purabi Rani Sharma, AAG ------ For the respondent No. 1.
parties:
Fahmida Akter Jusi and Others
Vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Represented By the Secretary, Ministry of Education and Others
full_judgment:
J.B. M. Hassan, J: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned decision dated 14.11.2016 taken by the Bangladesh Medical & Dental Council under the joint signatures of its Chairman and the Registrar (Annexure-K) refusing to grant registration of the petitioners in the Bangladesh Medical & Dental Council for the MBBS Course in the Academic Year 2012-2013 as students of the Northern (Pvt.) Medical College, Rangpur under the University of Rajshahi and also recommending to file case against the petitioners and prohibiting them from attending and continuing the classes and to sit for the examinations should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondents No. 7-9 and 11 should not be directed to allow the petitioners in the final year MBBS course for the academic course 2012-2013 and to appear in the MBBS course examinations and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 2. Pertinent facts leading to issuance of the Rule Nisi, inter alia, are that the petitioners having their Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) appeared in the admission test for the Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) course conducted by the University of Rajshahi for both the Government and Private Medical Colleges for the academic year 2012-2013. The petitioner No.1, Fahmida Akter Jusi obtained merit score 95.15; petitioner No.2, Md. Alamgir Kabir obtained merit score 106.24; petitioner No.3, Jannatun Noor Sworna obtained merit score 92.12; petitioner No. 4, Md. Amirul Islam obtained merit score 79.84 and petitioner No. 5, Md. Rubel Islam obtained merit score 108.49. Due to their such merit scores the petitioners could not get admission in the Government medical colleges. The Northern (Pvt) Medical College, Rangpur (the College) offered the petitioners for admission in the vacant seats of the course 2012-2013 and the College authority also intimated that they have special permission from the concerned authority to admit a few students relaxing the test score requirement in accordance with the Nitimala, 2011. The College authority also informed that to get the opportunity the aspirant candidate has to pay extra money along with the normal admission fees. 3. Accordingly, the petitioners having their aim to become doctors paid Tk. 16,42,000/- each instead of regular admission fee of Tk. 13,41,000/-. After getting admission the petitioners have been pursuing their studies on payment of other charges and monthly tuition fees and in course of their academic sessions they successfully passed 1st professional examination on completion of two years and after completing four years the petitioners also appeared in the written examination of the 2nd professional examination. But at the end of written examination the Registrar of the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (the BMDC) issued a letter bearing memo no. বিএমডিসি/১০-এফ-২০১৬/৪৭৫ dated 28.09.2016 addressing the Principal of the College informing that the submitted test score and merit position of certain students (the petitioners) were found inconsistent with the records lying with the Health Directorate and that by the said memo, the Principal of the College was asked to explain in this regard failing which registration would not be provided to those students. But the College instead of reply to the said letter restrained the students from appearing in the viva-voce examination of the 2nd professional examination. Although from 12.11.2016 the 5th year class (final year) had already been started, yet the petitioners were not allowed to attend the classes. 4. In the circumstances, the petitioners through their learned Advocate served a notice demanding justice on 14.11.2016 requesting the respondents to allow them to continue their respective courses. The respondents did not respond to the said notice and on the other hand the petitioners came to know from online newspaper on 25.11.2016 that the BMDC would not provide registration to the petitioners. In this regard no copy of the said decision having been provided by the BMDC, the petitioners through Information Commission obtained a decision from the BMDC on 14.11.2016 whereby they had decided not to provide registration to the petitioners for the session 2012-2013 bringing allegations of forgery. In this backdrop, the petitioners filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule Nisi. 5. The Registrar, Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (the BMDC) as the respondent No.9 appearing in the Rule has filed an affidavit in opposition controverting the statements of the writ petition. Contentions of this respondent, in brief, are that section 5 of “বাংলাদেশ মেডিকেল ও ডেন্টাল কাউন্সিল আইন, ২০১০” (shortly, the BMDC Act, 2010) authorizes the BMDC to register students of the medical courses, to identify any fraudulent representation and to take step for punishment in this regard. The Principal of the Northern (Pvt.) Medical College by his forwarding dated 22.09.2016 sent 68 registration Forms filled up by the respective students for registration in the session 2012-2013 along with applicable fees. From the aforesaid registration Forms the BMDC detected anomaly relating to five Forms of the petitioners. Thereafter, this respondent obtained the actual roll numbers of those students from the records maintained by the Director General of the Health Service and found the following inconsistencies:

6. After detecting aforementioned inconsistencies, the BMDC issued a letter on 28.09.2016 to the Principal of the College specifying discrepancies in respect of roll number, test score and merit position of the petitioners and accordingly requested the Principal to explain about the discrepancy. Thereafter, the Principal by his letter dated 13.10.2016 intimated that the petitioners committed fraud in submitting information and thus, have dishonestly admitted themselves into the College and that due to failure of the concerned persons the untrue statements provided by the students at the time of admission could not be detected. Although the students and their parents were notified to provide their respective papers but they did not respond. Subsequently, the BMDC issued another letter on 17.10.2016 requiring the Principal of the College to inform the BMDC as to whether they took any action against those students. In reply to the said letter, the College supplied a resolution of its academic council taken on 23.10.2016 to the effect that due to submission of wrong information the College cancelled their admission and suspended their academic curriculum. On receipt of the letter dated 24.10.2016 along with the decision of the College, the BMDC by its 192 meeting of the Executive Committee took decision not to provide any registration to those five students (the petitioners) for resorting to fraud by submitting false information at the time of admission as well as in submitting the registration Forms to the BMDC. The BMDC also requested the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on 21.12.2016 to take appropriate legal action against the petitioners and the College Authority including cancellation of the registration of the College. 7. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate with Ms. Nasima K Hakim and Mr. M. Ashraful Islam, the learned Advocates appear for the petitioners. After placing the writ petition and other materials on record, the learned Advocate submits that by the impugned decision the petitioners were debarred from pursuing their academic career. But in taking such drastic decision they have not been given any opportunity of being heard about the allegations of fraud. He further submits that fraud, if any, was committed by the College authority who admitted the petitioners taking excess amount with the regular fees for admission and so the College is liable instead of the bonafide petitioners. He also submits that on furnishing the academic certificates and information the petitioners .got admission in the College and were pursuing their studies and that the registration Forms submitted to the BMDC were prepared and submitted by the College authority having no control over the same by the petitioners and as such for any untrue information provided in the said Forms, the petitioners can riot be liable. He again submits that as per the Nitimala the College have 5% quota to provide admission relaxing the required merit score and the petitioners being covered by the said quota, question of fraud as to their merit position and score does not arise. 8. Mr. Ali further submits that in the meantime the petitioners have completed four years of their academic courses and that at the far end of their course the impugned action shall harshly affect the rest life of the petitioners and therefore, on humanitarian ground the petitioners may be allowed to continue their remaining part of the academic course. He lastly submits that the circular for admission was published on 16.09.2012 and the test examination was held on 23.11.2012 and therefore, the subsequent circular dated 04.12.2012, requiring cut off mark-110 for admission, cannot be applicable in respect of the petitioners' admission criteria. In view of the facts, all the petitioners inspite of having below the cut off mark-110, were being eligible for admission, the alleged forgery did not benefit them and as such they cannot be liable for the alleged forgery. In support of his submissions, the learned Advocate refers to an unreported decision in Civil Appeal No. 147 of 2015 with Civil Petition For Leave to Appeals No. 1110 and 1111 of 2015. 9. Mr. Tanjibul Alam, the learned Advocate with Mr. Kazi Ershadul Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the Registrar of the BMDC (respondent No.9) at the very outset has drawn our attention to the Annexure-8 series to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition affirmed on 07.05.2017. He contends that apparently the mentioned registration Forms (Annexure-8 series) show that those were filled up by the petitioners themselves by putting their respective signatures on the upper part and that the lower part of the said Forms were filled up by the Principal of the College satisfying the statements made by the petitioners as to correctness thereof. Therefore, the petitioners cannot avoid their responsibility in respect of contents of the said Forms. He further contends that the BMDC on examination of the records lying with the office of the Health Directorate, found inconsistencies regarding registration number and merit position mentioned in the aforesaid registration Forms (Annexure-8 series) and thereby forgery and fraud having been detected, the BMDC took the action in accordance with law. He also contends that the Admission Guideline, 2011 incorporates 5% quota for the Governing Body of the College in order to admit maximum 5(five) students relaxing the merit position subject to having minimum merit score, at least 110 i.e the cut off mark and that the petitioners having not the minimum required score, inserted false merit score as well as merit position resorting to forgery in order to overcome the requirement of cut off mark. He again contends that since the petitioners are the beneficiaries of the aforesaid forgery committed in the registration Forms, they cannot eschew the liability of the said forgery. 10. Mr. Alain also contends that the forgery detected on the registration Forms (Annexure-8 series) have been admitted by both the students and the College but both of them tried to skirt round the liability of the same and that since the forgery is apparent from the admitted facts in the registration Forms submitted by the petitioners under their signatures, service of show cause notice upon them is not required as fraud vitiates everything. He further contends that the cited case as referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioners is not applicable in this particular case in view of its distinguishable facts. Referring to an unreported judgment passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3372 of 2016, Mr. Alain contends that earlier the College, namely, the Northern (Pvt.) Medical College, Rangpur also committed similar fraud because of which the Appellate Division imposed a penalty of Tk. I (one) crore upon them and in the instant case also it has committed fraud in connivance with the petitioners in admitting them in the MB13S course inspite of having no requisite qualifications. He lastly submits that the petitioners were supposed to submit the registration Forms immediately after their admission but they sent those registration Forms before the BMDC through the College on 22.09.2016. After submitting those Forms, within the short span of time the fraud having been detected the action was taken but in the mean time they completed four years without submitting the registration Forms before the BMDC and thereby this wrong having been committed by the petitioners themselves, they cannot be allowed to take advantage thereof. In support of his submission, Mr. Alain refers to a case of the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, Secretariat Building, Dhaka Vs. Mrs. Momtaz Begum and another reported in 10 MLR (AD) 23. 11. We have gone through the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No.9 and the supplementary affidavits thereto filed subsequently by both the petitioners and the respondent No.9. 12. It appears that the petitioners got admission in the MBBS course for the session 2012-2013 in the Northern (Pvt.) Medical College, Rangpur (the College). Admittedly, in the admission test the petitioners could not obtain the requisite score for admission either in the government medical college or in the private medical college. It is the petitioners' assertion that the College authority offered them to get admission stating that they have a special permission to admit the students in some vacant seats relaxing the requisite score for admission and that indisputably the petitioners got admission in the College on payment of extra amount of Tk. 3 (three) lac in addition to the regular admission fees of Tk. 13 lac 41 thousand. 13. In this regard Mr. A. J. Mohammed All submits that pursuant to Admission Nitimala, 2011 the Governing Body of the College has got 5% quota (maximum 5 students) to admit students beyond the merit position. But by the circular dated 04.12.2012 (Annexure-D) it was provided that to fill up the 5% quota, a student has to score minimum mark (cut off mark)-110. Admittedly, the petitioners did not have minimum score-110. Learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that requirement of minimum score- 110 is not applicable to the petitioners' case as this requirement was introduced on 04.12.2012, after the admission circular and admission test held on 16.09.2012 and 23.11.2012 respectively. But this submission does not hold good inasmuch as the requirement was imposed upon the Governing Body of the medical colleges in the enjoyment of their privilege, 5% admission quota and it was introduced long before the petitioners' admission. Although, the score mark has to be obtained by the students and thereby they are related to it, but it does not impact upon the examination of the students. Realizing this aspect, the petitioners and the College authority altered the score mark above 110 in the registration Forms (Annexure-8 series) resorting to forgery although none of the petitioners, scored-110 mark and that in order to show the score-110, they had to change their roll numbers and merit positions as those were taken from other candidates. 14. From the Annexure-8 series to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it appears that the roll number, test score, merit score and merit position of the respective petitioners are different from that of the actual position. The petitioners do not deny that the information of the said Forms are untrue and those were taken from other students. Their only contention is that those were not filled up by the respective petitioners; rather those were prepared by the College authority. On the other hand, the letter dated 13.10.2016 (Annexure-2) written by the College authority addressing the BMDC reflects that the petitioners made the aforementioned untrue statements in their respective Forms. 15. We are not here to enter into such dispute as to who filled up those Forms putting the forged and untrue information. But the facts remain that on examination of the aforesaid Forms, we find that the petitioners put the signatures below the contents of the Forms and therefore, admitting those signatures, they cannot avoid the responsibility for the contents of those Forms. Moreover, these petitioners are the beneficiaries by making such untrue information inasmuch as from these Forms it appears that the merit scores are all above 110, while admittedly all the petitioners got the merit score below 110 and in view of the facts it is apparent that in order to overcome the required cut off mark 110, the petitioners inserted the aforesaid untrue information by committing forgery taking from other candidates. 16. The BMDC under the Act, 2010 is authorized to register the students of the medical courses and having found the untrue statements resorting to forgery, the BMDC refused to register the petitioners and as such we do not find any impropriety in the action of the BMDC in not registering these students when it is the admitted fact that the registration Forms submitted by those students contained the forged statements regarding their merit position and merit score. 17. Moreover, admittedly the petitioners' score marks are below 110 and so, they cannot be admitted in exercise of 5% quota given to the Governing Body. Further, Annexure-2 to the supplementary affidavit shows that the College authority does not claim that the petitioners were admitted under the said 5% quota. Rather the College authority admits that forgery was committed in filling up the registration Forms submitted to the BMDC. 18. As to the submission of Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali that at the far end of their academic career the BMDC took drastic decision in not registering the petitioners while it ought to have been done at the earliest opportunity i.e immediately after the admission of the petitioners, it is on record that they got admission in the College in the year 2012 and that the College authority for the time sent the registration Forms of the petitioners to the BMDC on 22.09.2016 (Annexure-9 to supplementary affidavit in opposition). On receipt of the same, the BMDC proceeded and finally took the decision on 13.11.2016 (minutes signed on 14.11.2016). Therefore, it is not true that the BMDC took action at a belated stage allowing the petitioners to continue their course for the last 4 (four) years and that it is apparent that the BMDC had no laches in taking the impugned decision. Rather it is the petitioners and their College who sent the registration Forms at a belated stage and in view of their own wrong they cannot take the advantage of the same. This view of ours finds support from the case of the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Secretariat Building, Dhaka Vs. Mrs. Momtaz Begum and another reported in 10 MLR (AD) 23. 19. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali vehemently submits that the impugned decision curtailing the petitioners' right to study was taken without issuing any show cause notice. In this regard, we find that the BMDC by their letter dated 28.09.2016 asked the College to explain regarding the allegation. In reply to said letter, the College authority wrote the letter on 13.10.2016 (Annexure-2) stating that they asked the petitioners and their parents to explain regarding the allegations but they did not respond. Rather, by the said letter the College authority asserted that the petitioners committed fraud by way of furnishing their academic information. Thus, it is apparent that through the college the petitioners got an opportunity to explain about the allegation of forgery brought against them. 20. Over and above, from the records and the admitted facts, it appears that the registration Forms submitted by the petitioners with their signatures, were filled up resorting to forgery and taking benefit of said forgery the petitioners tried to continue their academic career inspite of having no requisite qualifications for getting admission in the medical college. Thus, this fraud having been detected, we do not find any substance in the submissions of Mr. Ali. In this context we find the case of Principal, Fulbaria College, Mymensingh Vs. Md. Helaluddin and others reported in 32 BLD (AD) 11 apposite wherein their Lordships held that fraud being detected the principles of natural justice would not be applied in taking action without show cause notice. Relevant portions of their Lordships observations are as follows: "The authority has the right to rectify the illegality without affording the writ petitioner an opportunity to explain his position against the proposed action since lie collusively procured the recommendation. Since the writ petition has acquired no right whatsoever to draw higher scale or post, he is not entitled to a hearing and thus the authority has not violated the principles of natural justice by reason of reduction of his pay scale and post." 21. Regard being had to the above, we are of the view that in such situation it would not be unjustified if the petitioners are refused to get registration with the BMDC without issuing any show cause notice. 22. Now the next question arises as to whether on the facts and in the circumstances, the petitioners would be allowed to continue their academic courses. In this regard, the learned Advocate for the petitioners refers to the decision in an unreported case of the Vice Chancellor, University of Rajshahi, Rajshahi and others Vs. S. M. Ariful Haque and others in Civil Petition For Leave to Appeal No. 3372 of 2016 wherein by judgment dated 15.12.2016 their Lordships allowed the respective petitioners to continue their academic courses subject to payment of a fine of Tk. 1(one) Crore to be paid from the account of the College only. In this particular case, the petitioners who obtained below the required minimum numbers in the admission examination were refused to get the registration card from the University. The College Authority admitted those students in violation of law and eventually by the interim order this Court allowed them to continue their courses. Although the apex Court found that the College authority in violation of rules admitted the students but considering the doctrine of necessity allowed those students to continue their courses. But here in this case, it is apparent that resorting to forgery the petitioners themselves submitted their registration Forms and that both the College authority as well as the petitioners themselves admitted this fact of forgery. In such circumstances, the cited case is not applicable in this particular case and as such, we are unable to accept the submission of Mr. A J Mohammad Ali to allow the petitioners to continue their courses. 23. Another aspect as we find here is that earlier the Appellate Division by judgment dated 15.12.2016 passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 3372 of 2016 imposed a fine of Tk. 01(one) Crore upon the College, namely, Northern (Pvt.) Medical College, Rangpur in respect of same misdeeds admitting some students in violation of the rules and that in the said judgment the apex Court cautioned them not to commit so in future. The same wrong has again been detected in the same college admitting the present petitioners despite having their no requisite score in the admission test. Further, it appears that inspite of being a respondent the College has not appeared in the Rule Nisi to explain their position. Although it appears that the academic council of the College by making resolution is trying to shift the burden of such misdeeds upon the students but they cannot avoid their responsibility to admit those students on acceptance of their academic papers and test score below the cut off mark. In particular, when it is apparent that taking extra money from the students (petitioners) the College authority for their personal gains have gambled with the petitioners. In view of such consistent misdeeds of the College authority, we consider that they should be dealt with severely otherwise they would repeat similar violation in future. At the same time the respondents No. 1-10 shall take proper action against the College authority including its Principal. 24. Having regard to the above, we are of the view that the College authority should be ordered to pay an exemplary fine in favour of any cancer hospital within a given time frame. 25. In view of the above discussions, we do not find any merit in this Rule Nisi. 26. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The Governing Body and the Principal of the Northern (Pvt.) Medical College, Rangpur are directed to pay a fine of Tk. 2,00,00,000.00 (Two Crore only) in favour of Ahsania Mission Cancer & General Hospital, Dhaka Ahsania Mission of House #19, Road # 12 (New), Dhanmondi R/A, Dhaka-1209 within 02 (two) months from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment. 27. Communicate a copy of the judgment and order to the respondents at once. End.

caseno: Appeal from original Decree No. 73 of 1967.
lawyer:
Abdus Salam Khan, Advocate ------  For the Appellant. 	
Fazlul Karim, Advocate ------ For the Respondent
parties:
Lal Banoo and ors  ------  Appellants.  
Vs. 
Md. Yasin Abdul Aziz and ors  ------  Respondents.
full_judgment:
Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman, J.: This appeal at the instance of defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo (wife of defendant No. 10 Amjad Ali) is directed against the judgment and decree passed by Mr. Nasiruddin Humayun Chowdhury. Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka on 16.5.67 in Title Suit No. 153 of 1964.

2. In this suit plaintiffs 1-30 as heirs of original owner Faloo's two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi claimed l/3rd share in the suit property. According to the plaintiffs C.S. plot No. 545 measuring .63 acre, C.S. plot No. 232 measuring .38 acre, C.S. plot No. 676 measuring .22 acre C.S. plot No. 953 measuring .15 acre, and C.S. plot No. 640 measuring .34 acre (total area = 1.72 acre) of C.S. Khatian No. 48, Touzi No. 192 of mouza Jatrabari, P.S. Kseraniganj, District Dhaka originally belonged to Faloo (see Ext.1). Similarly C.S. plot No. 533 measuring .34 acre. C.S. plot No. 678 measuring .21 acre., C.S. plot No. 667 measuring .15 acre; C.S. plot No. 630 measuring .47 acre, C.S. plot No. 954 measuring .16 acre, C.S. plot No. 973 measuring .30 acre and C.S. plot No. 989 measuring .17 (total area = 1.80) of Khatian No. 53, Touzi No. 112 of Mouza Jatrabari, P.S. Keraniganj, District Dhaka belonged to Faloo alias Sk. Faloo as Jote Faloo (রায়তিস্বত্বে স্থিতিবান)= occupancy raiyat. Fa- 100 had 16 annas raiyaty right in the aforessid plots of the said two Khatians, While he was owning and possessing the aforesaid lands in assertion of his right and title, he died before the last settlement operation leaving behind his two sons, namely Khadem and Chamoo and his two daughters namely, Joy tonnessa and Anwara Bibi as heirs to his aforessid jote. Each of his sons (Khadem and Chamoo) got 1/3rd share and each of his two daughter (Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi) 1/6th share in the said properties (described in the schedule of the plaint including amendment made in the plaint) left by Faloo. The aforesaid two sons and two daughters of Faloo had been in joint ownership and possession of the properties in their respective snare. Khadem, as the eldest son of Faloo, taking advantage of the confidence of his two sisters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi got his name surreptitiously recorded in the last settlement record as 16 annas owner of the aforesaid C.S. Khatian No. 48 containing C.S. plot Nos. 545, 632, 679,953 and 740. Similarly Sk. Chamoo, the second son of late Faloo, got his own name recorded as 16 ann as owner' of C.S. Khatian No. 53 containing the aforesaid C.S. plot Nos. 533, 678, 667, 630, 954, 973 and 989 in the last settlement record. It is apparent that the last settlement records showing Khadem as exclusive owner in possession of the aforesaid plots of Khatian No. 48 and showing Chamoo as exclusive owner in possession of the aforesaid plots of Khatian No. 53 is wrong. While Khadem, Chamoo, Joytonnessa and Anwara were in joint possession and ownership of the suit properties in their respective shares, Chamoo died leaving three sons, namely, late Magon, Danajuddin (defendant No. 3) and Moghal Mia (defendant No. 2) and two daughters, namely Safura Bibi (defendant No. 8) and Late Hazera Bibi. Thus the entire share of Chamoo devolved upon his aforesaid sons and daughters. Thereafter Hazera Bibi died leaving her sole heir Azimuddin (defendant No. 9). Thereafter Magon died leaving one son, namely, Shahabuddin (defendant No. 4), two daughters, namely Latifan and Ashrafan (defendant Nos. 5 and 6 respectively) and window Ayesha Khatun (defendant No. 7). After the death of Chamoo, his sister Joytonnessa died leaving one son Korban, three daughters, namely Akmolnessa, Orfan and Sayera Khatun. One sixth (1/6th) share of Joytunnessa thus devolved upon her said son Korban and the said three daughters-Akmolnessa, Orfannessa and Sayera. Thereafter Akmolnessa died leaving her son Afajuddin (defendant No.8) as her only heir to her estate. Thereafter Orfannessa alias Orfa died leaving two sons, namely Serajuddin (plaintiff No. 97 and Jahed Ali and one daughter Seha Bibi (plaintiff No. 11) as her heirs in the suit properties. Then Jahed Ali, son of late Orfannessa, died leaving his son Tahed Ali (plaintiff No. 10) as his sole heir to his estate. Late Joytonnessa's daughter Sayera Khatun thereafter died leaving her two sons, Safajuddin (plaintiff No. 12) and Osimuddin (plaintiff No. 13) and one daughter Asadan Bibi (plaintiff No. 14) as heirs to her estate. Late Joytonnessa's son Korban Ali died leaving behind six sons, namely Abdul Aziz, Aminuddin, Amiruddin, Abdul Hye, Wajuddin and Hafizuddin (plaintiffs 1-6 respectively) and a widow Aimon Nessa (plaintiff No. 7) as his heirs.

3. The further case of the plaintiff is that late Faloo's son Khadem died leaving a daughter Lal Banoo (defendant No. 1) and a widow Korfunnessa as his heirs to his estate and thereafter late Khadem's widow Korfunnessa died leaving her daughter (defendant No. 1) Lal Banoo as her only heir.

4. Further case for the plaintiff is that after the death of Khadem, late Faloo's daughter Anwara Bibi died leaving one son, namely Kabir Khan and two daughters, namely Khatoon and Nazimoon. Thereafter Kabir Khan died leaving behind his three sons Bahadur Khan (plaintiff No. 15), Fatik Khan (plaintiff No. 16) and Shahad Khan. Shahad Khan thereafter died leaving one son plaintiff No. 17, Wahid Khan and his (Shahad's) widow, plaintiff No. 26 Rahatan. Thereafter, Faloo's daughter late Anwar's daughter Khatoon died leaving one son Akub Ali and four daughters, namely Mozahar Bibi, Monohar Bibi (plaintiff No. 19), Rafatun Bibi (plaintiff No. 20) and Seraton (plaintiff No. 21). Thereafter, said Mazahar Bibi died leaving two sons Ebadat Khan and Nannu Khan and two daughters, namely Bahani Bibi (plaintiff No. 28) and plaintiff No. 29 Bibi Ayesha. Thereafter, Ebadat died leaving one minor daughter, namely, Jahanara (plaintiff No. 25 represented by her guardian cousin plaintiff No.18 Nadu Khan, son of late Nannu Khan) and two sisters, namely defendant No. 25 Jahanara and defendant No. 27 Falani. Nannu Khan (son of late Muzahar Bibi) died before Ebadat Khan leaving his sole heir (son) Nadu Khan (plaintiff No.18.). Late Anwara's daughter's son Akub Ali thereafter died leaving three sons namely plaintiff No. 22 Mohar Ali, plaintiff No. 23 Jaman and plaintiff No. 24, Litkoo and a widow plaintiff No. 27 Falani. Thereafter, late Anwara's another daughter Najimon died leaving her only son plaintiff No. 30 Ful Chan as her only heir.

5. Thus according to the plaintiffs 1-30, they are joint owners of 1/3rd of the total share in the suit properties and they are in constructive possession thereof without any partition by metes and bounds of their respective shares.

6. The further case for the plaintiff is that while the plaintiffs were in joint ownership and possession of the suit properties aforesaid C.S. plots No. 545, 632 and 679 of Khatian No. 48 and C.S Nos. 533, 678, 630 and 989 of Khatian No. 53 were acquired by the Collector of Dhaka in L.A. Case No. 92 of 1963-64 for WAPDA Project. The plaintiffs learnt on 27.11.64 that the defendants have surreptitiously got the award prepared in their names and arc trying to get all the compensation money for the acquired plots of land fraudulently suppressing the fact that the plaintiffs are also co-sharers to the extent of 1/3rd share of the compensation money.

7. As the defendants did not pay any heed to the request of the plaintiffs to effect partition of the ejmali properties amicably by metes and bounds and allow them to have 1/3rd share of the compensation money, the plaintiffs were compelled to institute the present suit on 10.12.64.

8. Defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo (daughter of late Khadem) and defendant No.10 Khoaj Bibi, another daughter of late Khadem, contested the suit by filing two separate written statements. Defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo contended that she is the daughter of Khadem through Khadem's second wife Korfulnessa and that defendant No.10 Khoaj Bibi alias Makhari is the daughter of Khadem through Khadem's 1st wife Soal Bibi. During the life time of Khadcm he, on 28.2.1917 corresponding to 16th Falgoon, 1322 B.S., gifted by heba-bil-ewaj to Korfulnessa dag No. 953 (homestead with hut), dag No.545 and dag No. 632 of khatian No. 48 of Mouza Jatrabari. Korfulnessa in her turn made a gift on 7.6.1939 A.D. corresponding to 24th Jaistra1346 B.S. of plot No. 953 (having tin hut), plot No. 545 and plot No. 632 of Mouza Jatrabari (Khatian No. 48) to her daughter defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo and her son-in-law and Lal Banoo's husband, added defendant No. 20, Amjad Ali by registered deed of gift. Defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo and her husband defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali are in exclusive possession in the said three plots by virtue of gift and by adverse possession and the plaintiffs have no subsisting shares or interest in the said three plots. Though defendant No. 1 claimed to have paid rent in her name and in her husband's name but no rent receipt could be produced by defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 20 at the time of trial.

9. Defendant No. 10 Khoaj Bibi alias Mukhari contested the suit by filing a written statement to the effect that late Khadem's first wife Soal Bibi died leaving her daughter defendant No. 10 Khoaj Bibi alias Mukhari as her heir. Khadem transferred during his life time C.S. plot No. 740 of Khatian No. 48 to Kazimuddin on 9.12.18 and also gave C.S. plot No. 679 of Khatian No.48 to his daughter Soal Bibi after whose death her daughter Khoaj Bibi alias Mukhari possessed plot No. 679 exclusively for more than 30 years adversely by paying rent. Transferee Kazimuddin died leaving behind his son defendant No. 21 Mullak Chand as his sole heir. During the pendency of the suit defendant No. 21 Mullak Chand died leaving behind his heir defendant No. 21(a) Pari Banoo, wife of Bojumkar Ali.

10. The plaintiffs and defendants 2-9 who are the heirs and successors of late Faloo's son late Chamoo filed a petition of compromise on 26.1.65 agreeing to the genealogy as given by the plaintiffs and also admitting the entitlement of 1/3rd share of the plaintiffs in both the suit Khatian Nos. 48 and 53 as heirs successors of late Faloo's two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi.

11. To meet the objection as to the defect of parties and non-inclusion of certain properties in the hatchpotch the plaintiff filed petition to meet the objection which were allowed. Thus, undisputedly there remains no defect of parties and no properties of the plaintiffs and defendants have been left out.

12. Plaintiffs examined two witnesses P.W. 1 Abdul Aziz (plaintiff No. 1) and P.W. 2 Dadan Miah. On behalf of the contesting defendants six witnesses were examined, namely, D.W. 1 Lal Banoo (defendant No. 1), D.W. 2 Mohabbat Ali Sarder, D.W. 3 Amjad Ali (defendant No. 20), D.W. No. 4 Khoaj Bibi alias Makhari (defendant No. 10), D.W. No. 5 Shamsuddin and D.W. No. 6 Reajuddin. Both the parties filed certain Exts. Ext. 1 is the certified copy of C.S. Khatian No. 48 of Mouza Jatrabari. Ext. D is the certified copy of C.S. khatian No. 53 of Mouza Jatrabari. Ext. A is the certified copy of the registered deed of Heba-bil-Ewaj executed by late Faloo's son late Khadem on 28.2.1917 in favour of his wife Korfulnessa, but for obvious reason it contained no plot number. Ext. A(1) is another deed of gift executed by Korfulnessa to her daughter defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo executed on 7.6.1939 in favour of Korfulnessa and her husband defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali transferring plot Nos. 953, 545 and 632 measuring 1.31 acre. Ext.B-B(5) are provisional rent receipts showing payment of rents for the Bengali Year 1362, 1363,1364, 1365, 1366 and 1368 showing payment of rent by Amjad Ali (defendant No. 20) and Lal Banoo defendant No. 1 in respect of 1.16 acre of land of khatian No.48 of mouza Jatrabari. Ext. No. C is the certified copy of the registered deed showing transfer of 34 acre of plot No. 740 of khatian No. 48 of mouza Jatrabari by Sk. Khadem on 9.12.1918 A.D. in favour of late Kazimuddin, father of defendant No.21 Mullak Chand.

13. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the suit is maintainable in its present form as undisputedly all necessary persons having interest in the suit properties have been added as parties to the suit and also because all the joint properties have been brought into the hatchpotch since the plaintiffs made necessary amendments in the plaint and in the schedule to the plaint to meet the objection raised by the contesting defendants in their written statement that the suit properties originally belonged to Faloo from whom his two sons Khadem and Chamoo and his two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi inherited the suit properties, that although the name of Khadem is recorded in khatian No. 48 and the name of Chamoo is recorded in khatian No. 53, but it is also recorded in the khatian that the joie in the said two khatians belonged to Faloo and that therefore the share of two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara by inheritance 1/3rd share remained unaffected; that the defendant failed to prove that Faloo made any gift of the suit properties in favour of his two sons Khalem and Chamoo to the exclusion of his two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi, that even if it is believed that Khadem made a gift of some land of the suit properties and that Khadem's wife Korfulnessa in her turn made a gift of the same to her daughter Lal Banoo and her son-in-law defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali, the fact remains that Khadem is not entitled to make any gift to his daughter beyond the share to which he is entitled to in the suit properties and consequently Khadem's daughter Korfulnessa could not have made any gift to defendant No.1 Lal Banoo and Lal Banoo's husband defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali beyond the 1/3rd share of Khadem in the suit property, that the plaintiffs being co-sharers by inheritance must be and still are in constructive possession of the suit property when there is no total ouster either by stranger or by other co-sharers including contesting defendant and defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali in assertion of their exclusive title, that as the contesting defendants have failed to prove that there is total ouster of the plaintiffs from the suit properties by possession of the defendants by openly denying the title of any sort of the plaintiffs within their (plaintiffs) knowledge; that therefore the fact that the co-sharer out of physical possession remains in constructive possession of the suit land through the other co-sharers remains unrebutted, that the suit by the plaintiffs is therefore not barred by adverse possession by the defendants and the plaintiffs are entitled to 1/3rd share of the suit property as heirs of Faloo's two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi.

14. The learned Subordinate Judge on 16.5.67 decreed the suit in preliminary form on contest with costs against the defendants 1-10 and ex pane against the rest and declared 1/3rd share of the suit property in favour of the plaintiffs. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the defendant No.1 and her husband defendant No.20 came up with this appeal.

15. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the two appellants submits that the suit land is in possession of the defendant appellants for more than 50 years, that the defendant-appellants are in possession of plot No. 943 measuring.15 acre of Khatian No. 48 of Mouza Jatrabari on the basis of their deed of gift, that they are also in possession of plot No. 545 measuring .36 acre and plot No. 632 measuring .38 acre of said Khatian No. 48 which have been acquired by the government and that the trial Court erroneously held that Faloo did not transfer the suit land in favour of his two sons. Thus he argued that the two defendant-appellants possessed the said three plots adversely to the exclusion of the plaintiff for more than 12 years and thereby acquired title in the said land by adverse possession.

16. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondents supported the judgment of the learned subordinate Judge. He how-ever pointed out that it is apparent on the face of the record that the correction of plot No. 953 of khatian No. 48 by substituting plot No. 935 is not correct and is a clerical error in view of the khatian Ext. 1 and that the said plot should continue to be read ac plot No. 953 of khatian No. 48 in the schedule to the plaints as it was originally so.

17. In this case P.W. 1 Abdul Aziz (plaintiff No. 1) deposed that the plots belonged to Faloo who died leaving behind two sons, namely, Khadem and Chamoo and two daughters namely, Joytunessa and Anwara Bibi. He supported the genealogy given in the plaint. He stated that the suit properties remained ejmali and undivided and that the plaintiff as the heirs and successors of Faloo's two daughters Joytonnessa and Anwara Bibi are entitled to 1/3rd share in the suit property including 1/3rd share in the compensation awarded by the Government in respect of the acquired plots. In his cross examination he stated that he goes to the houses of Khadem and Chamoo on visit and went there also after the suit was filed and that it is not a fact that they did not go there from the time of their grandmother Joytennessa.

18. P.W.2 Dadan Miah stated that the suit plots belonged to Faloo who died leaving behind two sons Khadem and Chamoo and two daughters Joytunnessa and Anwara and that the said two daughters of Faloo and the heirs of the said two daughters of Faloo used to visit the house of Khadem and Chamoo occasionally. In his cross-examination he has stated that it is natural that sisters would come to the houses of their brothers.

19. D.W.1 Lal Banoo (defendant No. 1) stated that her mother Korfulnessa got land by gift from her father Khadem and that her mother Korfulnessa made a gift of that land to her. She stated that she paid rents and the receipts have been filed by her in Court.We find that the six rent receipts Ext. B-B(5) are provisional rent receipts showing payment of rent for 1.16 acre of land of khatian No.48 of Mouza Jatrabari by defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo and her husband defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali for the period from 1362 B.S. to 1372 B.S. It is significant to note that the contesting defendant appellants failed to produce any rent receipt whatsoever for any period before 1362 B.S. From the six provisional rent receipts Ext. B-Ext. B(5) no presumption of possession can be made.

20. D.W.2 Mohabbat Ali Starder stated that Korfulnessa made a document in favour of defendant No. 1 Lal Banoo and Lal Banoo is wife of defendant No. 20 Amjad Ali. In his cross-examination he has stated that he is not an attesting witness in the document and that he heard about the document only. His evidence thus has no evidentiary value in respect of the execution of the deed of gift of Korfulnessa, in respect of possession by Korfulnessa or by defendant No.1 and defendant No.20.

21. D.W.3 Amjad Ali (defendant No.20) stated that his mother-in-law Korfulnessa made a gift of some land in his favour and in favour of his wife Lal Banoo (defendant No. 1) in lieu of Jainamaz and that they possessed the land. It is significant to note that neither D.W. 1 Lal Banoo (defendant No. 1) nor her husband D.W. 3 Amjad Ali stated anywhere that they possessed the land of Hebanama Ex.  A(1) (allegedly executed on 7.6.39) adversely or adversely to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and their predecessors.

22. D.W.4 Khoaj Bibi (defendant No. 10) is not an appellant. She has stated nothing in favour of the defendant-appellants.

23. D.W.5 Shamsuddin Ahmed who deposed on behalf of defendant No. 10 Khoaj Bibi has also not deposed in favour of the defendant-appellants.

24. D.W.6 Reajuddin Ahmed stated that he wrote the Hebanama Ext. 1(1) which was executed by Korfulnessa by putting her thumb impression. He further states that Khadem executed a kabala Ext. C in favour of Kazimuddin and that the said kabala was written by his khalu. Kazimuddin is dead and late Kazimuddin's son Mullak Chand added in the plaint by amendment as defendant No. 21. Mullak Chand, as heir of Kazimuddin, did not contest the suit.

<u>25. From the discussion of the oral and documentary evidence made above we find that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly found that the plaintiffs being co-sharers by inheritance from Faloo's two daughters' namely Joytunessa and Anwara Bibi continued to remain in constructive possession of the suit plots as the defendants failed to prove in any way that there was total ouster of the plaintiffs by any of the defendants in assertion of their hostile title. This view finds support in the decision in the cases of Maharaja Bhupendra Chandra Singha Sarma and other Vs. Sudhindra Ch. Singha and ors 5 DLR 142; Mst. Ghulam Ilahi Vs. Muhammad Waris Khan, 10 DLR (FC) 174; Abdul Gani Talukder alias Md. Abdul Gani Talukdar and others Vs. Rushan and others 12 DLR. 40; Kutijan Bibi Vs. Zulmat Khan and others 19 DLR 20; C.R. Vs. Corea Vs. M.I. Appuhamy and another AIR 1914 (PC)243; W.P. Tamel and others Vs. H.A. Anohamy and others. AIR 1918 (PC)339; and Abdul Jalil Sikdar and others Vs. Korshed Ali Dakua and ors. 27 DLR (A.D)143; In the case of Most. Ghulam Ilahi Vs. Muhammad Waris Khan, 10 DLR (FC)174 it was held:-</u>

<u>"The principle of law is that possession is not to be considered adverse if its origin can be referred to a lawful title whenever that is possible, because a person who claims to have entered into possession as a trespasser will be presumed not to have done so if at the time he so entered he had some lawful title to possession."</u>

<u>In the case of Abdul Gani Talukdar Vs. Rushan and others 12 DLR 40 I.H. Chowdhury, J. held as follows:-</u>

<u>"There is no doubt that every co-sharer is entitled to enjoy a joint property and, if he enjoys to the exclusion of the other co-sharers and in excess of his own share, he cannot be forcibly evicted from the joint land.</u>

<u>The remedy of the co-sharer not in actual possession is to bring a suit for partition and get a decree for possession of his specific share on partition."</u>

<u>In the case of Abdul Jalil Sikdar and others Vs. Khorshed Ali Dakua and others, 27 DLR (AD)143 it was observed:—</u>

<u>"Ouster is necessary to constitute adverse possession by a co-sharer. Mere sole possession of a joint estate by any one of the co-shares affords no evidence to the exclusion of the co-sharers having interest. There is also authority in support of the proposition that uninterrupted possession of a property must be referred to the lawful title possessed by the co-sharer of the joint estate and cannot be regarded as an assertion of a right to hold it as separate so as to assert an adverse claim against other co-sharers having interest therein. When the question arises as to whether the possession is either lawful or unlawful, it must be assumed, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that possession is lawful not only on his behalf but on behalf of his co-sharers. In support of this proposition reference may be made to two decisions of the Privy Council, C.R. V.S. Corea Vs. M.I. Appuhamy (AIR 1914 PC 243) and W.P. Tamel Vs. H.A Anohamy (AIR 1918 PC 339)".</u>

<u>Thus it is clear that right, title and interest of the plaintiffs to the extent of 1/3rd share of the suit property as heirs of Faloo's aforesaid two daughters has not been extinguished by any ouster or adverse possession by the appellants. The Yearned subordinate Judge, therefore, has rightly declared the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs to the extent of 1/ 3rd share of the suit including C.S. plot No.953 of Khatian No.48 of mouza Jatrabari.</u>

In the result the appeal is dismissed without costs. The Judgement and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka is affirmed.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 114 of 1982.
lawyer:
Abdur Rashid ---- For the appellant.
Syed Badrul Alam --- For the respondent.
parties:
Md. Azharul Islam ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Md. Idris Ali and anr ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
Fazle Hussain Mohammad Habibur Rahman, J.—This appeal it the instance of the plaintiff-appellant is directed against the judgment and decree passed by Mr. M.A. Salam, Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Mymensingh on 30.4.82 in O.C. Suit No. 137/80 which is a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of immovable property.

<u>1. The suit was decreed in favour of plaintiff Mohammed Azharul Islam against defendant No. 1 respondent Md. Idris Ali in the following terms ; "The plaintiff shall get the kabala deed executed from the contesting defendant on payment of Tk. 95,000,00 to the contesting defendant including Tk. 50.000 as compensatory cost in view of the real valuation of the suit property. The plaintiff is directed to pay the kabala consideration to defendant No. 1 within 2 months from the date and defendant No. 1 is directed to execute the kabala deed in respect of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff within 3 months from the date in default of payment of the balance consideration money within 2 months to defendant No. 1 the suit shall stand dismissed. If the defendant fails to execute and register the kabala deed within 3 months on receipt of the kabala consideration money, the plaintiff shall get the kabala deed executed and registered through court on depositing the balance consideration money and on furnishing requisites, stamps and other fees.</u>

2. The case for the plaintiff appellant Mohammad Azharul Islam is that the suit property measuring 0.03 acre of land situated in Mouza Mymensingh Town, P. Kotwali comprising of one pucca room, one pucca latrine and two dakhila tin sheds belonged to this defendant No. 1 Md. Idris Ali who told the plaintiff that he was in urgent need of money and that he wanted to sell the suit property to the plaintiff at the highest market price. The highest market price of the suit property was fixed at Tk. 50.000 between the plaintiff and the defendant and accordingly defendant No. 1 Md. Idris Ali executed the bainapatra Ext. 1 on 1.6.79 in presence of P.W. 2 Narayan Chandra Dey, P.W. 3 Md. Abdul Ahad, P.W. 4 Abul Kasem and one Abul Hossain. P.W. 3 Md. Abdul Ahad is the scribe of the document. In presence of the said witnesses defendant No. 1 Md. Idris Ali executed the said bainapatra Ext. 1 accepting Tk. 5,000/- in the majlish as earnest money. Defendant Idris Ali by the said bainapatra agreed to execute the registered safkabala within 10 months from 1.6.79. The plaintiff used to run Star Medical Hall in the suit premises as a tenant under defendant Idris Ali. In spite of repeated demands the defendant No. 1 did not execute the required kabala in favour of the plaintiff. The plaintiff has been always ready with the balance amount of consideration money to be paid to the defendant. The plaintiff then sent a legal notice Ext. 2 through his advocate to the defendant on 31.3.80. The said legal notice was served on defendant No. 1 on 16.4.80. Defendant No. 1 by his Advocate's letter Ext. 2 (ga) dated 24.4.80 replied that the defendant No. 1 did not enter into a contract to sell the land in question to the plaintiff for an amount of Tk. 50,000/- on 1.6.79, that the question of receiving Tk. 5,000/- as earnest money by the defendant from the plaintiff does not arise at all and that as the plaintiff did not agree to pay the increased rent at the rate of Tk. 75/- per month for the said premises, the plaintiff was asked by the defendant to vacate the premises. Thereafter the plaintiff through his Advocate sent a letter Ext. 2 (gha) dated 29.4.80 to defendant No. 1 stating that if the defendant did not execute the kabala in favour of the plaintiff within 7 days, the plaintiff would be compelled to file civil suit for execution and registration of the kabala. Thereafter the plaintiff instituted the present suit on 9-5-80 praying for a decree for specific performance of contract by execution and registration of sale deed by the defendant No. 1 in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit property on receipt of remaining amount of Tk. 45,000/-, in default to execute and register the kabala through court.

3. Defendant No. 1 Idris Ali contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations and contending, inter alia, that the father of the plaintiff since 1950 has been possessing the suit property as a monthly tenant on payment of Tk. 38/- per month. After his father the plaintiff has been possessing the suit property on payment of monthly rent at first at the rate of Tk. 75/- per month. The plaintiff has been running his pharmacy in the name and style of the Star Medical Hall in the suit premises. The defendant No. 1 found the plaintiff to be undesirable tenant. He used to delay in the matter of payment of rents. Defendant No. 1 wanted to run his own business in the suit premises and asked the plaintiff to vacate the premises. Thereafter on creating a forged and fabricated Bainapatra the plaintiff sent his advocate's letter dated 31-3-80 to defendant No. 1 asking him to transfer the suit property by executing and registering a deed in his favour. The plaintiff never paid Tk. 5,030/ to the defendant as earnest money and defendant No. 1 also never agreed in any majlish on 1-6-79 to sell the suit property to the plaintiff at a price of Tk. 50,000/-. The defendant No. 1 never executed any Bainapatra. The alleged Bainapatra is forged and fabricated. The defendant No. 1 further asserted that the market price of the suit property should be Tk. 2,00,000/-. The suit is, therefore, liable to be dismissed.

4. At the time of trial the plaintiff examined four witnesses including himself as P.W. 1. The defendant No. 1 examined 2 witnesses including himself as D.W. 1. The plaintiff filed documents Ext. 1 and 2 series and defendant filed counter foils of rent receipts Ext. A-Ext A (4).

5. The learned Subordinate Judge on a consideration of the evidence on record found that the bainapatra was genuine, that it was duly executed by defendant No. 1 on 1-6-79 in presence of the witnesses on respect of a consideration money of Tk. 5.000/- out of the stipulated amount of Tk. 50,000/-, that in view of the fact that the price of the property at the time of the hearing of the suit had gone up the plaintiff should pay Tk. 1,00,000/- for the suit property to defendant No. 1 instead of Tk. 50,000/- as its price and that he accordingly decreed the suit against defendant No. 1 asking the plaintiff to pay Tk. 95,000/- instead of Tk. 45,00% to the contesting defendant including Tk. 50,000/- as "compensatory cost" in view of the present price of the suit property and accordingly directed the plaintiff to pay the balance consideration money to the defendant, in default, he directed that the suit shall stand dismissed. Thereafter the plaintiff has preferred this appeal.

6. Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant submits that once it has been proved and once it has been accepted by the trial court that the bainapatra or for that matter, the contract is genuine and true, there is no provision in law empowering the trial court to direct the plaintiff to pay Tk. 50,000/- more than the stipulated amount as compensatory cost to defendant No. 1 in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff and that the said part of the judgment and order of the trial court being illegal must be set aside He further submits that the trial court has virtually substituted the contract entered into by the parties by a new contract with new terms and thus acted beyond its jurisdiction. He also submits that the trial court acted arbitrarily and without jurisdiction by asking the plaintiff to pay an additional amount of Tk. 50,000/- for execution and registration of the kabala.

7. Mr. Syed Badrul Alam, the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1- respondent concedes that as defendant No. 1- respondent has not filed any cross-objection under Order 41, rule 22 C.P.C., he cannot challenge the decree on merit. But he submits that under Order 41, rule 33 C.P.C. the appellate court has inherent power to see whether the bainapatra Ext. 1 is genuine or false and fabricated. This is indeed a queer submission specially in view of the fact that after having told a big lie in the trial court in this respect the plaintiff himself is ashamed to repeat the lie by filing a cross-objection and has justly accepted the correct finding of the trial court regarding the genuineness of the bainapatra Ext. 1.

8. D.W. 2 Jamaluddin does not speak anything about the bainapatra. He has only been brought to speak about the market price of the suit property. D.W. 1 Md. Idris Ali, defendant No. 1 deposed that the bainapatra Ext. 1 is forged and that it was not signed by him P.W. 1 Azharul Islam (plaintiff) P.W. 2 Narayan Chandra Dey, P.W.3 Md. Abdul Ahad (scribe) and P.W. 4 Abul Kasem have proved the defendant No.1 Md. Idris Ali voluntarily and duly executed the bainapatra on 1.6.79 in their presence on receipt of Tk. 5,000 promising to sell the suit land at the highest market price of Tk. 50,000/-and also promising to execute and register the deed of sale in favour of the plaintiff within 10 months from the date of execution of the bainapatra.
