The trial court compared defendant No. 1's signature in the bainapatra with other available signatures of defendant No. 1 and came to the finding that the bainapatra Ext. 1 contains the genuine signature of defendant No. 1 and that P.W. 1, P.W.2, P.W 3 and P.W.4 have deposed truly that the defendant No. 1 executed the bainapatra on 1.6.79 accepting Tk.5 000/- as earnest money promising to sell the suit property for Tk. 50,000/-. We have also compared the signatures of defendant No. 1 (DW.1) in the bainapatra Ext. 1 with his signatures in the plaint filed in the trial court, in the power filed in the trial court as well as in this Court and the signature put by him below his deposition recorded in the trial court. We find that there is no difference in the style and manner of execution and writing between the said signatures and the signatures of the executant in the Bainapatra in question. There is thus no manner of doubt that defendant No. 1 genuinely put his signatures in the Bainapatra Ext. 1 which was written by P.W.3. P.Ws. 1-4 have proved that defendant No. 1 agreed to sell the suit property at the highest market price of Tk. 50,000/- and received Tk. 5,000/- as earnest money on 1.6.79 in their presence from the plaintiff P.W. 1 and executed the bainapatra Ext. 1. So we find that defendant No. 1 has not been able to make out any special case calling for our interference under Order 41 rule 33 C.P.C. As already stated, we find that defendant No. 1 in the trial court had made a false statement when he denied to have executed the Bainapatra Ext. 1 and that by not filing the cross-objection he has rightly and justly accepted the correct finding of the trial court that he had in fact genuinely executed the Bainapatra.

<u>9. The trial court has not held that at the time of the execution of Bainapatra dated 1.6.79 Ext. 1 the prevailing market price of the suit property was Tk. one lac Plaintiff's witnesses 2-4 have said like plaintiff P.W. 1 that that price of the suit property was fixed on 1.6 79 at the highest market price of Tk. 50,000- and that accordingly Bainapatra was executed by defendant No. 1 accepting the earnest money of Tk 5,000/. on the date promising to sell the suit property to the plaintiff for a total consideration money of Tk. 50,000/-. Plaintiff P.W. 1 said while deposing on 13.3.83 (that is, about 3 years after the date of contract) as follows:-</u>

<u>বায়না পত্রের সময় দাম ৫০০০০/- টাকা ছিল, বতমার্নে বাড়িয়া দুই লক্ষ টাকা হইতে পারে।</u>

<u>(At the time of execution of the Bainapatra (in June 1979 the (market) ) price was Taka 50,000/-. No (in March, 1983 the (market) price might have increased to Taka two lacs.")</u>

10. On the basis of this statement the learned Subordinate Judge observed, 'Plaintiff P.W. 1 himself admitted that the present price of the suit property is about taka two lacs and defendant D.W 1 and D.W.2 assert that the valuation of the suit property is not less than taka two lacs. I do hold that if defendant No. 1 is compelled to sell the suit property at Tk. 50,000.00 only, an injustice would be done upon defendant No. 1. In a suit for specific performance of contract, passing of a decree is a discretion of the court under the provision of Specific Relief Act and as such I think justice will be met if the plaintiff pays taka one lac as consideration money of the suit property to defendant No. 1. In the light of findings and observations made above I am inclined to award compensatory cost in favour of the defendant No. 1".

<u>11. In the case of Ram Chandra Das and others Vs. Md. Khalilur Rahman and another reported in 37 (1985) DLR (AD) 21 it has been held by the Appellate Division,</u>

<u>"The contention that it would cause hardship to the defendant if specific performance is ordered after the lapse of so many years particularly when the prices of land have gone up considerably since the date of contract, cannot be accepted for the simple reason that the Court in such cases is to give effect to the bargain struck between the parties. The intention of the parties to a contract would then vanish. All formal transactions like a contract of sale of property are solemnly entered and cannot, therefore, be trifled with."</u>

12. We have already shown above that the plaintiff has been able to establish without any manner of doubt that a genuine and straight-forward contract was entered into between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 on 1.6.79 on the basis of written Bainapatra' executed by defendant No. 1 and that the said contract was not obtained by the plaintiff from the defendant No. 1 within the meaning of section 28 of the Specific Relief Act by any fraud, undue advantage, misrepresentation, concealment, unfair practice influence or mistake of fact, misappropriation or surprise or that the stipulated price was in any way grossly inadequate with reference to the state of things existing at the date of contract. Explanation to Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act specifically provide that unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall presume that the breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by compensation in money. Illustration to Clause (c) of section 12 of the said Act is as follows ;-

"A contracts with B to sell him a house for Taka 1,000. B is entitled to a decree directing A to convey the house to him, he paying the purchase money."

13. Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act empowers the Court to award compensation for breach of contract in certain cases to the person suing for the specific performance of contract whether in addition to, or in substitution for, such performance. The said section 19 (without the Explanation and illustrations) Is quoted below:—

Any person suing for the specific performance of a contract may also ask for compensation for its breach either in addition to, or in substitution for such performance.

If in any such suit the court decides that specific performance ought not to be granted, but that there is a contract between the parties which has been broken by the defendant and that the plaintiff is entitled to compensation for that breach. it shall award him compensation accordingly.

If in any such suit the court decides that specific performance ought to be granted, but that it is not sufficient to satisfy the justice of the case, and that some compensation for breach of the contract should also be made to the plaintiff, it shall award him such compensation accordingly. Compensation awarded under this section may be assessed as the court may direct.

Explanation..............

Illustrations………..

14. Regarding the provisions of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act Pollock and Mulla in their book on the Contract and Specific Relief Acts (Eighth Edition Page 798) commented, 'Our section 22 with its sub-divisions and illustrations is really more like an elementary lecture than legislation. We are far from saying that an explanation of this kind was not required or at least useful in 1877. It must not be supposed to be exhaustive," The provisions of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act are as follows:

The jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the Court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so; but the discretion of the Court is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal.

The following are cases in which the court may properly exercise discretion not to decree specific performance:-

1. Where the circumstances under which the contract is made are such as to give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant, though there may be no fraud or misrepresentation on plaintiff's part. Illustration (d)—A's property is put up to auction. B requests C, A'S attorney, to bid for him. C does this inadvertently and in good faith. The persons present, seeing the vendor's attorney bidding, think that he is a mere puffer and cease to compete. The lot is knocked down to B at lower price. Specific performance of the contract should be refused to B.

II. Where performance of the contract would involve some hardship on the defendant which he did not foresee,

whereas its non-performance would involve no such hardship on the plaintiff. ……………….

Illustration (h)—A contracts with II to sell him certain land, and to make a road to it from a certain railway station. It is found afterwards that he cannot make the road without exposing himself to litigation. Specific performance on the part of the contract relating to the road should be refused to B, even though it may be held that he is entitled to specific performance of the rest with compensation for the loss of the road. ………………………

III. The following is a case in which the Court may properly exercise a discretion to decree specific performance. Where the plaintiff has done substantial acts or suffered losses in consequence of a contract capable of specific performance."

<u>15. It may be stated here that within the meaning of part 11 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act subsequent rise or fall in price of immoveable property is not considered to involve 'some hardship" on the defendant which he did not foresee, whereas its non-performance would involve no hardship on the plaintiff. This is because both the parties are bound by the bargain struck between the parties in a genuine contract for sale of immoveable property and subsequent fluctuations in price, that is, rise or fall in the price of such property after the date of contract is not considered to be a ground to refuse specific performance of either party. (See Sassoon Vs. Ardeshir, AIR 1926 Bombay 189 ; Ardeshir Vs. Sassoon, AIR 1928 P.C. 208). In the said case of Ardeshir Vs. Sassoon, Plaintiff Ardeshir on 19 December 1919 accepted defendant Sassoon's of offer Rs. 18 lacs as price of a house in the Malabar Hill of Bombay and received Rs. one lac as earnest money and communicated it to defendant on 29 Dec. 1919. But another party who had offered up to Rupees 15 lacs pressed his offer and raised it to Rupees 25 lacs till 19 January 1920. The defendant accepted it then and completed the sale. The plaintiff filed suit against the defendant for specific performance of contract on 10.1.1921 due to which the defendant could not dispose of the property. After about three years the plaintiff altered the prayer, gave up the prayer for specific performance of contract and prayed for compensation and damages simpliciter and thus converted it into a suit for breach of contract. Mirza, J. the learned Judge who tried the suit in the original side of the Bombay High Court awarded Rupees eight lacs as damages to the plaintiff. The Division Bench of the Bombay High Court in appeal (judgment delivered by Macleod. C.J.,) only allowed the plaintiff return of the earnest money, but in the facts and circumstances of the case did not allow any compensation to the plaintiff. The Privy Council upheld the High Court's decision with certain observations regarding amendment of a plaint of a suit for specific performance or damages in the alternative into one for damages only. In a properly framed suit (in view of the provisions of the Specific Relief Act) the plaintiff purchaser may be awarded compensation in substitution for specific performance. It is however clear from this decision that if the plaintiff purchaser did not alter his prayer and continued with the prayer for specific performance of contract and if the plaintiff purchaser could prove that the defendant vendor herself entered into the contract or through her duly authorised agent, specific performance would have been decreed in favour of the plaintiff purchaser together with any compensation for any loss the court might have thought the plaintiff had suffered owing to defendant's refusal to complete the transaction. The fact that within a month after the contract between plaintiff and defendant on 19.12.1919, defendant got another party agreeing to pay much higher price of Rs. 25 lacs in place of Rs. 18 lacs, that is, Rupees seven lacs more for the same property on 19.1.1920 is no ground for refusing specific performance of contract between plaintiff and defendant at the price stipulated on 19.12.1919. Secondly, although in the specific Relief Act there is no express statement, yet in a suit for specific performance of contract the plaintiff purchaser is required to prove a continuous readiness and willingness from the date of the contract to the time of hearing to perform the contract on his part, but the Court may in its discretion grant his alternative prayer for return of the earnest money and any further amount the court thinks proper to award as compensation to the plaintiff. In such cases of subsequent rise in the price of the immovable property in granting specific performance of contract to the plaintiff, the question of giving compensation to the defendant vendor owing to subsequent rise in price does not arise, just as in a case of subsequent fall in price the plaintiff vendor can ask for specific performance of contract at the already stipulated higher price by the defendant purchaser in spite of the fall in price and the Court may in its discretion grant plaintiff vendor's alternative prayer for appropriate compensation for breach of contract by the defendant purchaser.</u>

<u>17. A reference may also be made to the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Davis Vs. Maung Showe Con 15 C.W.N. 935 ; 38 Calcutta 805 ; 14 C.L.J. 50 wherein Mr. Ameer Ali delivering the judgment of the Privy Council observed</u>

<u>"It has been strongly urged by Counsel on behalf of the defendant that as a decree for specific performance of contract is discretionary, their Lordships, having regard to the onerous character of the bargain, should not affirm the decision of the Chief Court. In the absence of evidence of fraud or misrepresentation on the part of the plaintiff which induced the defendant to enter into the contract, their Lordships see no reason to accede to the argument. The bargain but there is nothing unconscionable."</u>

18. An unreported decision dated 28.2.85 by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No. 274 of 1984 in the case of Imperial Chemical Industries (Bangladesh) Ltd. vs. M/s. G.K. Brothers has been noticed by us. The judgment of the Division Bench of the High Court Division, Chittagong Bench in the said case of I.C.I. (Bangladesh) Ltd. vs. M/s.G.K. Brothers, reported in 36 DLR 114 was delivered by me. In the said suit for specific performance of contract by the defendant in respect of sale of house property including the hill in Chittagong the price of the suit property had gone up several times higher when on 7.6.74 the suit was instituted than the price of Taka 3,30,000/-stipulated on 17.8.70. The suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff purchaser M/s. G.K. Brothers by the trial court and the said decision was palled by the High Court Division in appeal. Neither in the trial court nor in the appellate court the defendant (Bangladesh) Ltd, prayed for any solatium on any ground in view of the defendant's case the that contract dated 17. 8.70 entered into by the Imperial Chemical Industries (Pakistan) Ltd. with its Head Office in Karachi Whose properties were declared abandoned properties under P.O. No. 16 of 1972 and later handed over to the newly formed defendant company Imperial Chemical Industries (Bangladesh) Ltd, is not enforceable against the defendant company an d that the plaintiff having failed to complete transaction with regard to the sale of the property within the period of validation of Income Tax Clearance Certificate, that is, within 31.12.71, the contract stood rescinded and the plaintiff forfeited the right to obtain the sale deed under the contract. Due to the unusual and extraordinary situation prevailing in the country in consequence of the war of liberation the plaintiff requested the Imperial Chemical Industries (Pakistan) Ltd. by its letter dated 17.4.71 and obtained extension of validity of the Income Tax Certificate which was first extended up to 30.6.71 and then up to 31.12.71 to facilitate the execution of the deed of sale. The plaintiff during that abnormal period had to remain in hiding to save his life from the Pakistani Occupation Army. After the war of Independence ended on 16.12.71 and Bangladesh came into being as an independent sovereign state, the assets and properties in Bangladesh of the Imperial Chemical Industries (Pakistan) Ltd. (registered in Karachi) became abandoned properties and vested in the Government which later released the said assets and properties from the category of abandoned properties and the defendant company, that is, the Imperial Chemical Industries (Bangladesh) Ltd. took over the business management of the company. In the circumstances when the defendant company through their learned advocate in the Appellate Division prayed for some compensation in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and the plaintiffs agreed to pay a solatium of Tk. 1,00,00/- the Appellate Division dismissed the petition for Special Leave subject to the payment of Taka one Iac by the plaintiff by a bank draft (in addition to the balance consideration money of Taka 2,97,000/- which had already been paid by that time to the defendant by a bank draft within a month whereupon the defendant was directed to execute and register the necessary kabala. The unusual and extraordinary facts of the said case of Imperial Chemical Industries (Bangladesh) Ltd vs. M/s. G.K. Brothers are not at all attracted in the present case so as to justify the granting of any solatium(compensation) to the defendant vendor who was at fault while the plaintiff has proved his continuous readiness and willingness from the date of the contract to the time of hearing of the suit to perform the contract on his part.

19. We have noticed the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Jogesh Chandra Das and others Vs. Farida Hasan reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 315 where although it was proved by the plaintiff purchaser that the defendants on receipt of the entire consideration money of Tk. 3000 on 27.12.63 executed two separate kabalas and made over the title deeds and khatians of the suit land to the plaintiff, but did not turn up to effect registration and also did not deliver possession of the suit property, the Appellate Division did  not grant specific performance of contract on the ground that consideration money of Tk. 3000/- for sale of 5.29 acres of land was abnormally low and that it was executed at a time when there was civil disturbance in the country and the members of the minority community were contemplating to migrate from this country and that specific performance in the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case would give an undue advantage over the defendant. The Appellate Division modified the decree asking the defendants to return the consideration money of Tk. 3000/- and pay Tk. 30,000/- as compensation to the plaintiff within six months in default, the plaintiff's suit stands decreed in full. The facts and circumstances of this decision in the case of Jogesh Chandra Das end others Vs Farida Hasan, 1933 MD (AD) 225 have no manner of application in the present case.

<u>20. In the present case we have good and reliable evidence on record that the defendant vendor as an ordinary prudent man with his eyes open agreed to sell the suit property by duly executing a written bainapatra on 1-6-79 at a price of Taka 50,000/- without being influenced by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake of fact etc. There is also no reason to hold that the stipulated price was in any way grossly inadequate with reference to the state of things existing at the date of contract. As the defendant No. 1 did not execute the kabala as per agreement, the plaintiff after due service of his advocate's notice on 31-3-80 on the defendant, instituted the present suit in time on 9th May, 1980 and before institution of the suit he also served notice on defendant No. 1 on 29-4-80 on receipt of defendant no. 1's reply. Since the price fixed on I-6-79 between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 was not in any way grossly inadequate or influenced by misrepresentation, fraud, unfair practice, mistake of fact, misapprehension, etc., there is absolutely no reason to hold that there is any ground for asking the plaintiff to pay any compensation or solatium to defendant No. 1. We find that the trial court had no justification whatsoever to ask the plaintiff to pay any compensatory cost" to defendant No. 1 or any extra amount over an above the stipulated amount of Tk. 50,000/- out of which Taka 5,000/- had already been paid. So we set aside the direction of the trial court asking the plaintiff to pay an additional compensatory cost of Tk. 50000/- over and above the balance amount of Taka 45,000/-.</u>

21. In the result, the appeal is allowed in the following terms without any order as to costs. The suit is decreed on contest against defendant No. 1 and ex-parte against defendant No. 2 Government of Bangladesh. The plaintiff shall get the kabala deed executed by the defendant on payment of the remaining amount of Tk. 45,000/-. The plaintiff is directed to pay the balance consideration money of Tk. 45,000/- to defendant No. 1 Within 3 months from the date of receipt of the record by the Subordinate Judge and defendant No. 1 is directed to execute and register the kabala in respect of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff whereupon the defendant shall execute and register the necessary kabala. If the defendant fails to execute and register the kabala on receipt of the said balance consideration money, the plaintiff shall get the kabala executed and registered through court on depositing the balance consideration money of Taka 45,000/- in Court.

Mohammad Abdur Rouf, J.-- I agree

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakrborty, Adv. with Mr. Sanjib Kumar Chowdhury, Adv. (in person) ----- For the petitioners. 
Mr. Kamal-ul Alam, Advocate with Mrs. Shahanaj Akther, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Sontosh Kumar Chowdhury and Others
Vs.
Pranab Kumar Chakraborty and Others
full_judgment:
Soumendra Sarker, J: The Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties No.1-3 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 18.05.2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No. 380 of 1990 disallowing the appeal and thereby affirming those of dated 31.05.1990 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Additional Court, Sadar, Chittagong in Partition Suit No. 25 of 1990 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the predecessor-in-interest of the present petitioners namely Brojendra Lal Chowdhury as plaintiff instituted the original Partition Suit being No.131 of 1978 in the 3rd Court of learned the then Sub-ordinate Judge, Chittagong which was subsequently transferred to the 1st Court of learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong and renumbered as 149 of 1984. The suit was again transferred to the 3rd Additional Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong for hearing and disposal and it was again renumbered as Partition Suit No. 25 of 1980, contending inter alia that the disputed property corresponding to schedule No.1 of the plaint originally belonged to one Monmohon Dutta. At the demise of Monmohon Dutta his one son Nogendra Lal Dutta and wife Tarongini Dutta succeeded him. Tarangini Dutta in the year 1963 made her portion of land demarked in a Partition Suit No.10 of 1963. For want of getting cost of that suit in an Execution Case being No. 13 of 1967 the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 auction purchased the land of Nogendra Lal Dutta in equal share and the plaintiff after erecting his homestead in some portion of that land possessing the same as of his dwelling house. In the remaining portion of land the defendants do possess. In the land of schedule No. 2 of the plaint out of 51/2 koras of land the plaintiff in his equal share obtained two gondas three koras. In fact; the auction purchased land was never partitioned by metes and bounds among the plaintiff and defendants. The plaintiff while asked the defendant No.1 to make partition through “দখল দেওয়ানী” (delivery of possession) the defendant No.1 denied; showing excess land in his portion, which constrained the plaintiff to institute the original suit.

3. The contrary case of the contesting defendants No.1 and 6 in short is thus that the plaintiff is the “কার্য কারক” of the defendant No.1 and he used to work on behalf of the defendant No.1 The plaintiff taking advantage of that; at the time of auction purchase collusively created a "boynama" in his name as auction purchaser with the name of the defendant and in the subsequent “দখল দেওয়ানী” proceedings, the plaintiff admitting his collusive act begged pardon and prayed for one gonda land in his favour, at which the defendant at the request of the plaintiff gave him one gonda land in the suit holding. The further case of the defendants is such that in the corresponding “দখল দেওয়ানী” of the aforesaid `boynctma' the plaintiff admitted the case of the defendants, and there is a mention to that effect in the “দখল দেওয়ানী” wherein the plaintiff admitted that he has obtained only one gonda land in the suit holding. Suppressing the facts on false allegations subsequently the plaintiff instituted the original suit for partition to grab the property of the defendants.

4. The case of the defendant No.6 in a nutshell is such, that he has purchased 03 koras land by way of a kabala deed dated 01.02.1980 from the defendant No.1 and after his purchase he is possessing that 03 koras land in the suit holding.

5. The learned trial court during trial of the original suit after examining two witnesses from the side of the plaintiffs and 03 witnesses from the side of the defendants on perusal of the evidence produced therein and evaluation of the same dismissed the suit on contest by his judgment and decree dated 31.05.1990.

6. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred a Partition Appeal being Other Appeal No.380 of 1990 in the court of learned District Judge, Chittagong, which was transmitted to the 4111 Court of learned Additional District Judge, Chittagong for hearing and disposal and the learned appellate court hearing the appeal disallowed the same affirming the judgment and decree passed by the trial court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 18.05.2000.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate court, the heirs of Brojendra Lal Chowdhury, who was the original plaintiff have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

8. During hearing of this Rule Mr. Tapan Kumar Chakraborty with Mr. Sanjib Kanti Chowdhury, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. Kamal-ul Alam with Mrs. Shahanaj Akther the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

9. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that, both the courts below during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed illegality and infirmity. The learned Advocate further submits that without assigning any cogent reason the learned trial court as well as the appellate court in deciding the fate of the case committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate also submits that the specific contention of the plaintiff to the original suit was such that he along with the defendant No.1 auction purchased the suit land in equal share in the execution proceedings of Auction being No.13 of 1967 on 10.01.1968 A.D. at a cost of Taka 895/-(Eight hundred and ninety five) and the boynama' showing the purchase of the plaintiff and the defendant in equal share has been duly effected. In some portion of the suit property the plaintiff to the suit after- erecting his homestead used to reside with his family members. It was further contended from the side of the plaintiff specifically that in the subsequent “দখল দেওয়ানী” the defendant No.1 collusively entried excess land depriving the plaintiff in getting equal share pursuant to auction boynama' which has been marked as Exhibit-`A'. The learned Advocate argued that the specific case of the defendants has been raised in paragraph No.10 of their written statement, which is not proved by any tangible evidence. The learned trial court at the time of disposal of the original suit analyzing the papers on record arrived at a conclusive decision after framing seven different issues that the suit is maintainable in its present form and it is not barred by limitation. It was further decided by the trial court that the valuation of the suit and payment of court fees are proper and adequate and that there is no defect of parties and all the ejmali properties has been brought into hotchpotch. Against the aforesaid decision of the trial court neither any appeal was preferred nor any cross objection was filed from the side of the contesting defendants in the appellate court and thereby they have waived any counter claim on the findings and decisions of the trial court on the issues No.1- 5. The learned Advocate lastly submits that, the courts below only on one point which is the alleged admission of the plaintiff in the “দখল দেওয়ানী” with regard to his only 01 gonda land in the suit holding dismissed the suit. The learned Advocate submits that in “দখল দেওয়ানী” Exhibit-'D' despite it is found that the defendant gave possession of 01 gonda land in the suit holding in favour of the plaintiff, but it is not conclusive evidence and the alleged “দখল নামা” Exhibit-'D' has not been effected yet. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred some decisions of this Court and our Apex Court.

10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule controverted the argument advanced from the side of the petitioners and submits that neither the trial court nor the appellate court during disposal of the original suit and its subsequent appeal committed any sort of illegality, infirmity or irregularity resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned trial court and the lower appellate court in their observation and findings concurrently held adverting evidence on records that, pursuant to auction sale in the “দখল দেওয়ানী” the predecessor of the present petitioners namely Brojendra Lal Chowdhury clearly admitted that; he is not entitled equal share with the defendant No.1 . It is also admitted that in the suit holding he has right, title, interest and possession in only one gonda land and both the courts below concurrently decided after proper assessment of evidence that the claim of the plaintiff is barred by the principle of estoppels. Under section 20 of the Evidence Act the plaintiff is estopped in getting his share as prayed for in the partition suit. The leaned Advocate lastly after referring some decisions of this Court and our Apex Court submits that the boynama' of the auction sale is not a collusive piece of evidence and the final proceedings of the auction depends upon “দখল দেওয়ানী” viz. “দখল নামা” which apparently disproved the case of the plaintiff.

11. Considering the submissions of the learned Advocates having gone through the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and the judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate court below along with the evidence led from the sides of the respective parties it transpires that the contention of the plaintiff in his pleading in the suit for partition is such that the plaintiff Brojendra Lal Chowdhury who was the predecessor-interest of the present petitioners along with the predecessor of the defendant-opposite parties namely Satish Chandra jointly purchased the disputed property in equal share in an auction measuring 05 gondas, 02 koras on 10.01.1968.

12. The contrary case as alleged from the contesting defendants No.1 and 6 is such that Satish Chandra the predecessor of the defendants in fact alone auction purchased the suit land through his tadbirker Brojendra Lal and taking advantage of that, Brojendra Lal included his name collusively along with the name of Satish Chandra and inserted his name with ill motive in the `boynamai. The Other contesting defendant No.6 raised his plea that he has purchased 03 koras land from the defendant No.1 by a kabala deed dated 01.02.1980 finding the actual physical possession of the defendant No.1 pursuant to auction “দখল নামা” locally known as “দখল দেওয়ানী”.

<u>13. On perusal of the documentary evidence produced from the side of the parties it appears that Exhibit-`A', the boynama' dated 10.01.1968 shows that the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 were the auction purchasers in equal share. Pursuant to auction it also appears that an application for getting possession of the auction purchased land dated 05.03.1968 was filed by the auction purchasers jointly marked as Exhibit-`E' and this very document shows that the plaintiff Brojendra Lal admitted the defendant No.1 as an auction purchaser of 04 gondas 02 koras of land and he (plaintiff) has acquired 01 gonda land, for which he is claiming possession of that land. It also appears that, pursuant to that documentary evidence there has been delivery of possession, which is commonly known as “দখল দেওয়ানী” and this paper is Exhibit-'D'. This document proves that the plaintiff to the original suit took delivery of only one gonda land according to his prayer and the defendant obtained 04 gondas, 02 koras land in the suit holding. The certified copy of the final order of the Execution Case No.13 of 1967 is marked as Exhibit-`D(1)' dated 01.04.1968. This documentary evidence goes to show that the predecessor of the present petitioners who was the plaintiff to the original suit was given 01 gonda land and the defendant was given the rest 04 gondas 02 koras land pursuant to the auction sale by the concerned the then Sub-ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong. The Other Execution Case No.13 of 1967 was finally disposed of on full satisfaction without objection inasmuch as the connected Writ of D.P. under Order XXI, Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure duly executed [vide Exhibits D(1) and E].</u>

14. Having gone through the evidence on records I find that the predecessor-in-interest of the defendants Satish Chandra thereafter filed an application before the competent authority stating as to how he has acquired title and interest in the land, for correction of the B.S. khatian which was allowed in presence of Brojendra Lal, followed by recording of 01 gonda land in the name of Brojendra and 04 gondas, 02 koras land in the name of Satish Chandra, without any challenge (vide Exhibit 'C'). In that act of law; the entire previous proceedings were reflected.

15. On meticulous assessment of the evidence adduced from the sides of the respective parties I find that to substantiate the case of the plaintiff he has examined two witnesses. Between these 02 witnesses, P.W.1 is the plaintiff himself Brojendra Lal Chowdhury. From the testimony of the plaintiff it is apparent that the plaintiff admitted at a stage of his examination-in-chief that, pursuant to the auction dated 19.02.1968 he went into possession through court. It further appears that the plaintiff asserts that in the last part of August, 1978 the defendants tried to construct house in the vacant land and in spite of his protest the defendants have erected two houses therein. P.W.1 during his deposition in reply to a question from the side of the defendants admits that the defendant No.1 have dispossessed him after institution of the suit from the vacant land and he further admits that no amendment was sought for to that effect by him and it was not even informed to the trial court. The plaintiff states at a stage of his deposition that against the B.S. khatian he lodged objection, but his objection has been rejected. At a stage of his testimony the plaintiff admits that pursuant to the final order passed in Execution Case No.13 of 1967 (Exbt.-`D') they filed an application for possession and the certified copy of that application has been identified by the plaintiff Brojendra Lal. From his admission it was marked as exhibit-'E'. The plaintiff with regard to the quantum of the land; which is under his possession and being used by him as of his own homestead; failed to state anything. P.W.1 at a stage of his deposition testified that in the year 1968 he was a clerk of an Advocate Mr. Umesh Chandra Chowdhury and at the time of giving deposition he is also working as an Advocate's clerk of Advocate Mr. Bisheshor. The plaintiff testifies before the court that against the “দখল দেওয়ানী” no step was taken by him before any court of law.

16. P.W.2 Parimal Kanti Das has testifies in his examination-in-chief that he knows the parties and the suit land and in the year 1968 the plaintiff along with Satish Babu auction purchased the suit property jointly. This witness further testifies in his examination-in-chief that at the time of payment of money of auction Satish Babu called him and he has seen that the plaintiff handed over half auction money in the hand of Satish Babu and the total amount of the auction money was Tk.895/-. In the cross-examination P.W.2 testified that since 1952 he is an Advocate's Clerk. This witness in a reply to a question with regard to auction purchase frankly admitted that, besides the money he knows nothing about the auction.

17. On the contrary; D.W.1 Pronab Kumar Chakraborty who is the son of defendant No.1 deposed after the death of his father the defendant No.1 Satish Chandra Chakraborty. In support of their pleadings he testified that, Brojen Babu at the time of auction was a "kormachari" of his father Satish Chandra and he was entrusted to auction purchase on behalf of his father Satish Chandra Chakroborty and taking advantage of that, Brojen Babu committed breach of trust with his father and managed to insert his name along with the name of his (D.W.1) father. Subsequently; Brojen Babu admitted his misdeed and prayed for one gonda land to reside with his family members in the suit holding from his father and his father being pleased gave him (Brojen Babu) 01 gouda land.

18. The witness No.02 for the defendants is Kiron Sankar Chakraborty. This witness in his testimony testified before the Court that he knows the parties and the suit land. The plaintiff is residing in his present homestead since the year of liberation of Bangladesh. This witness further testified that it is not a fact that he is deposing falsely. The last witness is Sumita Chakraborty, who is the defendant No.5. This witness testifies in support of her registered sub-kabala deed executed and registered by the defendant No.1 in favour of her for 03 koras land in the disputed holding. This witness further testified that for her purchased land she paid rent which is Exhibit-B (1). D.W.3 further testified that the plaintiff use to possess 01 gonda land and the plaintiff has no other land in the disputed holding other than this 01 gonda land. During cross-examination from the side of the plaintiff this witness in a reply to a question testifies that in the year 1966 she came to Chittagong Town and since then she is residing in the present property and prior to her purchase her husband was a tenant under Satish Babu.

19. In the instant suit; it is evident to note that practically it is not denied from any corner that the suit land had been owning and possessing originally by the admitted owner of the property Monmohon Dutta who died leaving behind one son Nogendra Lal Dutta and wife Torongini Dutta. It is also an admitted position that in a Rent Suit the property was put to an auction and purchased by the auction purchaser. Lastly it was finally disposed of in Execution Case No.13 of 1967 on 01.04.1968 A.D. The `boynama' of the auction sale stands in the names of the plaintiff and the defendant no.1- in equal share. In this regard; it is the specific contention of the defendant that the plaintiff was the “কার্যকারক” of the defendant No.1 who was entrusted to auction purchase the suit land in favour of the defendant No.1 and taking advantage of that, the plaintiff managed his name inserted as one of the purchasers with the defendant in the boynama' which has been marked as Exhibit-'A'. The fact remains that, pursuant to boynama' there was delivery of possession and prior to that; admittedly the auction purchaser defendant along with the plaintiff jointly filed an application on 05.03.1968 in the 3rd Court of the then Sub-ordinate Judge, Chittagong under Order 21 Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The plaintiff as P.W.1 admitted the said application before the concerned court in connection with the auction purchase. In that application there was a recital, which reads as follows:

“আমরা ১/২ নং নিলাম খরিদ্দার প্রার্থিকগণ দাইকের নিম্ন তপশিলের স্থাবর সম্পত্তি ১০/১/৬৮ ইংরেজী তারিখে আদালতে প্রকাশ্যে নিলামে নিম্ন লিখিত মতে খরিদ করিয়া বয়নামা প্রাপ্তি মালিক হইয়াছি। আমরা প্রার্থিকার তপশিলের জমি নিম্ন লিখিত মতে দখল পাওয়ার আবশ্যক।

অতএব প্রার্থনা যে, নিম্ন তপসিলের দাইকের স্বতীয় সম্পত্তি নিম্ন লিখিত মতে আইনতঃ ২১ অর্ডার ৯৫ রুল মতে দখল দেওয়ার আদেশ হয়। ইতি-

তপশীল

১। মৌজা মাদার বাড়ী থানা ডবলমুরিং মহল ১৪৬৯৮ নং হাল ৯৬০৫ জিং কিমাং কাঠা ও ৩৪২৪ নং জিং বদু ও R.S. জরিপের ৪৪৯ নং খতিয়ানের ৩০৬৪ দাগের ও R.S. জরিপের ৫১৫ নং খতিয়ানের ৩০৬৪/৩২৫৭ দাগের আং P.S. জরিপের ১৬১৪ নং খতিয়ানের ৩৪৮৫ দাগের ও ১৬১৩ নং খতিয়ানের P.S. ৩৪৮৬ দাগের R.S. ও P.S. উভয়ের দাগের ৫।। কড়া জমির মধ্যে আমি ২নং নিলাম খরিদ্দার প্রার্থিকের আমরা ১/২ নং প্রার্থিক নিলাম খরিদ্দারের আপোষ মতে আমি ২নং প্রার্থিকের সর্ব দক্ষিণে চলাচল রাস্তার সংলগ্ন ১ এক গন্ডা তৎ উত্তরে আমি ১নং প্রার্থিক নিলাম খরিদ্দারের অবশিস্ট ৪।। চারিগন্ডা দুই কড়া সর্ব মোট ৫।। পাঁচ গন্ডা দুই কড়া জমি।”

20. The certified copy of this application which is an attested document from both the parties has been marked as Exhibit-' D'. Pursuant to that application the concerned court vide his order dated 01.04.1968 passed an order and in compliance of that order the process-server delivered possession. All these papers have been duly proved and after admission from the side of the plaintiff those have been exhibited. In this context; it is required to be mentioned that the plaintiff to the suit is an Advocate's Mohorar who supposed to be a well acquainted person having knowledge about auction and its subsequent proceedings upto the final order passed by the executing court.

21. The learned courts below after proper assessment of the relevant evidence on records and appreciation of law arrived at a concurrent decision that the claim of the plaintiff-petitioner is barred, inasmuch as he is stopped by law from claiming the suit property as prayed for in the schedule of the plaint from his side.

22. Section 20 and 21 of the Evidence Act, 1872 provides admission by persons expressly referred to by party to suit and proof of admissions, against persons making them, and by or on their behalf. Our Apex Court in the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar —vs.- Mahiuddin & others, VI BLD(AD) 224, opined admission between the parties made in another proceeding-such admission whether binds a party in a subsequent proceeding-Respondent's admission that he was a tenant under the appellant extops him from denying appellants' title in the suit premises. Admission by way of statements made in documents certified to be true copies by an authorized officer of the Government are admissible in evidence.

23. In the case of Birendra Chandra Saha —vs.- Sashi Mohan Saha, 27 DLR(SC)89, it was decided by their lordships that, admission is a substantive evidence.

24. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions referred to from the sides of the respective parties, consulting the same meticulously with the facts and circumstances along with the material evidence on records, I have the reason to inclined such a view that among the decisions referred to from the sides of the learned counsels, the case laws reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 224 have got nexus in our instant case because of its identical character. In the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar —vs. - Mahiuddin and others 6 BLD (AD) 224, it was held by their lordships in paragraph No.9 (quote):

"Mr. Asrarul Hossain has laid considerable stress on Exts. 4 and 4(a) which purportedly contains an admission of the respondent (defendant No. 1) that he was atenant under the appellant. These exhibits are certified copies of two applications of the respondent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) praying for settlement of the suit-premises from the Government, the ultimate owner. Both the appellant and the respondent (defendant No. 1) prayed for settlement from the Government in 1973 where upon two separate Cases were started which ended ultimately in favour of the appellant, obviously in view of the appellant's possessory right from Gagan Ali Bepari for a long time. The question raised here, however, is-not as to who got the settlement from the Government. In both these applications, Exts. 4 and 4(a), filed about six years after his father Kala Mia's death, the respondent (defendant No. 1) stated that he was a tenant of the appellant. Haji Abdus Sattar who by misrepresentation, had created the tenancy though he had no title, that because of this defect of of title, he was offering himself as a candidate for settlement in view of the fact that he had been running a cloth shop in the premises for a long time. This is a clear admission and estops him from denying the appellant's title in the premises. To wriggle out of this tight corner, he has contended that the documents Exts. 4 ctr 4(a) are not correct copies of his applications to the Revenue Authorities. The learned Single Judge has observed that these copies of the applications were not legally proved that they are private documents and further that attention of the respondent was not drawn to the statement contained in these applications, and as such the question of binding him with the statement therein does not arise. This observation, we find, got no legal or Actual basis. For these are certified copies of applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner for settlement, who after necessary endorsement, incorporated them into the record of the Settlement Case and issued certified copies thereof in accordance with law; the originals of the applications cannot be produced or obtained by anybody unless a Court calls for them. These certified copies were filed as exhibits in this suit in presence of the respondent who then raised objection, but the Court ignoring his objection marked them as exhibits- 4 and 4(a). Again, while deposing in Court as D. W. 1 he himself drew his attention to these documents stating in his examination-in-chief that these were not true copies of his applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner. In the circumstances, there was no necessity for drawing his further attention to them during cross-examination. As to the authenticity of these certified copies the respondent did not apply to the Court to lodge a complaint under section 195 Cr. P.C. against the appellant on a charge of forgery who produced or filed in evidence these documents in a judicial proceeding. Such a complaint may be filed under section 195(1)(c) Cr. P.G. even now if the respondent deres to move the Court for that purpose. These documents issued and certified to be true copies by an authorized officer of the Government are admissible in evidence. The statement contained therein as described above is admission within the meaning of section 20of the Evidence Act and the respondent is bound by his admission that he was a tenant of the appellant who allegedly got no valid title to the premises."

25. Apart from this; with regard to sale certificate in the case law reported in AIR (31) 1944 Nagpur 305, in the case of Degdulal Tilokchand Gangrade and another —vs.- Ramesharar Ramkaran and others, their lordships held that,

Sale certificate-It is merely prima facie evidence of title and not conclusive-Schedule of property in application for attachment, order directing sale and sale proclamation are the crucial documents to be seen.

The sale certificate is not conclusive. It a, fjords only prima facie evidence of title and it can always be shown that the sale certificate is wrong even when there is no ambiguity in it. A court sale is nothing but an offer and an acceptance, the offer being made by the Court in the sale proclamation. The drawing up of the sale certificate is only a ministerial act and not a judicial one, and so, if it does not correspond with what was offered for sale and purchased it is of no avail. The crucial documents are (a) the schedule of property in the application for attachment, (b) the order directing the sale and (c) the sale proclamation. [Not village in suit but some other village held was sold]; 41 Cal. 590 (P. C); 27 Born. 334 and (25); 12 A.I.R. 1925 Pat. 615, Bel.

26. From the above mentioned case laws the principles, which has enunciated by their lordships definitely lies against the case of the present petitioners and supports the opposite parties.

27. In the foregoing narrative as spelt out in the discussions and findings referred to above; I have the reason to draw such inference that the concurrent findings and decisions of both the courts below with regard to the right, title and interest of the present petitioners since their predecessor-in-interest Brojendra Lal Chowdhury is not proved by any tangible evidence, rather; the concurrent findings of facts arrived at by both the courts below is not warranted any interference of this Court in absence of any such misreading or non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Under the ambit of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure no such infirmity or non-consideration of material facts is noticed by which the impugned judgment and decree can be interfered with. Besides this; the matter of adjudication as already decided makes it clear that in the instant civil revision the plaintiff-petitioners have got no such merit by dint of which the Rule issued can be made absolute.

28. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The impugned judgment and decree dated 18.05.2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Chittagong in Other Appeal No.380 of 1990 disallowing the appeal and thereby affirming those of dated 31.05.1990 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Additional Court, Sadar, Chittagong in Partition Suit No. 25 of 1990 is hereby affirmed.

29. However; there will be no order as to costs.

30. Let a copy of the judgment along with the Lower Court's Record be sent down at once.

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and order dated the 31.7.79 passed by the High Court Division in S.M.A. No. 6 of 1970
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—The question raised in this appeal by special leave is whether the period of limitation under Article 182 of the Limitation Act for filing an application for execution of a decree runs from the date when the final decree was passed or from the date when the said decree was engrossed on stamped paper and signed by the judge, the intervening period being 12 years 5 months 22 days.

2. Facts of the case are as follows: Respondents got a preliminary decree on September 15, 1945 in Partition Suit No. 30 of 1938 of the Court of Munsif, Noakhali and the final decree was passed on November 30, 1954, but the decree was drawn and signed on May 22, 1965 when the requisite stamped paper was put in. Thereafter, on May 9, 1967 Title Execution Case No. 36 of 1967 was filed to which an objection was raised by the defendants-appellants under section 47, Civil Procedure Code taking a number of grounds the principal ground being that the execution case was barred by limitation as not having been filed within the period of three years from the date of the final decree which is November 30, 1954. The learned Munsif rejected this ground and dismissed the objection petition under section 47, Civil Procedure Code holding that limitation would start in this case from May 22, 1965 when the decree was drawn and signed. The learned Subordinate Judge in appeal, relying on the decision in Kishori Mohan Pal vs. Provash Chandra Mandal AIR 1924 Cal. 351, reversed the Munsif's order and held that though the decree was drawn and signed on May 22, 1965 it would bear the date of the passing of the final decree i.e. November 30, 1954 and that limitation would run from that date. The plaintiffs appealed, and the High Court Division, by the impugned order dated July 31, 1979, set aside the order of the lower appellate court and restored that of the trial court and directed that the execution proceeding should proceed. Special leave has been granted to see whether this order of the High Court Division is well founded in law in the circumstances as set out above.

<u>3. Mr. Abdul Wadud Miah, the learned Advocate, has appeared for the defendants-appellants. Mr. M.G. Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, has appeared for the plaintiff-respondents while Mr, M. H. Khondker, learned counsel has appeared as amicus curiae in order to assist the court in arriving at a correct decision on this question about which conflicting views have been expressed for over a long period. The question is what is the date of a decree for the purpose of putting it into execution or, for that matter for preferring an appeal there from. Period of limitation prescribed in Article 182 for filing an application for execution is three years from the date of decree. Order XX, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that "the decree shall bear the date the day on which the judgment was pronounced", i.e. date of the judgment will be the date of the decree. This tends to show that if the decree is not prepared and signed on the day on which the judgment is announced but is drawn and signed at a later date still it shall bear the date of the judgment. In the instant case final decree was passed on 30-11-54 but the decree was drawn and signed on 22-5-65. The decree could not be drawn and signed earlier as the required stamp-paper was not put in. A decree in a partition suit is an instrument of partition which is chargeable with stamp duty under article 45 of the Stamp Act, 1898, and unless it is duly stamped the decree is not admissible in evidence as provided in section 35 of the Stamp Act. The Privy Council held in Ram Rattan vs. Parma and 50 C.W.N. 367, "Unstamped memoranda of a partition which require to be stamped as constituting an instrument of partition cannot be admitted in evidence even for any purpose". Contention of Mr. A. W. Miah is that the plaintiff who got the final decree should have filed the execution case within the period of three years from 30-11-54 without waiting for the drawing and signing of the decree. Answer to this contention is that a decree cannot be enforced before it sees the light of the day. Decree cannot be prepared unless the required stamped-paper is supplied. But there is no law under which the decree-holder is bound to supply the stamped paper within a particular time for drawing up the decree. It, of course, lies in his interest to put in the stamp-paper for getting the decree drawn up and signed but he is not under any legal obligation to do so within a particular time. Similarly, the decree-holder is not required by any law to put in any application for a copy of the decree which has not yet come into existence, for a decree comes into existence, for practical purposes, only when it is engrossed on a stamped paper and signed by the Judge.</u>

4. Mr. M. H. Khondker has submitted that under Order XLI, rule 1, C.P. Code appear from a decree cannot be filed without a copy of the decree and that though the appellate court may at its discretion dispense with the copy of the judgment the court cannot dispense with the copy of the decree. Mr. Khondker is of the view that no application for execution of a decree can be filed without a copy of the decree. It is also not the duty of the court which has passed the decree to compel any party to put in the required stamped-paper within a particular time for drawing the decree. If the requisite stamped-paper is supplied by the party interested in the decree after long delay still the decree will have to be drawn and signed. In Raghubir Sahu vs. Ajodhya Sahu AIR 1945 Pat. 482, it has been held:

"There is no time limit prescribed by the statute for the engrossment of a partition decree on stamp of requisite value. Therefore, mere delay in engrossment of the decree on stamped paper of the requisite value will, not in any way affects the interests of the parties in respect of the properties though changes may have taken place in regard to the properties since the decree has been made".

In situations like this it is to be seen whether this period can be covered up by the period required for preparation of the decree.

5. Mr. M. H. Khondker has referred to a number of decisions in support of his view that the period of limitation for filing an application for execution of a decree runs from the day when it is drawn up and signed and that till the decree is drawn up and signed the suit itself remains pending. In Jotindra Mohan Tagore vs. Bajoy Chand Mahatap AIR 32 Cal. 483 it was held:

"A suit for partition, even when the report of the Commissioners is confirmed and a decree is directed to be drawn in accordance therewith, is a pending litigation until the Court signs the final decree  A decree for partition, to be operative, must be engrossed on stamped-paper as required by the Stamp Act, and until the Judge signs the decree so engrossed, it cannot be said that the suit has terminated; and an order directing a party to be added under section 32 of the Civil Procedure Code (1908) can be made in such a suit before it has actually terminated."

According to the principle laid down in that case it is the drawing and signing of the decree on a stamped-paper in a partition suit which concludes a suit and that announcement of the judgment is not enough and as such the two date though notionally the same, are different in fact. The Privy Council in Lachmi Narain Marwary vs. Balmalanid Marwary 29, C.W.N. 391 observed:

"After decree, it is open to any party to a suit, to whose interest it is that further proceedings be taken to initiate the supplementary proceedings in order to have the decree enforced, though in the ordinary case it is the Plaintiff who moves.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Mian has relied upon the decision in Kishori Mohan Pal vs. Provash Chandra Mondal AIR 1924 Cal 351, in which it was held by the Calcutta High Court: "The date of the decree under Art. 182 Limitation Act is the day on which the judgment is pronounced, and limitation begins to run from that date although no formal decree can be drawn up in a partition suit until paper bearing a proper stamp under Art. 45 of the Stamp Act is supplied to the Court". This view also found favour with the Karachi Bench of the West Pakistan High Court in East and West Steamship Company vs. Queensland Insurance Company, PLD, 1960, Kar. 840.

7. But the Pakistan Supreme Court dissented from this view and held in the case. of Government of West Pakistan vs. Niaz Mohammad, (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 236= PLD 1967, S.C. 271, that the Limitation under Article 156 of the Limitation Act runs from the date of the decree. In that case final decree was awarded by a judgment announced on May 30, 1964 and it was directed that the final decree would be prepared after collecting deficit court-fee stamps. The decree was prepared and signed on 1st September, 1964 when the deficit of of stamp duty was paid application for certified copy of the decree was made on October; 6, 1964 and the copy was delivered after three days and the appeal was instituted on November 28, 1964. It was contended that the appeal was barred by limitation as it was filed beyond 90 days from the date of the judgment and decree, May 30, 1964. The contention was overruled and it was held that the decree bears the date of the judgment only "notionally" and that the time which elapses between the announcement of the judgment, and the signing of the decree should be accommodated in the time requisite for obtaining a copy of judgment and the decree. Having drawn the distinction between the date of judgment and the date of decree their Lordships further observed:

"The relevant law appears clearly to distinguish between the judgment and the decree which follows upon it, and this distinction cannot be allowed to be obscured on assumptions, such as, that a decree "in a legal sense" comes into existence as soon as a judgment is pronounced, or that "in its essence" a decree is not a thing separable from the judgment."

<u>8. On a careful consideration of views expressed in the cases cited above, we are inclined to the view taken by the Pakistan Supreme Court as it appears to be based on realistic interpretation of the relevant provisions of law. A decree, before it is prepared, drawn and signed according to law, cannot be put into execution. The decree cannot be drawn except on a requisite stamped paper, but as there is no law compelling a person interested in the decree to supply stamp, paper within a particular period of time nor any provision to cancel or set aside the decree or dismiss the suit on this ground, the drawing of the decree may be delayed beyond the period of limitation for its execution. In such circumstance limitation will start from the date the decree is drawn and signed or it becomes executable.</u>

<u>In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
This revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 10-10-1994 and 16-10-94 respectively passed by Mr GR Basak, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 165 of 1984 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and decree dated 19-7-84 and 25-7-84 respectively passed by AKM Serajul Islam, Upazila Munsif now Assistant Judge Gournadi in Title Suit No. 352 of 1984, decreeing the Suit.

2. The opposite party No.1 as plaintiff on 1-1-79 instituted the suit being Title Suit No. 2 of 1979 in the Court of Munsif, 6th Court, Barisal for a decrees of specific performance of contract of sale regarding 0.81 acre of land as described in the schedule 'ka' of the plaint, subsequently the suit was transferred in the court of the Upazila Munsif Gournadi and renumbered as Title Suit No. 352 of 1984.

3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is as follows:

The properties appertained to SA Khatian Nos. 321 and 124 covering area of 0.81 acre of mouza Goila under PS Gournadi belonged to the plaintiff who transferred out the same in favour of the defendant No.1 vide deed dated 4-1-67 with a consideration of Taka 1200.00 but with the stipulation to recovery the same within 12 years and accordingly, the defendant No.1 on the same date executed and registered a deed of agreement in favour of the transferor (the plaintiff). That the plaintiff instituted Redemption Miscellaneous Case No. 36 A of 1974 before SDG (Sadar) Barisal in pursuance of President's Order 88 of 1972 and on 7-11-74 got an order accordingly. That defendant No.1 amicably handed over possession of the agreed land to the plaintiff. Thereafter in the month of Choitra, 1381 BS the plaintiff went to cultivate the land but confronted interruption from the defendant No. 2 with the utterance that he has purchased the suit land from defendant No. 1 and on inquiry defendant No. 1 also admitted it. Defendant No. 1 executed the said deed in favour of the defendant No. 2 illegally, unlawfully. Defendant No. 1 has no locus standi to sell out the suit land in favour of the defendant No. 2 and no right, title and interest has accrued with that kabala in favour of the defendant No. 2. Meanwhile the plaintiff remained silent as President's Order 88 of 1972 was declared void ab initio by a judgment of this court. The plaintiff repeatedly requested defendant Nos.1 and 2 to execute and register Kabala deed as per terms and conditions agreed upon on acceptance of the consideration money but on the 13th day of Agrahayan 1385 BS the defendants finally turned down the proposal. Hence, the suit.

4. Added defendant Nos 4-8 contested in the suit upon filing a joint written statement wherein they denied the right, title and interest of the plaintiff contending that plaintiff sold out the interest of his agreement in favour of defendant No. 2 Salamat with a consideration of Taka 2500.00 on 16-11-70. Defendant No.1 Abdul Mannan sold out the suit land in favour of the defendants by dint of a kabala 17-9-69 AD and inducted possession of the same with them. That defendant No. 2 became insane and from 1971 his whereabouts are unknown. That the plaintiff has got no locus standi to file the suit. That the plaintiff intentionally did not state about selling out his interest of the agreement in favour of Salamat Ali (defendant No. 2). That the averment of surrender of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff by the defendant No. 1 and the interference by the defendant No. 2 are false, frivolous, concocted and got up story.

5. For the aforesaid reasons the defendants prayed for dismissal of the suit.

6. In the trial Court the plaintiff examined 3 witnesses and defendants examined 2 witnesses in support of their respective cases. After conclusion of the trial, the trial Court by the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-7-84 and 25-7-84 respectively decreed the suit.

7. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant Nos. 4-8 as appellants preferred Title Appeal No. 165 of 1984 in the Court of the learned District Judge Barisal which was ultimately heard by the learned. Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal who by his judgment and decree dated 10-10-94 and 16-10-94 respectively dismissed the appeal.

8. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the said Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge 1st Court Barisal in Title Appeal No. 165 of 1984 the defendant Nos. 4-8 as petitioners have filed and moved the present revisional application.

9. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners has submitted that the plaintiff transferred his land to the defendant No. 2 Salamat Ali Sheikh but suppressing the fact the plaintiff instituted the suit and, as such, the plaintiff did not come in the court with clean hands and he is not entitled to get decree.

10. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner that Sonamuddin predecessor of defendant Nos. 4-8 was a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration and that he has no knowledge about the deed of alleged reconveyonce.

11. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the plaintiff transferred the suit land to the defendant No. 1 with an agreement to recovery the same within 12 years and, as such, the plaintiff instituted Redemption case before the SDC (Sadar), Barisal in pursuance of President's Order 88 of 1972 and on 7-11-74 got an order in favour of him. So subsequent suit for specific performance of contract is not maintainable.

12. It has been further submitted that Ext. 1 (a) of the defendants is the kabala deed dated 16-11-70 executed by the plaintiff in favour of the defendant No. 2 and the same was found forged by the learned trial Court but the learned appellate Court considering the evidence on record held that the suit deed is not forged, so the plaintiff's case for specific performance of contract of sale is not maintainable.

13. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners that the court of appeal below with erroneous findings reached to a wrong decision occasioning failure of justice.

14. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1, has submitted that the plaintiff transferred his property to defendant No. 1 with an agreement for reconveyonce within 12 years for specific performance of contract of sale regarding 0.81 acre of land as described in the schedule 'Ka' of the plaint and the suit filed by the plaintiff was quite maintainable.

15. It has been further submitted by Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party that it was true that he filed Redemption Miscellaneous Case No. 36 A of 1974 before the SDO (Sadar), Barisal and got the order in his favour and amicably he got possession from the defendant No. 1 but when defendant No. 2 and others were creating obstruction in his peaceful possession, the plaintiff has filed the present suit and in the facts and circumstances of the case the suit is quite maintainable. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party that the Kabala dated 4-1-67 was executed by the plaintiff in favour of the defendant No. 1 and on the same date defendant No. 1 executed an Ekrarnama (Agreement) in favour of the plaintiff with a condition to recovery the suit land in favour of the plaintiff within 12 years and, as such, the kabala dated 4-1-67 in favour of the defendant No. 1 by the plaintiff was not an out and out sale rather it was a mortgage deed and for violating the terms of the Ekrarnama (Agreement) by defendant Abdul Mannan having transferred the suit land to Sunamuddin (the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 4-8) is of no value and defendant No. 1 Abdul Mannan had no right and title to transfer the suit land to Sonamuddin and Sonamuddin acquired no title by purchasing from Abdul Mannan by the Kabala dated 17-9-69, Ext. 1 of the defendants.

16. Mr Mansur Habib further submitted that the appellate Court only reversed the finding of the trial Court in respect of the kabala dated 16-11-70, Ext. 1 (a) of the defendant found to be forged one by the trial Court is not proper finding of reversal as the court of appeal below relied on the averments in paragraph 2 of the plaint which is not a proper one and in this respect the finding of the appellate Court is of an erroneous view, which is liable be to set aside and the trial Court actually has given reasons for saying the deed dated 6-11-70 Ext. 1(a) of the defendants as forged. by saying that the stamp of the said deed dated 16-11-70 has been purchased on 22-3-69, it has been executed on 15-4-70 and it has been placed for registration firstly on 4-7-70 and it was registered on 24-11-70 (under section 75 of the Registration Act vide order dated 16-11-70) and moreover, the ink of executions of the said kabala dated 16-11-70 are different and with those reasons the trial Court came to the correct finding that the aforesaid kabala dated 16-11-70 Ext. 1(a) of the defendants was forged.

17. Mr Mansur Habib finally submitted that when Sunamuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos 4-8 (the present petitioners), found that the kabala in his name dated 17-9-69 (Ext. 1 of the defendants) would be of no values they created a forged kabala dated 15-11-70 in favour of Salamat Ali (the defendant No. 2) and by the aforesaid 2 deeds dated 17-9-69, Ext 1 of the defendants and the forge kabala dated 16-11-70 Ext. 1 (a) of the defendants created no rights, title in favour of defendants and the trial Court rightly decreed the suit and the appellate Court though differed in one point that the kabala dated 4-7-70 (registered on 16-11-70) was not forged one, still, in fact, the appellate Court agreed with the conclusion of the trial Court and has rightly dismissed the appeal and upheld the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif.

18. I have heard both the sides at length, perused the revisional application and the judgments and decrees passed by the learned Munsif as well as the learned Subordinate Judge and I have gone through the record of the case.

19. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, in support of his argument has referred to 39 DLR 322 and has argued that reversing the finding of the trial Court is incumbent upon the lower appellate Court to discuss the evidence led by the parties on the points upon which the findings of trial Court are given, reasons by the trial Court may be accepted as good one and the confirming judgment need not go into every piece of judgment. Lower appellate Court when either confirming or reversing the judgment of the trial Court it is incumbent upon the lower appellate Court to discuss the evidence led by the parties on the points upon which the findings of the trial Court were given and to advert to the reasonings of the trial Court for such findings.

20. In the instant case in which the judgment of the trial Court has been affirmed by the court of appeal below in fine, differing only on the point that whether a particular document dated 16-11-70 was forged or not, I find that the reasons by both the courts below are concurrent.

21. Mr Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate, also referred to 39 DLR (AD) 70 and has submitted that sale deed in question is evidence of outright sale of the suit land by the plaintiff for a consideration of Taka 1200.00 and it contains that the executed sale deed was an out and out sale.

22. In the facts and circumstances of the case I find that the above 2 decisions do not help the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners.

23. On the other hand, Mr Mansur Habib appearing for the plaintiff- opposite party, has referred to 46 DLR 96 and has submitted that the restriction created in Ekrarnama (Agreement) is quite valid and in the instant case by the Ekrarnama an obligation has been created and annexed to the ownership of transfer under section 40 of the Act (Transfer of Property Act) and that is why the interest created by this transaction cannot be said to be absolute one which is required as a pre-condition for application of section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act.

<u>24. In view of the above discussion in the decision I am in agreement with the submission of Mr Mansur Habib that the sale deed dated 4-1-67 made by the plaintiff in favour of the defendant No. 1 was not an absolute one rather it was annexed to the Ekrarnama (Agreement) in question and the defendant No. 1 is bound by the Ekrarnama and if any kabala has been made from defendant No. 1 Abdul Mannan Khalifa to defendant Md. Sonamuddin (predecessor of the defendant-petitioners) by the Ext. 1 of the defendants that has not given any bonafide title to the said Md Sonamuddin or his successors and, as such, neither Sonamuddin nor his successors (the defendant Nos 4-8) have acquired any ostensible ownership in the disputed lands and they cannot be said as bonafide purchaser for value with consideration and again by Ext. 1(a) dated 16-11-70 whether defendant No. 2 Salamat Ali acquired any title is a matter of great doubt as the trial Court with reasonings as discussed above found the said document dated 16-11-70 to be a forged one and for that the trial Court has given sufficient reasons. Though the court of appeal below has differed in this respect but ultimately decreed the suit dismissing the appeal being in agreement with the trial Court in other respects of the suit.</u>

25. I also find that signature of Syed Ali in Ext. 1(a) of the defendants i.e. kabala dated 16-11-70 has not been compared at the instance of the defendants whether it is a genuine one and I find that the defendant have failed in their duty to prove the signature of Syed Ali in the aforesaid Kabala dated 16-11-70 in favour of defendant No. 2 Salamat Ali and the defendants cannot get any benefit of the document Ext. 1(a) dated 16-11-70 (of the defendants).

26. The court of appeal below rightly found that in the instant case we do not find any iota of documents or evidence that Sonamuddin made any inquiry or search before purchasing land by way of kabala deed dated 17-9-69 AD. So, I cannot decide that Sonamuddin was a bonafide purchaser for value without notice, Moreover, the kabala deed in the name of his son Salamat Ali Sheikh dated 14-11-70 also speaks a volume."

27. And I find that the court of appeal below after application of mind has correctly dismissed the appeal and from the facts and circumstances as discussed above. I am in agreement with the submission of the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party that when Sonamuddin found that the kabala dated 17-9-69 Ext. I of the defendants would be of no value created a forged kabala dated 16-11-70 Ext. 1(a) (of the defendant).

28. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, has also referred to 15 DLR 634 and has argued that,

Agreement to repurchase does not create interest in land but creates an obligation annexed to ownership thereof."

And Mr Mansur Habib further submits that benefit arising out of a contract of repurchase is assignable. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate, further submitted that the mortgage property could not be transferred by the defendant No. 1 (Abdul Mannan) in any way and defendant Md Sonamuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 4-8, has not acquired any title by purchasing the mortgaged property from said Abdul Mannan.

29. In view of the discussion made above I find that the defendant-petitioners did not acquire any title either by the aforesaid kabala dated 17-9-69 Ext. 1 (of the defendant) or by the kabala dated 16-11-70 Ext. 1 (a) of the defendants.

In the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that when the plaintiff found that by the order he got in his favour from SDO (North) in Redemption Case No. 36 A of 1974 dated 7-11-74 to clear the doubt in his right and title on the disputed land as mentioned above he has filed the suit which is quite maintainable and I find no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the court of appeal below.

Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
