Trustees of the Port of Chittagong ------Appellant
Vs.
K. Mahbub Hossain & ors ------Respondent
full_judgment:
Syed Mohammad Ali, J.—This appeal is at the instance of defendant No. 1, the Trustees of the Port of Chittagong against the Judgment and decree dated 29.3.75 passed by Mr. Bazlur Rabman. Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Money Suit No. 130 of 1972. The respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Money Suit No. 130 of 1972 in the Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for satisfaction of his claim amounting to Taka 14,108.22 paisa as market price of the Car and interest by way of compensation at the rate of 10% per annum from the date of institution of the suit till recovery.

2. The plaintiff alleged inter alia in the plaint that he was deputed to England by the then East Pakistan Government for training under the Colombo Plan for one year from 28.9.69 to 23.9.70. Out of his foreign exchange savings in U.K. the plaintiff purchased a Volkswagen 1200 Sedan 1971 Model Car through defendant No. 3 namely Messers Modern Motors Ltd. who happened to be the sole distributors of Volkswagen in Pakistan It was agreed between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 that the plaintiff would pay the costs and freight for the said Car direct to the manufacturers in West Germany but the plaintiff would pay insurance charge in. cured by defendant No. 3 to insure the Car covering all necessary risk and the defendant No. 3 would arrange clearance of the car on arrival at Chittagong and would deliver to the plaintiff in ready and worthy condition.

3. In pursuance of the agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3, the plaintiff remitted a sum of D. M. 4,900 being the C & F, Chittagong value of the aforesaid car to the defendant No. 3's principal in West Germany with due intimation to defendant No. 3. Accordingly one Volkswagen Car covered by invoice No. 16323 dated 21-10.70 was shipped at the Port Hamburg per S. S. Trafalgar for delivery at the port of Chittagong and was consigned to defendant No. 3 under Bill of Lading No. 11 dated 31-10-70. The said ship arrived at the port of Chittagong on or about 3-2-71 and the said car was discharged at the Chittagong Port on 6-2-71 under the care and custody of the defendant No. 1 as statutory bailee. The plaintiff paid all necessary dues for clearance of the car in suit and to deliver the same to the plaintiff.

4. The defendant No. 4 namely Messrs. Ahmed Shippers and Traders is authorised Customs Clearing and Forwarding Agent at the Chittagong Port for the defendant No. 3. The defendant No. 3 by letter dated 19.3.71 informed the plaintiff that due to abnormal situation and other difficulties the car of the plaintiff was not cleared till then. On further enquiry the defendant. No. 3 for the first time by their letter dated 25.5.71 informed the plaintiff that due to the alleged continuous disturbances in Chittagong the car of the plaintiff could not be cleared and that car was not traceable and it might have been taken by the defence service people.

5. The plaintiff made repeated demands to defendant No. 1 for delivery of the car or for compensation but without any effect. The plaintiff ultimately served one notice on 22-4-72 under section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act upon the defendant No. 1 who received the said notice on 24.4.72 but in spite of long expiry of the period of notice the defendant No. 1 neither delivered the car nor paid compensation of the lost car. The defendant No. 1 by its letter dated 26.9.72 repudiated the claim of the plaintiff alleging that many car etc were missed from the port area during the alleged abnormal condition from 24.3.71 to 6.12.71 and that the Pakistani Army and other miscreants took away many cars etc, to Karachi and other destination. The car was lost due to negligence, carelessness of defendant No. I and its officers and staff. The car could not be taken away by anybody from the port which is a protected area without the connivance of the defendant No. 1 and its officers and staff the defendant No. 1 is therefore liable to compensate the loss at the plaintiff.

6. It was stated in the plaint that the defendant No. 3 was responsible for the clearance of the car in suit in due time of their own risk and responsibility. The plaintiff made all necessary payment to defendant No. 3 as required by them by 21-12-70. It transpires that the defendant No. 3 appointed defendant No. 4 as clearing agent for clearance of the car from the Chittagong Port and the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 were required to take prompt action for clearance of the car when all payments required to be made by the plaintiff were paid to defendant No. 3 on 21.12.70. If necessary action would have been taken by defendant No. 4 in due time, there could not be any loss of the car. The defendant No. 3 or 4 were negligent and the loss of the car was due to their negligence. In arranging for clearance of the car from the Chittagong Port in due time. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant No. 2 Sadharan Bima Corporation with whom the car was in sure covered risk of loss of the car as per their open policy No. 5-230122-34 dated 22-1-69 read with endorsement dated 23-2-71. The plaintiff claimed that the loss of the car was covered by policy issued by the defendant No. 2 who is bound to indemnify the loss of the plaintiff due to loss of the car under the terms and conditions of the policy.

7. The plaintiff further alleged that he purchased and imported the car in suit for his personal use. Market value of the car at the relevant time was Taka 20,000/- and the present market value of the said car is much more than Taka 30,000/-. Due to the loss of the car the plaintiff has sustained a loss of Taka 20,000/- which was the market value at the relevant time.

The plaintiff got refund of the custom duty etc. amounting to Taka 5,891,78. So by adjustment of refund of custom duty the plaintiff suffered not loss of Taka 14,108.22. The plaintiff lodged claim against the defendant and made repeated demand for settlement of the claim but in vain. The defendant No. 1 specifically repudiated claim of the plaintiff and as such he has been compelled to file the suit.

8. The plaintiff in his plaint has shown that the cause of action of the suit arose first on the date of discharge of suit car on 6-2-71, and on the date of first information of the loss of the car on 25-5-71, on all dates of demand, on the date of service of notice upon the defendant No. 1 under section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act on 24-4-72, and on the date of repudiation of the claim on 26-9-72 at the Chittagong Port premises.

9. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 (Port Trust and the New Mampalife Insurance Co.) by filing separate written statements. The defendant Nos. 3 and (Modern Motors Ltd, and M/S Ahmed Shippers and Traders) also contested the suit by filing joint written statement.

10. The defendant No. 3 and 4 in their joint written statement contended inter alia that the plaintiff having obtained refund of custom duty is not entitled to go the compensation from them, that the suit is not triable in this court but in Norwejan, Swedish or Denish Court and they denied the allegation of the plaintiff that there was ample time to clear the car from Chittagong port. They also denied that the plaintiff has suffered any loss due to their negligence. Hence they are not responsible for the loss either jointly or separately. They also challenged the price of the car at the relevant time. Defendant No. 3 is the indented and the defendant No. 4 is the clearing agent, that due to the want of original bill of lading the car could not be taken delivery of from the Port Authority. On various correspondence with the consigner and the Steamer Company it could not be recovered. Ultimately the car was found to be missing. The Steamer Company agreed to accept Bank guarantee on 27.3.71 and thereafter the situation was such that the car could not be taken delivery of. They asserted that they tried their best to take delivery as quickly as possible but could not be taken delivery of for want of original bill of Lading on the refusal of the Steamer Company to accept Bank Guarantee and abnormal situation in the paralised port beyond the control of the defendants. They also denied any negligence on their part.

11. The defendant No. 2 in their written statements denied any manner of liability in respect of the alleged loss of the car under the policy in question. The alleged loss of the car is not covered by the policy. The relief if any for the loss could be had if at all is against the former Pakistan Insurance Corporation. It was further asserted that Insurance Corporation is not responsible for the loss and if this defendant is found to be liable, that would be to the extent of Taka 6,370/- that is the value of the car shown in the policy.

12. The defendant No. 1, the Trustee of the Port of Chittagong in their witness statements contended that the suit is not maintainable, that the alleged notice under Section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act is not a proper and valid notice, the suit is barred by limitation and that there is no cause of action against this defendant. The defendant No. I denied any liability for the alleged loss for the non-delivery of the said consignment. The entire port area and the cargo were under absolute control of the occupation forces and non-local and under the abnormal condition and circumstances prevailing beyond the control of the port administration at that time. During the war of liberation many cars, jeeps, trucks and buses etc. and other imported consignments had been missing from the port area. It is common knowledge that the Pak army and the allied miscreants took away many of those vehicles to Karachi and other unknown destinations and all efforts to locate such vehicles hardly met with success. The car obviously was the victim of the circumstances and the plaintiff was informed accordingly. The defendant asserted that there was no negligence or carelessness on the part of the staff of this defendant and no loss occurred for any fault on the part of the present port administration.

13. In the suit before the trial court four issues were framed which are as follows:-

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the suit barred by limitation?

3. Is the plaintiff entitled to get a decree for money? If so to what extent and against whom?

4. What relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled to?

The plaintiff and the defendant filed certain exhibits. The plaintiff examined himself as P.W. 1 this case. The defendant No. 1 examined one witness namely D W. 1 Gafur. The defendant No. 3 examined one witness namely D.W. 2 N. R. Das. The defendant No. 4 also examined one witness namely D.W. 3 Nurul Islam.

14. Upon a consideration of the evidence and other material on record, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 were negligent and due to their negligence the car was not taken delivery of. As such defendant No. 3 and 4 liable for the loss sustained by the plaintiff. He also found that the car was discharged at the port of Chittagong in the care of defendant No. 1. He could not rely upon ext. A and B filed by the defendant No. 1 and found that the defendant No. 1 was also responsible for the missing of the car. The learned Subordinate Judge further found that the defendant No. 2 is not responsible in any way for the loss of the car and as such be decreed the suit in part against defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 for Taka 4,930/. with costs and C & F value for the disputed car interest at the rate of 10% upon the said decrital amount pendent elite till realisation from defendant No. 1.

Being dissatisfied with and aggrieved by the said Judgment and decree dated 29.3.75 passed by the trial court in the said Money Suit No. 130 of 1972, the defendant No. 1 has preferred this appeal.

15. Mr. Moqbul Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for Mr. Muzammel Huq, the learned Advocate for the appellant argues that the learned trial court should have found that the notice under section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act is not proper notice and that the suit is barred by limitation. No further argues that in view of Section 50, Sub-section 2, the claim of the plaintiff is not maintainable, that the trial court failed to note that the delivery of the car was not taken within 5 days of the landing of the consignment and as such the defendant No. 1 was not at all liable. He has further argued that the trial court having failed to note that the port was during the disturbed period under the occupation of the Pak army and as such the alleged loss has not been caused due to the negligence of the port employees.

16. In this case the plaintiff as P.W 1 has, in his deposition stated that he paid clearing charges amounting to Taka 5,500/- on 21.12.70. The car was landed under the car and custody of defendant No. 1 on the 5th/6th Feb, 1971. The defendant No. 4 was appointed by defendant No. 3 as clearing agent. He stated that he made correspondences with defendant No. 3 and 4 for delivery of the car. But by letter dated 25.5.71 defendant No. 3-4 informed him that due to disturbance in the country the car could not be taken delivery and the said car was not traceable in the said port area. Subsequently he received information that the delivery order could not be issued as the defendant No. 3 did not receive the original Bill of Lading. He stated that he laid claim after the defendant No. 1 repudiated that the car was not traceable. He issued notice upon defendant No. 1 under section 109 of the Port Act. He stated that he sustained loss amounting to Taka 14,108.22. Defendant No. 1 specifically did not inform him as to the fate of the said car. In cross examination by defendant Nos. 3 and 4 this witness stated that at the moment he had no tally sheet or landing certificate with him. This witness admitted that he had no knowledge of the formation to be observed in case of delivery of care from the jetty. This witness admitted that he got back the custom duty.

17. D.W. 1 Abdul Gafur on behalf of defendant No. 1 is his deposition stated that he was Jetti Inspector in 1971 from 2nd March to 24th March. He stated that activities of this port were controlled by Messers M.R. Siddiqul, Commandar Mamtaz and Brigadier Majumdar. Civil employees of the Port Trust did not attend their duties at that time. The civil employees began to resume their duties after direction by Radio in April, 1971. Still Port was being operated. The suit car landed into the cars of the Port Tres Building was found missing. He proved Ext. A; the statement of missing car (F. shed). He also proved Ext. B. He stated that they informed the parties for the missing car. Defendant No. 4 filled shed release order for delivery of the suit car for the first time on 23.3.71 which is marked Ext. C. The delivery order filed on 24.3.71 is marked Ext. D. This witness further admitted that they tried diligently to find out the suit car but in vain. In his cross-examination by defendant Nos. 3 and 4 this witness stated that lefty Superintendent of the relevant time was still in service and the staff of the F: Shed were available then. Delivery order was beins issued on production of shipping documents including the original Bill of Lading. From 2nd March, 1971 they started non-cooperation movement. This witness denied the suggestion that they have created Ext. A and B for the purpose of the suit. In cross-examination by the plaintiff this witness stated that he was Jetty Asst. Superintendent of claim since March, 1972. Before that he was Jetty Inspector incharge of court cases. The suit car was landed in the Jetty on 6.2.72. He further stated that they have nothing to show that the car was not available up to 24.3.71. They made missing report if and when consignee endorsed for not found and the cargo was lost by theft etc. In the instant case nobody endorsed. On 12.7.71 Shed Officer made missing report. There was an inventory of missing and available good of the port at the relevant time.

18. Ext. A. is the missing report. He admits they have not filed any document to show that they made any missing report earlier than Ext. A. The endorsement of Ext. A were not signed by any officer. Ext. A, with endorsement were over written by hand but they were not initialed. He cannot say who and where Ext. A and B were prepared. He filed Ext. A and B. etc. on the date of his deposition i.e. 18.3.75. They had no document to show that the said document was sent to the traffic Manager. They were directed to resume duties by 21st April, 1971. This witness was Inspector-in-charge of court cases before March, 1972 and from the evidence of this witness it appears that the Jetty Superintendent and the staff of the 'F' shade at the relevant time are available but they have not been produced to depose in this case. So, this witness is not a competent witness to depose about what happened at the relevant time in the port area in respect of the occurrence taking place in 'F' shade. According to the evidence of this witness there is no inventory of missing goods earlier than Ext. A which was not signed by any officer and that was over written by hand without any initial and that document found light of the day only on 18.3.75 for the first time and this witness could not say who prepared Ext. A and B. The learned Subordinate Judge who tried the case has rightly held that these Exts. A and B were prepared for the purpose of the suit. This witness has not been corroborated by any other oral evidence and he has not proved that the suit car was available before 24.3.71 and it was found missing after the civil staff resumed their duties on the 21st April, 1971. Therefore the plea taken by defendant No. 1 that the suit car might have been taken away to Karachi or to some other destination by the Pak Army or non-locals is not tenable.

19. The D.W. 2 Mr. N.R. Das was examined on behalf of defendant No. 3. In his deposition he stated that he was in-charge of the accounts of the defendant. They did not get the official documents of the car in suit because of the port strike at the relevant time. They got the duplicate document from the plaintiff and handed over the same to the clearing Agent on 16.2.71. Delivery order was not passed by the Shipping Company for want of original documents. They agreed to furnish security on the basis of duplicate document. They got the delivery order on 22.3.71. They could not get the delivery of the car on 23.3.71 as it was a holiday and there were disturbances there. During Pakistan period no car could be imported worth more than Taka 5,000/-. This witness admits that they handed over shipping documents to clearing Agent on 16.2.71. Delivery order was issued against their guarantee.

20. D W. 3 Md. Nurul Islam is an employee of defendant No. 4. He stated that he was engaged as clearing Agent by defendant No. 4. The defendant No. 3 could not give him any original document in spite of repeated requests. The defendant No. 3 agreed to furnish the security to the Steamer Company who did not agree to accept the same. They presented the delivery order on 24.3.71, but due to disturbances they could not take delivery order. Minimum one week is necessary to release any consignment if original documents are available. In cross-examination of the plaintiff this witness stated that they did not receive the original Bill of lading. But they received original of other documents before taking delivery order. They paid custom duties on 27.2. 71. They came to know on 16.27.1 that the original Bill of Lading was not available. On a consideration of the evidence of these two witnesses it app. ears that they could not get the clenreonce of the car due to non-availability of the original Bill of Lading. After instruction from defendant No. 3 and on furnishing guarantee they were given the delivery order on 22.3.71. Thereafter due to disturbances they could not get the clearance of the Car in suit and the car was not available for delivery which was intimated to the plaintiff by this defendant on 25.5.71. It is the admitted fact, even admitted by the defendant No. 1 that cargo was discharged in the care of the defendant No. I. It was the responsibility of defendant No. 1 as bailee. Therefore it cannot be said that these defendant Nos. 3 and 4 are liable for the loss of the car found by the trial Court.

21. It appears from ext. 2 dated 16.3.72 written by the plaintiff to the clearing agent, the defendant No. 3 wherein he stated that clearing agent tried to say once that for want of the original Bill of Lading the delay was caused. Similarly United Liner Agencies Ltd. in their letter to the plaintiff dated 11.12.72 (Ext. 5(a) informed the plaintiff in clearing the car in suit from the port, the delay, if any, may have occurred in obtaining delivery order from them owing to the non-receipt of original Bill of Lading from the supplier. In the letter written by the plaintiff to the defendant No. 3 ext. 5(a) dated 15,6.71 the plaintiff stated that he has already paid to the defendant No. 3 the custom duty and clearance on 21.12.70 and that other documents are always ready for production. So, from all these exts it appears that the original Bill of Lading was not available with the defendant No. 3 and 4. So, in view of the oral and documentary evidence in this respect, it can safely be concluded that the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 are not liable for the alleged loss of the car in suit. If the plaintiff would have incurred any loss by way of demurrage or paying other taxes or ware-house charges, the plaintiff can realise that amount from these defendants for their negligence and that aspect cannot be gone into this suit. Here the main question is the liability of the bailee. Unless the bailee proves affirmatively that it has discharged the duty as bailee it is liable for any loss of the Cargo.

22. Now as regards the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the suit is barred by limitation Mr. Makbul Ahmed during his argument could not show or point out anything from the notice that the notice was not served or that notice was not a proper notice as contemplated under Section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act. The learned Advocate strenuously argued that the plaintiff knew about the arrival of the Cargo and the discharge of the Cargo with the defendant No. 1 and that the plaintiff had definite know-ledge of the loss of the car from defendant No. 3 on 25.5.71 and that therefore from that date this suit is barred by limitation.

23. Mr. M.A. Jalil the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent submits that in view of the facts and circumstances of the case the suit is not barred by limitation. In this connect the learned Advocate cited before us the case of Chittagong Port Authority Vs. Md. Ishaque and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 364 in support of his contention.

24. It appears from ext. 5(q), a letter dated 25.5.71 written by the defendant No. 3 to the plaintiff wherein the plaintiff was in-formed that on enquiry from the clearing agent the defendant No. 3 has been informed that the suit car is not traceable in the port and that it might have been taken away by the defence service people. This letter gives preliminary information that clearing agent on completing formalities could not locate the suit car. But from Ext. A(2), a letter dated 6.7.71 written by the plaintiff to the Chairman of the Port of Trust of the Port of Chittagong. It appears that the plaintiff intimated to him that the plaintiff has been informed that his imported car reached the port in perfectly good condition but soon after conclusion of formalities by Custom Clearance they found that the suit car is not available in the Jetty for clearing. Thereafter on receipt of the notice dated 24.3.71 under Section 109 of the Chittagong Port. Act by the plaintiff to the defendant No. 1, the Port authority by its letter Ext. A(3) dated 17.7.7)119.7.11 informed the plaintiff that it has come to light that many trucks, buses etc. have been missing from the Port and suit car also appears to be the victim of such circumstances. Investigation was said to be gill in progress regarding the missing of things from the part which is a protected Area. On completion of investigation reference was likely to follow. Thereafter as per letter or Ext. A(4) dated 26.9.72 written by defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff, the plaintiff was informed that Pak Army and other miscreants took away the vehicles from the part. The car in question was said to be the victim of such circumstances. From Ext. A(3) it appears that the defendant No. 1 did not deny his liability but tried to give an indication to the plaintiff that they were investigating to locate the suit car and ultimately by Ext. A (4) dated 26.9.72 they have tried to say the finality of their effort, The plaintiff filed 'the suit showing the cause of action considering this letter as the date of repudiation of the liability of defendant No. 1 as a Bailee. So on consideration of these materials read with the evidence of D.W. 1 we are of the view that the plaintiff gave the notice in time and the suit is not barred by limitation. In this regard Subsection (2) of section 109 may be quoted which runs as follows:—

"Every such suit shall be commenced within six months next after accrual of the right to sue and not after-wards".

25. Sub-section (1) of section 109 of the said Act provides for a notice in writing to give jurisdiction to the court to try the suit and unless that notice is proved the court shall dismiss the suit. He will not proceed with the trial of the suit, but Subsection (2) deals with the period of limitation.

26. From a reading of this sub-section (2) of section 109 of the said Act it appears that the suit shall be commenced within six months next after the accrual of right to sue and not afterwards. In the case of the Chittagong Port Authority Vs. Sadharan Bima Corporation reported in B.C.R. 82 (SD) page 4 it has been observed that the expression accrual of the right to sue as used in Section 109 (2) of the Chittagong Port Act means the accrual of cause of action and that the plaintiff will be entitled to add the notice period under sub-section (1) of section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act to the period of limitation prescribed under sub-section (2) of the said Section 109. So we are inclined to hold that in the present case the right to sue accrues from the actual date of knowledge of the loss of the car. In this particular case the right to sue accused as soon as the defendant No. 1 who informed the plaintiff that their last attempt has failed on 26,9.72 vide Ext. A(4). Therefore we do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant so far as the question of bar of limitation under section 109 atilt Chittagong Port Act is concerned.

28. Mr. Makbul Ahmed next contends that the suit car was missing during the disturbed period. It appears that from the 2nd March, 1971 to 24th March, 1971 the operation of the port was being directed by Messers M. R. Siddique and others but thereafter the Pakistani Army took control of the port activities and the defendant No. 1 could not produce any scrap of paper to show that the suit car was missing soon thereafter. Civil employees resumed their duties by 21st April, 1971. In this connection the defendant No. 1 has tried to produce Ext. A., the missing report of the vehicle of F. Shade and present position of the missing car by Ext. B Needless to mention more than what has already been observed earlier in this connection. The said exts. A & B are not signed by any officer of the port. There were over-writings and those overwritings were not in tailed by any officer and D. W. 1 could not say by whom and where those exits were prepared. Those were produced for the first time when this D.W. 1 was produced in court. We have observed earlier that this D.W. 1 was Inspector in-charge of the court cases at the relevant time. The officers who dealt with the matter are available but they have not been produced and this witness is not a competent witness to depose regarding the facts about which he has got no knowledge. Apart from that this witness in his deposition has not said &single word about the missing of the car or non-availability of the car soon after the civil staff resumed their duties. The alleged lists were prepared in July 1971 long after the strike ceased to exist.

29. Mr. M. A. Jalil the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent on the other hand submits that defendant No. 1 as a bailee failed to discharge his duties in respect of the fact that they took proper measure for protection of the suit car. It is well settled that onus is on the bailee to show that missing, loss etc. happened because of the factors beyond the control of the bailee. Here in the instant case defendant No. 1, the statutory bailee has failed to discharge the said onus. This view finds support in the case reported in AIR 1957. Mysore, 55. Therefore, on a consideration of the materials facts and circumstances of the case we find it difficult to accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

30. Mr. Makbul Ahmed then replying upon Sub-section (2) of section 50B tried to show that defendant No. 1 is not liable for the alleged loss of the suit car. In this connection sections 50A, 50B, 63 and 64 of the Chittagong Port Act are to be read together. All these sections were inserted by Chittagong Port Ordinance Amendment of 1960. Section 50A, reads as follows:—

"The responsibility of the Board for the loss, destruction, or deterioration of animals or goods whether landed for import or received for export during such time as the same remains in the possession or under the control of the Board, shall, subject to other provisions of this Act, and in the case of animals or goods, received subject also to the provision of the Railway Act, 1890, be that of a bailee under sections 151, 152 and 161 of the Contract Act, 1872, omitting the words "in the absence of any Special Contract" in section 152 of the last mentioned Act."

31. This section has got clear reference to that of a bailee under section 151, 152 and 161 of the Contract Act as contemplated under section 50A of the Port Act.

Section 50B runs as follows :—

(i) "The Board shall, immediately upon the landing of any goods on the port take charge thereof, and store such of the goods as may be liable to damage or deterioration by exposure in any shed or warehouse belonging to the Board."

Sub-section 2 of section 50 runs as follows:—

(ii) "If any consignee or owner of the goods landing on the port, without any default on the part of the Board, fails to remove such goods not being goods stored in a warehouse licensed under section 16 of the Sea Customs Act. 1878 from the premises of the

Board, within five clear working days of their landing, such goods shall thereafter remain on the premises of the Board at the sole risk and expense of the consignee or owner."

Sub-section 3 of section 50 runs as follows:—

(iii) "The Board may give notice to such consignee or owner as aforesaid (if his address is known) by letter sent to his address by post or otherwise, that the liability of the Board, if any, in respect of such good has ceased to exist, and such notice may also be published in one or more daily newspapers shall specify as far as possible the number marks and description of such goods.

In Sub-section (4) of Section 4 of the Chittagong Port Act the term goods has been defined as goods shall include wares and merchandise of every description."

<u>32. In sub-section (I) of section 50B it has been provided that the port will take charge of the goods upon landing and store such of the goods as may be liable to damage or deterioration by exposure in any shed or Warehouse belonging to the port. Sub-section (3) of the said Section provides for a notice to be given to such consignee for owner. Sub-section (2) of said Section 50B provides that the consignee or the owner may be liable for the damage or deterioration by exposure if hoods are removed or stored and on receipt of notice under sub-section (3) the consignee or owner does not clear the goods within 5 clear, working days of their landing provided the fault on the part of the port is not proved. If the port can prove that it was not due to their fault and they took pre-emption to avoid damage or deterioration of the goods by exposure in that case such goods shall thereafter remain on the premises of the port after the expiry of the said five days at the sole risk and expenses of the consignee or owner. The bailee remains bailee but subject to the condition as aforesaid provided in section 50B of the said Act. It is not a case that the suit car in the instant case has not been cleared by the consignee and failure to do so has absolved the port authority, Here in this case it is a clear case of non-delivery of the car and automatically comes within the view of section 50A of the said Act. This principle finds support in the case.</u>

<u>33. The case of Central Bank of India Ltd. Versus-M/S-Jan Md. Hazi Ismail reported in 17 D.L.R. 582 Section 63 provides that where condition as laid down in Section 50B are fulfilled in that case trustees may cause such goods to be removed either to any warehouse belonging to them or with the consent of the Custom Collector of the Port, to the public warehouse and the removal in such warehouse shall be at the risk and expense of the owners of the said goods. Sub-section (2), (3), and (4) of section 63 of the Act provide for notice to be given to the consignee or owner of the goods by port and paper publication whenever any goods are removed and also provides for charging in case of removal of goods for warehousing or open storaging, Section 64 of the Act empowers the Port authority even to sell the goods at the expiration of two months from the time when the goods are placed in their custody public auction and in case of perishable goods within such period not less than 24 hours after the landing of the goods as they think fit. Defendant No. 1 as a bailee has failed to discharge his liability to take proper measure for protection. It has also failed to prove the conditions required to be fulfilled in taking the plea of bar of risk of the consignee or the owner within f. clear working days of their landing as required under section 50B of the Chittagong Port Act. As it is a case of loss of the suit car while in the custody of the statutory bailee, it does not come under the preview of Section 50B of the Chittagong Port Act. This finds support in the case of Chittagong Port Authority versus- Md Ishaque and others 35 DLR. (A.13) 36</u>4.

34. From our foregoing discussions we find that the defendant No. 1 alone is liable for the loss of the car as a baffles The defendant No. 3 & 4 against whom decree was also passed have not filed any appeal or cross objection. But in view of Order 41, Rule 33 C.P.C. this court as an appellate court can grant that relief to the respondent although they have not filed any appeal or cross-objection. Order 41 Rule 33 C.P.C. runs as follows:

'‘The appellate court shall have power to pass any decree and make any order which ought to have been passed or made and to pass or make such further or other decree or order as the case may require, and this power may be exercised by the court notwithstanding that the appeal is as to part only of the decree and may be exercised in favour of all or any of the respondents or parties although such respondents or parties, may not have filed any appeal or objection."

The trial court was not justified in decreeing the suit against defendant Nos. 3 and 4.

35. Accordingly the appeal is dismissed. The Judgment and decree of the trial court is modified and the suit be decreed against the defendant No.1 for Taka 4930/-plus interest at the rate of pendentilite till realisation from the date of institution of the suit.

Mohammed Habibur Rahman, J.—I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Delwar Hossain J: This first appeal at the instance of defendant No. 1 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 16-10-1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Tangail in Partition Suit No. 117 of 1984 decreeing the suit in preliminary form giving saham to the plaintiff to the extent of 13½ acre out of the suit property and also half of the dwelling house as was in existence at the time of purchase.

2. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff filed the suit for partition of the suit property stating, inter alia that he along with defendant No. 1 purchased the same on 30th July, 1965 from one Moniruddin Beg through his attorney Abdus Samad Khan. Both of them have been possessing the suit property in ejmali. The plaintiff has been possessing the eastern portion by constructing 'L' pattern tin shed house and defendant No. 1 has been possessing the western portion. As defendant No. 1 had been claiming more than what she owned the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the plaintiff was the benamdar of her husband Abdul Karim Khan, Advocate who purchased the suit property in his name with his money and also taking loan from various relatives. The suit property was requisitioned and she applied for de-requisition in which the plaintiff gave no objection. Accordingly, the suit property was de-requisitioned in her favour and possession was delivered to her. Defendant No. 1 has been possessing the suit property by paying rents to the Government. Earlier Title Suit No. 370 of 1968 was instituted by one Fazlur Rahman for partition in respect of one decimal of land out of the said land in which this plaintiff and defendant No. 1 were made parties as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 which was decreed giving saham of one decimal land to the plaintiff of that suit.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge framed the following issues:

(1) Whether the suit was maintainable in present form and manner?

(2) Was the suit property valued properly?

(3) Was the suit bad for defect of parties?

(4) Whether the plaintiff had title and possession in the suit property?

(5) Was the plaintiff entitled to get 13½ acres out of suit land and entitled to half of the dwelling house?

(6) What other reliefs the plaintiff was entitled to?

5. During trial the plaintiff examined 4(four) witnesses including the plaintiff himself and produced documentary evidence which were marked as exhibits. Defendant No. 1 examined 7(seven) witnesses and produced several documents which were also marked as exhibits. On conclusion of the trial the learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and decree dated 3-12-2008 decreed the suit. Hence this appeal.

6. Mr Subash Chandra Saha, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, took us through the plaint, written statement, evidence on record and the impugned judgment and decree. He submitted that the plaintiff was the benamdar of Mr Abdur Karim Khan, Advocate, husband of the defendant No. 1 who purchased 1/2 of the suit property in the name of the plaintiff for his own benefit along with defendant No. 1 jointly each having equal share as apparent from the fact that while she applied for de-requisition of the suit property to the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh the plaintiff gave no objection and the same was derequisitioned in her favour and accordingly, possession was delivered to her and from the further fact that the rents in respect of the said property was also paid in the name of defendant No. 1 alone. He further submitted that one Fazlur Rahman earlier filed Partition Suit being No. 370 of 1968 for partition of his share out of the suit land in which the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 were parties as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respectively. Since the said suit was decreed and the plaintiff did not challenge the decree passed in the suit, the same is binding upon him. So, the instant suit was not maintainable in law but the learned Subordinate Judge, on an erroneous approach in the case, misread and misconstrued the evidence on record and decreed the suit and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside and the appeal be allowed. In support of his contention Mr Saha has cited the case of Bina Rani vs Shantosh Chandra Dey reported in 51 DLR (AD) 81.

7. Mr Abdus Salam Khan, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Aftab Hossain and Mr Bivash Chandra Biswas for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submitted that defendant No. 1 being a 3rd party had no legal right to say that the plaintiff was benamdar of her husband as he never challenged the title of the plaintiff by filing a suit for such declaration and he also never took any step for adding himself as a defendant in the instant suit to claim the suit property. He further submitted that as the sale deed dated 20-3-1965 (Exhibit-'A') stands in the name of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 jointly and the plain-tiff being in possession in a portion of the suit property defendant No. 1 cannot say that the plaintiff was the benamdar of her husband. He further submitted that both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 jointly sold one decimal of land out of the suit land to Mirza Joynal Abedin, defendant No. 2 and subsequently by a registered partition deed dated 30-12-1969, Exhibit-1 confirmed the said transfer which prima facie proved that they are the joint owners of the suit property in equal share. He further submitted that by filing application dated 30-7-1965 (Exhibit-B) though the plaintiff stated that he had no objection if the suit property was de-requisitioned in favour of defendant No. 1 he did not extinguish his title to the suit property, inasmuch as in the said application plaintiff identified himself as a co-sharer. Mr Salam Khan further submitted that mere payment of rent by a co-sharer in his own name does not extinguish, title of another co-sharer, here the plaintiff. Mr Salam Khan lastly submitted that in the decree passed in Title Suit No. 370 of 1968 as saham was not allotted either to the plaintiff or to defendant No. 1 the plaintiff cannot be debarred from bringing the present suit for partition in respect of his 13½ acres of land, the court below rightly decreed the suit and, as such, no interference is called for by this Court with the impugned judgment and decree. Mr Salam Khan in support of his contention cited the case of Lal Miah vs Md Ibrahim Meah reported in 28 DLR (AD) 61.

8. In this appeal the points to be decided are as to whether the Trial Court was justified in decreeing the suit giving saham to the plaintiff and whether defendant No. 1 could prove that the plaintiff was the benamdar of the husband.

<u>9. We have perused the evidence on record. From the evidence on record it appears that the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 both jointly purchased the suit land by sale deed dated 20-3-1965 Exhibit-1A' from Moniruddin Beg through his Attorney Abdus Samad Khan. From the deposition of PW 2 Abdus Samad Khan, the attorney of Moniruddin Beg, it is found that he sold the suit land to both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 jointly. PW 4 Ali Akbar, the deed writer, corroborated PW 2 stating categorically that the deed was written in the names of both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1, PW 3 Mirza Joynal Abedin, a common relative of both, also corroborated PWs 2 and 4. By cross examining PWs 2-4 defendant No. 1 could not at all shake their credibility. Further, in view of the provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872, the oral evidence as sought to be adduced by the defendant cannot be relied upon.</u>

<u>10. Defendant's case was that her husband Mr Abdul Karim Khan, Advocate purchased 1/2 of the suit land in the benami of the plaintiff by his own money and also by taking loan from various relatives. But on behalf of the defendant none of such of the relatives was produced to substantiate the said fact. DW 5, Fazlul Karim Khan alias Makhan Miah deposed that he paid Taka 1,400 as loan to the defendant No. 1. But it does not mean that said money was given as loan for purchasing the suit land by the husband of the defendant No. 1 in the benami of the plaintiff. Even if we accept that the said amount of Taka 1,400 was given as loan, the same does not cover the whole amount. As defendant No. 1 took the plea that the plaintiff was the benamdar of her husband onus was upon her to prove the said fact but in the instant case we do not find any evidence by which it can be said defendant No. 1 dis-charged her said onus. One of the star documents produced by the contesting defendant was the application dated 30-7-1965 filed by the plaintiff to the requisitioning authority for de-requisition of the suit land (Exhibit-B), wherein he stated that he had no objection if the suit property was derequisitioned in the name of defendant No. 1 to show that had the plaintiff been the actual owner of the said property then he would not have written so. But a reading of Exhibit-B shows that the plaintiff identified himself in the application as a co-sharer with the defendant No. 1 in the suit property and, as such, it cannot be said that the plaintiff admitted the fact that he was the benamdar of the husband of the defendant No. 1. Further, from this application it does not show that the plaintiff gave up his claim to the suit property. The dakhilas Exhibits D-D2 show that rent in respect of suit property was paid in the name of defendant No. 1. Mere payment of rent in the name of one of the co-sharers cannot oust another co-sharer from the claim of title to a property who is in joint possession thereof. Further, the very fact that the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 jointly sold 1 (one) decimal of land to Mirja Nurul Islam by a registered kabala Exhibit-2 and that the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 jointly contested Partition Suit No. 370 of 1968 and in the written statement never took the plea that the plaintiff was the benamder of her husband. Not only that the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 jointly as first party executed a bainanama in favour of Joynal Abedin as second party in respect of his said 01(one) decimal of land. Besides the above, defendant No. 1 in her written statement also admitted that plaintiff's father gave Taka 4,000 at the time of purchase of the suit property and as she failed to return the said money so she gave up 1/4th portion of the suit property in favour of the plaintiff and though a deed was supposed to be executed and registered but was not made. This story of defendant No. 1 sounds a bit unusual and also does not at all fit in with the defendant's case that plaintiff was the benamder of her husband. All those prove that the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 are the joint owners of the suit property having equal share, so the plaintiff rightly filed the suit for his share.</u>

11. We also do not find any substance in the submission of Mr Shaha that as there was already a Partition Suit being No. 370 of 1968 and saham was given in the said suit so, the instant suit was not maintainable. As Partition Suit No. 370 of 1968 was filed by one Fazlur Rahman Khan for partition wherein the present plaintiff and defendant No. 1 were impleaded as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respectively and saham was given only to the plaintiff of that suit to the extent of 0.1 acre of land and no saham was given to defendant Nos. 1 and 2 that is, the present plaintiff and defendant No. 1 the decree passed in that suit cannot debar the plaintiff's claim of partition. Further since the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 are in joint possession of the suit property having equal share therein and there has been no partition by metes and bounds the plaintiff had/has every right to pray for partition of the same and the instant suit is maintainable in law. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the case reported in 51 DLR (AD) 81 as cited by Mr Saha being quite different and distinguishable from the facts of the instant case does not at all help Mr Saha to substantiate his contention.

12. From the discussions made above we do not find any reason to disagree with the findings given by the Court below in the impugned judgment in decreeing the suit.

13. In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree is hereby confirmed.

Send down the lower Court's record immediately.

End.
