full_judgment:
Mohammed Habibur Rahman, J:—This appeal by appellant defendant No.1 represented by present Mutwalli S.M. Anwar Hossain is directed against the judgment and decree dated 6.-9-79 passed by Mr. K.A. Majumder, Sub-ordinate Judge, First Court. Chittagong in Other Suit No. 27 of 1976 directing specific performance of contract dated 4-9-74 by defend ant No.1 by executing and registering a kabala in favour of the plaintiff respondent in respect of the suit land within sixty days from the date of deposit of Taka 6520/- by the plaintiff failing which the same shall be executed and registered through Court in due course of law. The plaintiff was directed to deposit the balance amount of Taka 6520/- by 20-9-79, in default the suit shall he dismissed. Accordingly on 8-9-79 the plaintiff respondent deposited the said amount in the trial Court by Chalan No. 1592 dated 8-9-79.

2. The case for the plaintiff respondent Haji Abdul Malek Sowdager is that defendant No.1 is a Wald Estate known as Haji Abdul Latif Sheristadar Wakf Estate. The said Wakf Estate was brought into existence by one Abdul Latif, retired Sheristadar by Wakfnama Ext. G dated 11-2-1919. The Wakf property consisted of 14.30 acres of urban as well as rural properties. During his life time the Wakif Abdul Latif was to be the Mutwalli. After his death his son Mia Mohammad Eahya became the next Mutwalli for first live years in term of the Wakf deed Ext. G. Mia Mohammad Eahya on behalf of the defendant appellant Wakf Estate made an application to defendant No.5 Chittagong Development Authority and on that application defendant No.5 C.D.A. allotted 276 acres (equivalent to 14.86 kathas—about 12 gandas) of land appertaining to commercial plot No.5 at C.D.A. Jubilee Road, Chittagong for giving lease of the same for a period of 99 years on the terms contained in the said letter of allotment. The premium for the said land was fixed at Taka 5,00,000/- per acre (i.e. Taka 10,000/- per ganda). The first installment of Taka 40,000/- was to be paid within 10 days from the date of the said allotment letter. The Defendant No.1 Wakf Estate was short of fund and was not in a position to pay the premium of the land to defendant No.5 C.D.A. The then Mutwalli Mia Mohammad Eahya made an application to proforma defendant No.4 Administrator of Wakf to transfer about 9 gandas of land out of the said alloted Land with a view to raise necessary fund to pay the premium to pro-defendant No.5 C.D.A. The Administrator of Wakfs (pro-defendant No.4) by memo No.1681 dated 30-3-66 Ext. X granted permission to the following effect: -

"To

Mvi. Md. Eahya (Mutwalli).

C/O. Radio Supply & Service House.

137, Bipani Bitan,

Chittagong.

With reference to his petition dated 28-3-66 on the above subject he is informed that he is permitted to transfer 9 (nine) gandas of land as prayed for out of 14 gandas allotted to the Wakf Estate by the C.D.A.

Sd/- Illegible

30-3-66.

For Administrator of Wakfs."

Mia Mohammad Eahya on behalf of the Wakf Estate, Chittagong took an advance from pro-defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum (wife of pro-defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan) by verbally entering into a contract for sale of 9.90 kattas of land to Mrs. Hamidi Begum pro-defendant No.6. Mia Mohammad Eahya, the then Mutwalli paid the first premium of Taka 70,000/- to pro-defendant No.5 C.D.A. who thereafter executed the registered lease deed Ext,5 dated 24-1-67 in favour of defendant No.1 Wakf Estate for the said 14.86 kattas of land of commercial plot No.5, C.D.A. Jubilee Road. The agreement Ext.1 between the Wakf Estate and defendant No.6. Mrs, Hamidi Begum for sale of 9.90 kattas (equivalent to 8 agandas 1 kara) in the northern portion of the said commercial plot No.5 C.D.A. Jubilee Road., Commercial Area in favour of defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum and an lrrevccable General Power of Attorney Ext.2 between the Wakf Estate (defendant No.1) represented by. Mutwalli Haji Mia Mohammad Eahya and defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan (husband of defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum) was executed on the same date 26-1-67 authorising him (defendant No.7) to construct a building on the same land at a cost of Taka 2,00,000/- and to execute a sale deed in favour of defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum after completion of the construction. For various reasons the said proposed building was not constructed and the sale deed was not executed and registered in favour of Mrs. Hamidi Begum. In the meantime defendant No.2 S.W. Siddique, son of Haji Mia Mohammad Eahya became the Mutwalli. It was settled between defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique, the previous Mutwalli and defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum that if the Wakf Estate defendant No.1 can arrange to refund the consideration amount of Taka 81,730/- to defendant No.6 Mrs Hamidi Begum, she shall release the Wakf Estate from the contract of said Ext.1 along with the Power of Attorney Ext.2. Defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique as the Mutwalli of defendant No I then proposed to sell the said 8 gandas 1 kara of the suit land and the plaintiff Haji Abdul Malek Sowdagar agreed to purchase the same. After negotiation the terms and conditions of sale and the price of the land were fixed and an advance of Taka 1,15,000/- was paid by the plaintiff to defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique representing defendant No. 1 Wakf Estate as per memorandum of agreement Ext.6 dated 4-9-74. It was agreed that the defendant No.1 Wakf Estate would sell to the plaintiff the said land @ Taka 25,000/- per ganda, that a power of attorney would be executed as usual, that Income-Tax clearance certificate would be obtained by defendant No.1, that the plaintiff would refund to defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum earnest money that was taken by defendant No.1 from defendant No.6 and that the plaintiff would take back the bainama Ext. l from the defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum. The Memorandum of agreement Ext.6 was written by the plaintiff in defendant No.2's letter-head sheet of his personal firm "Cine Services" in own hand and the Mutwalli defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique put his signature on the same with date 4-9-74. P.W.2 Sayedul Huq also signed the same on 4-9-74 as an attesting witness. On the same date 4-9-74 defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique handed over the original lease deed Ext.5 dated 24-1-67 granted by C.D.A. (defendant No.5) and other papers to the plaintiff. Defendant No.2 as Mutwalli of defendant No.1 for completion of the said sale transaction signed on that very date two applications for Income-Tax Clearance Certificate along with two duplicates Ext.10 series and handed them over to the plaintiff. Two separate schedules showing equal half of the suit land i.e. 4.80 kattas each Ext.10A series were also signed on that date by defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique. Defendant No.2 then sent P.W.3 Hemayetulla with the plaintiff to defendant No.7 and the plaintiff thereafter refunded Taka 81,730/- to defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begun on behalf of defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique in presence P.W.3 Md. Hemayetulla, an employee of defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan. P.W.4 and defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum on 5-12-74 executed the deed of cancellation of the agreement Ext.3. Defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan on 5-12-74 executed the Memorandum Ext.4 cancelling Irrevocable General Power of Attorney. Defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique, the Mutwalli again received a sum of Taka 3,000/- as per cheque No.313118 (counter foil Ext.8 dated 18-12-78) of the Eastern Marcantile Bank. The said cheque the counter foil of which has been marked Ext.8 was received by defendant No.2's employee Sree Kali Prasad Dey as per receipt Ext.9 by signing the same on 18-12-74 in respect of payment towards earnest money for the purchase of the same land. The pass Book Ext.19 of the plaintiff in respect of his account No.1114 of Eastern Marcantile Bank Ltd., Sadarghat, Chittagong has been exhibited to show that Taka 3000/- was in cash on 18-12-74. Thus in three instalments of Taka 1,15,000/-, Taka 81,730/- and Taka 3000/-the plaintiff in all paid Taka 1,99,730/- to defendant No.1 the Wakf Estate as part payment of consideration money out of a total consideration money of Taka 2,06,250/- at the rate of Taka 25,000/- per ganda for purchase of the suit land measuring 8 gandas 1 kara. In the meantime defendant No.5 C.D.A. passed the resolution dated 12-11-74 (Ext.18) to the following effect:--

"The authority (C.D.A.) after detailed dis cession decided that the transfer of plots may be allowed on the conditions:

(i) If the allotee makes full payment of all the dues and if the allotment was made at least five years before the date of application of transfer, transfer of unconstructed plot may be allowed provided a transfer fee Taka 500/- (Taka five hundred) only per katha or part is paid to C.D.A.

(ii) No transfer shall be allowed in case of an allotment which was less than five years old unless the party construct the house."

3. Thereafter the plaintiff requested defend-ant No.2 to execute and register the sale deed on receipt of the balance consideration money of Taka 6520/- as the bar for transfer without construction had been removed by defendant. No. 5 C.D.A. The defendant No.2 as Mutwalli started avoiding the execution and registration of kabala and also did not file application to defendant No.5 C.D.A. for permission to transfer the suit land inspite of repeated requests. The plaintiff in the meantime came to learn that defendant No.2 with malafide intention is trying to transfer the land to others to make illegal gain. The plaintiff ultimately through his Advocate served a demand notice Ext. 12 dated 22-1-76 on defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique as Mutwalli of defendant No.1 demanding execution and registration of kabala on receipt of the aforesaid balance amount. Defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique as Mutwalli of defendant No.1 gave a reply Ext.13 through his Advocate on 24-2-76 intimating that within a course of one week he would give a reply. On 6-2-76 defendant No.2 through his Advocate gave a reply Ext.13(a) denying the present contract and making out a new story of contract of sale at the rate of Taka 40,000/- per ganda and also introducing a new story of advance of Taka 21,000/- only in all by 2 instalments. Thereafter the present suit was filed by the plaintiff on 24-3-76 praying for specific performance of the contract.

4. Defendant No.2 on behalf of defendant No.1 filed written a statement on 17-9-76 stating that the suit is barred under section 23 of the Contract Act in view of the provision of clause 19 of the lease deed Ext.5 wherein it has been provided that the tenant shall not sell, charge, mortgage, exchange, gift away or otherwise assign, sublet, encumber or in any way part with or dispose of the demised property or any part thereof before the construction, and appurtenance covenanted to he erected and such transfer without construction shall be void. In view of the provision of section 29 of the Contract Act an agreement, the meaning of which is not certain, or is not capable of being made certain, is void. It is true that the defendant No.1 Wakf Estate through previous Mutwalli took lease of 14.86 kattas of lands in plot No.5 C.D.A. Jubilee Road, Commercial Area by lease deed dated 24-1-67 from defendant No.5 C.D.A. An agreement for sale dated 26-1-67 was also executed between defendant No.1 Wakf Estate and defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum. On receipt of Taka 81,730/- an Irrevocable Power of Attorney was also executed in favour of defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan. The defendant No.5 allotted the said plot at a premium of Taka 10,000/- per ganda. The then Mutwalli of the Wakf Estate arranged with defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan and his wife defendant No.6 Hamidi Begum to share in buying the plot as the Wakf Esate defendant No.1 did not have sufficient fund to buy the whole plot. It was decided that the whole plot would be bought in the name of the Wakf Estate and proportionate lands would he transferred later on to Mrs. Hamidi Begum defendant No.6 and for such purpose, necessary permission was obtained by the then Mutwalli from the Administrator of Wakfs, Dhaka (defendant No.4). As C.D.A. rules would not permit sale of portion of a plot to a third person unless constructions had been made, the then Mutwalli entered into an agreement with Mrs. Hamidi Begum and granted Irrevocable Power of Attorney of her husband defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan to transfer 8 gandas 1 kara of the suit plot with a building to be constructed by him. The then Mutwalli of the Wakf Estate died. Defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum and her husband defendant No.7 expressed their willingness to rescind the agreement due to the changed political situation in the country on repayment of Taka 81,730/- paid by defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum to the previous Mutwalli. Defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique agreed to the proposal and was on the look out for a possible buyer to raise fund for the purpose as well as for the purpose of construction in the remaining part of the lands. Defendant No.2 on behalf of defendant No.1 did not enter into any written contract such as Memorandum of agreement Ext.6 with the plaintiff. The plaintiff was known to the defendant No.2 from before. In the early part of 1974, the plaintiff proposed to purchase the 8 gandas 1 kara of land at the rate of Taka 40,000/- per gonda and also proposed to pay 50% of the total consideration money to defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique. It was agreed that the documents from defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum would be released on payment and necessary permission will be obtained from prescribed authorities by defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique and thereafter the agreement for sale would be made. These proposal were accepted by the defendant in the early part of 1974 on the express oral agreement making the time for completion of the transfer to be made by 31-12-74 and the time was the essence of the contract. During the time of negotiation defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique expressed his intention to purchase a scooter and asked the plaintiff to sell one to the defendant. In that connection the plaintiff stated that in order to sell a scooter, permission from the Deputy Commissioner is necessary. The plaintiff gave assurance to the defendant to obtain such permission and asked the defendant to give to the plaintiff some letter-head slips of the defendant duly signed by him for making necessary application to the Deputy Commissioner and other authorities as may be necessary in this connection. The defendant No.2 in good faith gave his signature in blank letter head sheet of his personal business firm "Cine Services" at 113A, Jubilee Road, Chittagong with his signature thereon, The plaintiff has fraudulently utilised the signed blank letter-head sheet for the purpose of fabricating the alleged agreement in order to make wrongful gain by causing wrongful loss to the defendants. Defendant No.2 did not enter into any such contract for sale nor did defendant No.2 grant any receipt for Taka 1,15,000/- as alleged by the plaintiffs. The alleged signed agreement (Ext.6) is fabricated and fraudulent. No contract for sale was made by the defendant No.2 on behalf of defend-ant No.1 with plaintiff on 4-9-74 on the basis of a consideration at the rate of Taka 25,000/- per ganda. No term and condition as alleged was written down on any paper on 4-9-74 and no acknowledgement receipt of Taka 1,15,000/-was made by the Defendant No.2 on 4-9-74 Gr on any other date. No papers were written or signed or filed on 4-9-74 for Income Tax Clearance nor any such paper was handed over to the plaintiff. The verbal negotiations and agreement for sale took place long before on 4-9-74 between plaintiff and defendant No.2. The plaintiff promised to complete 'the transaction within 31-12-74 at the rate of Taka 40,000/-per ganda and also undertook to pay 50% of the total consideration money as earnest money. It was agreed that after the payment of the present money by the plaintiff bainanama would he executed containing the terms and conditions for sale. The defendant No.2 signed blank Income Tax Clearance application well after 4-9-74 and not on 4-9-74 as alleged. The plaintiff failed to pay the 50% of the consideration money as .earnest money and at the expiry of 31-12-74 the said oral contract with the plaintiff fell through due to failure of the plaintiff to comply with the terms of the oral contract. So there is no subsisting contract. It farther appears that taking advantage of the circumstances the plaintiff without making payment to the Mutwalli Defendant No.2 as agreed upon has made fraudulent deals with Mrs. Hamidi Begum defendant No.6. The plaintiff came to the defendant No.2's business premises on 4-9-74 and paid Taka 15,000/- and requested the defendant to wait for sometime. The plaintiff was given receipt. For the said amount on the letter-head of the Wakf Estate, thereafter on 19-11-74 the plaintiff paid a further stun of Taka 10,000/-. Thus the plaintiff paid only a total sum of Taka 25,000/- in all in part payment of the agreed consideration money at the rate of Taka 40,000/- per ganda. No other payment was made by the plaintiff to defendant No.2. On the date of payment of Taka 10,000/- the plaintiff was given fresh receipt for total payment of Taka 25,000/- in the letter-head form of the Wakf Estate and defendant No.2 kept copy of the said text with himself. The plaintiff has collusively obtained documents from the defendant Nos.6 and 7. The alleged payment made by the plaintiff to defendant Nos.6 and 7 cannot bind the defendant Nos.1 and 2. The specific performance of contract is an equitable relief to which the plaintiff is not entitled. The Wakf Estate will suffer great injury if specific performance as prayed for is granted.

5. The present Mutwalli S.M. Anwar (brother of defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique) on behalf of the Wakf Estate fired additional written statement on 30-12-78 stating that the previous Mutwalli defendant No.2 committed acts against the interest of the Wald Estate. Defendant No.2 was removed by the Wakf Administrator from the office of Mutwalli and in his place S.M. Anwar the present Mutwalli was appointed by the defendant. No.4. As per Wakfnama the Mutwalli has got no right to transfer. The alleged permission given by the Administrator of Wakf defendant No.4 to the previous Mutwalli Haji Mohammad Yahya has lost its force with the death of Haji Md. Yahya. The permission was accorded to sell the property to a particular individual. As that contract has failed, the permission has lost its Force. The plaintiff is not entitled to get any benefit out of such permission. The permission was not accorded to defendant No.2 who therefore had no authority to enter into an agreement for sale on behalf of Defend-ant No.1 with the plaintiff. After Haji Md. Yahya Mr. A.N.M. Wahed became Mutwalli who also did not act on the alleged permission. The land is vacant. In terms of the lease between the Wakf Estate Defendant No.1 and the C.P.A. Defendant No.5 any agreement to transfer before any construction is prohibited and void. As such the agreement is an unenforceable.

At the time of trial the following issues were framed:

"(1) Is the suit maintainable?

(2) Is the suit bad for misjoinder of party and cause of action?

(3) Is the suit barred under section 23 of the Contract Act?

(4) In the suit barred under sections 21 and 22 of the Specific Relief Act?

(5) Is the plaintiff entitled to get a decree for specific performance of contract as prayed for?

(6) What relief, if any, is the .plaintiff entitled to?"

6. 4 witnesses were examined on behalf of the plaintiff. S.M. Anwar, the present Mutwalli was examined as the sole witness for the Wakf Estate defendant No.1.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge on a discussion of evidence found that the plaintiff on behalf of the Wakf Estate Defendant No.1 paid Taka 81,730/- to defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum, that Ext.6 (the memorandum of agreement) is a genuine document executed by defendant No.2 on behalf of defendant No.1, that the plaintiff paid Taka 1,15,000/- to defendant No.1 through its Mutwalli defendant No.2 on 4-9-74 in pursuance the contract of sale of the suit land, that the plaintiff paid Taka 3000/-in favour of defendant No.1 by issuing cheque (counter foil Ext.8) which was encashed on 18-12-74, that the application for Income Tax Clearance Certificates Ext.10 series are genuine and bear the signatures of defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique admittedly, that defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique was not removed from office of Mutwalli for any misconduct in con-section his deal with the plaintiff or for any other misconduct, that there is nothing to show that the ex-Mutwalli defendant No.2 acted in collusion with plaintiff and that defendant No. 1 through its Mutwalli defendant No.2 contracted to sell the suit land to the plaintiff for Taka 2,06,250/- at the rate of Taka 25,000/- per ganda and received Taka 1,99,730/- towards consideration money leaving a balance of Taka 6,520/- on payment of which the plaintiff is entitled to enforce the contract. On these findings the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff as aforesaid. Thereafter this appeal has been preferred by Defendant No.1.

8. Mr. S.C. Das, the learned Advocate for the defendant appellant argued that the learned Subordinate Judge misread and misconstrued the oral and documentary evidence and arrived at a wrong finding.

9. The plaintiff P.W.1 Haji Abdul Malek Sowdagar deposed that the Haji Abdul Latif Sowdagar Wakf Estate (Defendant No.1) took lease of 276 acre (14.86 kathas) including the suit land from Defendant No.5 Chittagong Development Authority under the original lease agreement Ext.5 dated 24-1-67 which was handed over to the plaintiff by the previous Mutawalli Defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique, brother of the present Mutawalli S.M. Anwar. Defendant Not also gave him Ext. X, the order of the Wakf Administrator giving permission to sell 9 gandas out of 14 gandas of suit plot. Permission of the Administrator of Wakfs Ext. X is dated 30-3-66 granted in favour of the previous Mutawalli Md. Yahia, father of S.M. Siddique and S.M. Anwar. P.W.1 also produced the undisputed lease agreement Ext.1 dated 26-1-67 executed by the previous Mutawalli Haji Md. Yahia in favour of defendant No.6 Hamidi Begurn in respect of 8 gandas 1 kara comprising the specific separated northern portion of C.D.A. plot No.5, Jubilee Road, Chittagong. He also produced the undisputed power of attorney Ext.2 dated 26-1-67 executed by Haji Md. Yahya in favour of defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan, husband of Defendant No.6. It appears from memo of agreement Ext.1 that Defendant No.6 paid Taka 81,730/- to Haji Md. Yahia, Mutawalli of the Wakf Estate Defendant No.1 as price of land and proposed to construct a building thereon at a cost of Taka 2,00,000/- in accordance with the duly approved plan of the C.D.A. But due to various supervening factors Defendant No.6 and Defend-ant No.7 did rot like to proceed with the contract and wanted to rescind the contract and get a refund of their money. Defendant No.7 M.A. Hasan has been examined as a witness in this case. In the meantime previous Mutawalli Haji Md. Yahia had died. Defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique as Mutawalli of the Wakf Estate proposed to sell the suit land to the plaintiff and informed him that if the money paid by defendant No.6 Hamidi Begum was paid back to her, Defendant No.6 (and her husband) would forego their claim. The plaintiff agreed to purchase the suit land. Defendant No.2 as Mutawalli agreed to sell the suit land to the plaintiff at the rate of Taka 25,000/- per ganda. The total price of the suit land was agreed by the defendant No.2 and the plaintiff to be Taka 2,06,250/-. On 4-9-74 P.W.1 paid Taka 1,15,000/- on the terms and conditions written in the letter-head sheet Ext.6 of Defendant No.2's firm "Cine Services". At the dictation of defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique plaintiff P.W.1 Haji Abdul Malek wrote the contents of the agreement Ext.6. Defendant No.2 put his signature beneath the contents of agreement Ext.6. The plaintiff put his signature also. P.W.2 Md. Sayedul Huq also put his signature as an attesting witness. P.W.2 Md. Sayedul Huq has deposed that in his presence P.W.I plaintiff paid Defendant Not S.M. Siddique Taka 1,15,000/- on 4-9-74 as earnest money for purchase of the suit land in the office or Defendant No.2, that defendant No.2 acknowledged the same by assigning below the contents of the letter-head sheet Ext.6 of his "Cine Services" that the price was settled between them at the rate of Taka 25,000/- per ganda and that defendant No.2 handed over the lease deed Ext.5, the map (construction plan Ext.7), permission Ext. X and other papers. Defendant No.2 did not come to the witness box to deny the genuineness of the agreement Ext.6 which was signed by him on 4.9.74. Defendant No.2 had given a story in his written statement that he had put his signature in his blank letter-head slip and gave the same to the plaintiff for obtaining permission of the Deputy Commissioner for the purchase of a scooter. Defendant No.2 thus had to admit that he put his signature in the letter head slip of his firm but wanted to explain it away by introducing a false story which story he did not come forward to state by becoming a witness at the trial. From the evidence of P.W.1 plaintiff and P.W.1's brother-in-law P.W.2 Md. Sayedul Huq the genuineness of the agreement Ext.6 is proved and the payment of Taka 1,15,000/-by the plaintiff to defendant No.2 out of the total price of Taka 2,06,250/- at the rate of Taka 25,000/- per ganda is also proved the plaintiff deposed that defendant No.2 handed over to him Exts. 1-5 Ext. X, building construction plan Ext.7, copy of C.D.A.'s certificate of handing over of possession of the suit plot (Ext.X-2), the allotment letter and Mutawalli Md. Yahia's affidavit Ext.X-3. Production of these documents in court from the custody of the plaintiff establishes the truth of the statement of P.W.1, the plaintiff. P.W.1, the plaintiff also produced before the court duly filled in applications to the Income Tax Officer Ext.10, 10(a), 10(b) and 10(c) and all of them have been duly signed by defendant No.2. Thus genuineness of the aforesaid agreement of sale Ext.6 between the parties as stated by P.W.1 is established beyond doubt.

10. P.W.1 the plaintiff states that according to the direction of defendant No.2 he paid Taka 81,730/- at Dhaka to defendant No.6 Hamidi Begum (through her husband defendant No.7) as further part payment of consideration money for the suit land. While deposing on commission at Dhaka in presence of the appellant Mutawalli D,W.1 S.M. Anwar witness M.A. Hassan staled, that P.W.1 the plaintiff paid Taka 81,730/- to his wife defendant No.6 through him in presence of his employee P.W.3 Hamayetullah who also stated in his evidence that defendant No.2 entered into contract to sell the suit land to plaintiff on the basis of prior agreement with defendant Nos.6 and 7, that defendant No.2 sent him to defendant No.6 at Dhaka along with the plaintiff and that after the plaintiff refunded the entire consideration money (Taka 81,730/-) of the earlier agreement to defendant No.6 and her husband, the latter returned the original agreement, power of attorney and that defendant No.6 also executed the deed of cancellation of agreement Ext.3 dated 3-12-74 in which the plaintiff, defendant No.7, ones Zahiruddin and P.W.3 Hemayetulla signed as attesting witnesses. P.W.3 Hemayetulla also stated that he filled in the Income Tax Forms Exts. 10, 10(a), 10(b) and 10(c), that the plaintiff wrote the attached schedules, that defendant No.2 made corrections in the schedules under his initials and defendant No.2 signed each of the said Income Tax applications in his presence. Thus from the evidence of P.W.1 the plaintiff, P.W.3 Hemayetulla and witness M.A. Hassan (Defendant No.7) it has been proved beyond doubt that the plaintiff paid Taka 81,730/- to defendant No.6 on behalf of defendant No.2 in pursuance of the agreement of sale of the suit land with defendant No.2 (Mutawalli of defendant No. 1 the Wakf Estate) for rescinding the agreement entered into by the previous Mutawalli Md. Yahia with Mrs. Hamidi Begum defendant No.6. This amount of Taka 81,730/-was paid by the plaintiff as further part payment of consideration money fixed for the purchase of the suit land.

11. P.W.1 the plaintiff also deposed that he paid a further sum of Taka 3000/- by Eastern Marcantile Bank, Sadarghat Branch, Chittagong cheque bearing E.C. 18/8 No. 313118 dated 18-12-74 of his Savings Account No.1114 in favour of the then Mutawalli S.M. Siddique (defendant No.2). The counterfoil of this cheque is Ext.8. P.W.1 the plaintiff handed over this cheque to defendant No.2's employee Kaliprasad Dey who received the same granting the receipt Ext.9 dated 18-12-74 stating that he received the same according to the instruction of defendant No.2 as part payment towards the price of the suit land. The Pass Book Ext.11 also shows that Taka 3000/- was encashed on 18-12-74. Therefore the plaintiff has also proved that he paid a further sum of Taka 3000/- on 18-12-74 to the then Mutawalli defendant No.2 as part payment of the consideration money for the suit land is pursuance of the earlier agreement Ext.6 dated 4-9-74. Defendant No.5 the Chittagong Development Authority by their Resolution dated 12-11-74 (Ext. 18) allowed transfer of unconstructed plots if the allotment was not less than five years old and if the allottee had made full payment of all the dues provided a transfer fee of Taka 500/- only per katha or part is paid to the Chittagong Development Authority defendant No.5. The plaintiff P.W.1 was always ready to pay the balance amount to defendant No.2, the then Mutawalli but no kabala was executed by defendant No.2 on behalf of defendant No.1 the Wakf Estate. The plaintiff P.W.1 through his Advocate Mr. A. Mannan sent the formal letter Ext.12 dated 22-1-76 to defendant No.2 (Mutawalli) to receive the balance consideration money, to obtain the permission of the C.D.A. (defendant No.5) and to execute the deed of sale in favour of the plaintiff. Defendant No.2 through his Advocate first gave the reply Ext.13 dated 24-2-76 intimating him that a reply would be sent by hint within a week. Defendant No.2 thereafter through his Advocate gave his reply Ext. 13(a) (wrongly dated 6-1-76) denying the contract as stated by the plaintiff and making out a false story of contract of sale of suit land at the rate of Taka 40,000/- per ganda and introducing a false story of advance of Taka 21,000/- only in all by two instalments. The plaintiff then instituted the present suit on 24-3-76 for specific performance of the contract.

12. In his evidence the present Mutawalli D.W.1 S.M. Anwar, (brother of defendant No.2 the previous Mutawalli) who became Mutawalli from 25-3-78 stated that his brother previous Mutawalli defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique did not enter into any agreement of sale and did not receive any money from the plaintiff for the suit land, that the agreement Ext.6 is a collusive creation, that the deeds of cancellation Ext.4 and Ext.3 are collusive creations that defendant No.2 got the suit filed by the plaintiff in order of grab the suit property, that defend-ant No.2 has been removed from Mutawalliship for such misconduct, that the Wakf Estate paid the money to Hamidi Begum (defendant No.6), that the suit land now sells at the rate of about Taka 70 or 80 thousand per katha and that the plaintiff is not entitled to got a kabala from the Wakf Estate defendant No.1. In view of the unimpeachable oral and documentary evidences produced by the plaintiff discussed above the aforesaid statement of D.W.1 S.M. Anwar, brother of defendant No.2 is palpably untrue. There is absolutely no reliable material whatsoever to show that defendant No.2 was removed from Mutawalliship for any misconduct. D.W.1 S.M. Anwar admits that he attended commission for taking the deposition of defendant No.7 M.A. Hassan, husband of D.W. No.6 Hamidi Begum and also identified the deponent. It is therefore clear that D.W.1 S.M. Anwar is on the contrary in collusion with his brother defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique in order to cheat the plaintiff and make illegal gain.

13. We have shown that it has been proved that Ext.6 is a genuine document executed by the defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique the previous Mutawalli in favour of the plaintiff agreeing to

transfer 8 gandas 1 kara of the suit plot in favour of the plaintiff on 4-9-74. It is clear that on 4-9-74 while executing Ext.6 defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique on behalf of Wakf Estate defendant No.1 received Taka 1,15,000/- from the plaintiff. The defendant No.2 S.M. Siddique has not denied his signature in Ext.6 by deposing in the Court. On the other hand he admitted in his written statement to have put his signature in his letter head slip but in a vain attempt to resile from the contract came with a false story that he put his signature in a blank letter head sheet. P.W.1 Abdul Malek Soudagar and P.W.2 Md. Sayedul Haque have proved the signatures and contents of the document Ext.6.

14. We have also shown that from the evidence of P.W.1 Abdul Malek Sowdagar (the plaintiff), P.W.3 Md. Hemayetulla and P.W.4 M.A. Hassan (defendant No.7) it has been proved beyond any doubt that the plaintiff paid. a further sum of Taka 81,730/- as part of the consideration money of the agreement Ext.6 dated 4.9.74 to defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum on behalf of the Wakf Estate to rescind the earlier agreement and to obtain the deed of cancellation.

15. Ext.3 the deed of cancellation corroborates the evidence given by P.W.1, P.W.3 and P.W.4 regarding payment of the said amount of Taka 81,730/- and taking hack of the agreement Ext.1 and the Power of Attorney Ext.2 from the defendant Nos.6 and 7 on cancellation of the earlier contract. That all these documents have been produced in the Court from the custody of the plaintiff P.W.1 is also a glaring fact establishing the truth of the statement of P.W.1, as already stated before.

16. From the evidence of P.W.1 and P.W.3 with the counter foil of cheque Ext.8, the

Receipt Ext.9 and the Pass Book Ext.11 it is also proved, as already shown, that the plaintiff paid Taka 30001- to the Wakf Estate defendant No.1 through the Mutawalli defendant No.2 on 18-12-74 as part of consideration money for the suit land.

17. Defendant No.2 has also admitted in his written statement that he signed the Income Tax Clearance Certificates. P.W.1 and P.W.2 have stated that defendant No.2 signed the Income Tax Clearance Certificates Ext.10 series. Therefore there is no doubt that the said Income Tax Clearance petitions are genuine documents duly signed by defend ant No.2 on behalf of defendant No.1.

18. Mr. S.C. Das, the learned Advocate for the appellant submits that clause 19 of the deed of lease Ext.5 dated 24-1-67 executed between the C.D.A. Defendant No.5 and the Wakf Estate defendant No.1 provides, "That the tenant shall not sell, charge, mortgage, exchange, gift away or otherwise assign, sublet, encumber or in any way part with or dispose of the demised property or any part thereof before the construction of the buildings, and appurtenances hereby covenanted to be erected and such transfers, etc., if any shall be void." He further submits that under this term the transfer before construction would be void and therefore the contract for transfer is also void. He relies on section 23 of the Contract Act and submits that the contract of transfer is void because the transfer if permitted would defeat the provisions of the agreement for lease which has the force of law and because the transfer is opened to public policy. It is difficult to accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lease agreement has the force of a law. The contention that the leasee is a statutory authority and therefore the terms of the lease have also the force of law is also not acceptable. The contract between the plaintiff and the defendant has to be examined in the light of the provisions of the Contract Act and the terms of the lease agreement. The contract is not hit by section 23 of the Contract Act as it in not in contravention of any law. The learned Advocate for the appellant refers to section 29 of the Contract Act and submits that the agreement is void for uncertainty because its meaning is not certain and is not capable of being made certain. We have gone through the memo of agreement Ext 6. The learned Advocate attacked it on the ground that it does not provide the exact situation of the 8 gandas 1 kara of land in the C.D.A. plot No.5. There is no evidence that there is any subsequent agreement between the parties specifying positively the land to be transferred. This however does not make the agreement uncertain. There can be a valid agreement with respect to an undivided quantity of land of a specific plot. In such agreement the subject matter is a specific share described in quantum out of a specific plot of which number and identity have been specifically given. There is no uncertainty about the suit plot. The instant agreement is therefore not hit by section 29 of the Contract Act also. It may be stated that admittedly the earlier agreement between Wakf Estate defendant No.1 and defendant No.6 Mrs. Hamidi Begum was in respect of specified northern portion (measuring 8 gandas 1 kara) of the C.D.A. plot No.5, Jubilee Road, Chittagong. The documents Ext. 1 and Ext.2 have been referred to in item No.7 of the memo of Ext. 6. Therefore it is clear that the parties intended to transfer the specified northern. 8 gandas 1 kara of the suit plot No.5.

19. As regards the contention of the learned Advocate that the contract of transfer if enforced would bring about a transfer which is hit by clause 19 of the C.D.A.'s lease agreement Ext.5 dated .24-1-67 under which transfer before the construction of the building has been prohibited and made void, it may be stated that this contention would have prevailed if subsequently the C.D.A. defendant No.5 would not have by resolution dated 12-11-74 Ext.18 provided that if allottes makes full payment of all the dues and if the allotment was made at least 5 years before the date of application of transfer of unconstructed plot or portion of a plot may be allowed provided transfer fee of Taka 500/-only per katta or part is paid to C.D.A. This resolution of the C.D.A. clearly waives the restriction on the transfer of unconstructed plot or part thereof as provided in clause 19 of the lease agreement Ext.5. The allotment in favour of defendant No.1 was made by the C.D.A. defendant No.5 much more than 5 years before the present agreement. The learned Advocates for both the appellant and respondent submitted that the entire consideration money for the suit plot have been paid by defendant No.1 to defendant No.5 C.D.A. Obtaining of permission for transfer in terms of resolution dated 12-11-74 Ext.18 on payment of the necessary transfer fee is now a matter of formality which does not stand in the way of enforcement of specific performance of contract against the defendant No.1 Therefore in view of the waiver of clause 19 of the lease agreement Ext.5 by the resolution of the C.D.A. dated 12-11-74 Ext.18 referred to above the said clause 19 now does not stand in the way of transfer of unconstructed plot or portion thereof and consequently specific performance of the present contract is enforceable. In this connection the decision in the case of Mansoor Husmain others V. Wali Mohammad & others, 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 369 P.L.D. 1965 (S.C.) 425 may be referred to. In that case it was argued that if the contract were enforced, it would violate certain provisions of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. The Pakistan Supreme Court held that reading the provisions embodided in the relevant section of the said Act it would appear that the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act does not forbid the making of contract which may contemplate doing a thing which is contrary to the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, for that a thing can still be done by expost facto permission of the State Bank of Pakistan. In the instant case the lease agreement between the C.D.A. and defendant No.1 does not forbid the making of a contract which may contemplate transfer of unconstructed plot or part thereof which is contrary to the original lease agreement between the C.D.A. and the Wakf Estate, as such provision may be waived and has in fact been waived by the resolution Ext.18 dated 12-11-74. On the principle enunciated in this decision reported in 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 369 also the contract between the plaintiff and defendant No.1 cannot be said to be hit by clause 19 of the agreement. In the decision reported in 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 369 the relationship between the parties was governed by the provision of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act and in the case before us the relationship between the parties is governed by the terms of the lease agreement. The principle involved however is the same.

20. The learned Advocate for the appellant Submits that no specific sanction of the Administrator of Wakf to transfer the suit land to the plaintiff has been obtained and in the absence of any permission the contract cannot be enforced. It appears from the sanction letter Ext. X dated 30-3-66 of the Administrator of Wakf defendant No.4 that previous Mutawalli Md. Yahia was permitted to transfer 9 gandas of land out of 14 gandas allotted to the Wakf Estate by the C.D.A. This sanction is a general sanction to transfer 9 gandas out of 14 gandas allotted to the Wakf Estate without any condition. The 14 gandas is identifiable with C.D.A. plot No.5, Jubilee Road which was admittedly the plot allotted by C.D.A. of the defendant No.1 Wakf Estate. The permission granted by the Administrator of Wakfs is general and does not say that permission to transfer is in favour of a particular person. Just because at the time the permission was obtained there was a contract of sale with defendant No.6 Hamidi Begum (wife of defendant No.7) it cannot be said that after the contract with defendant No.6 Hamidi Begum was rescinded, the sanction will not continue to remain valid for a transfer to any other person, in the instant case to the plaintiff. It is not the case of the defendant that the permission has been rescinded by the Administrator of Wakfs and the permission must, therefore, be held to hold good still. The learned Advocate could not show us any provision of law requiring that permission for transfer should be in favour of a particular person. It is evident that permission to transfer land by the Wakf Estate granted by the Wakf Administrator as reflected in the sanction letter Ext. X is sufficient.

<u>21. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that if the defendant is permitted to transfer 8 gandas out of 14 gandas, practically nothing of the plot allotted to the Wakf Estate will remain and if the contract is enforced it will cause extreme hardship to the beneficiaries of the Wakf Estate including the present Mutawalli. The learned Advocate has placed reliance on the decision in the case of Administrator of Wakfs and another V, Most. Sahera Begum Chwodhurani and others, 28 D.L.R. 238. In that case two residential houses in the city of Dhaka constituting the only tangible assets of the Wakf were to be transferred, the only other property being a cloth shop at Patuatully the business of which had come to complete stop by the time the suit for enforcement of the contract was being heard. A Division Bench of this Court held that it was a case of extreme hardship which was likely to result from the performance of the contract and further that having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case it was a fit case in which the discretionary power of the Court to refuse specific performance of contract should be exercised. Ext. G is the deed of Wakf dated 12-2-1919. In the case before us no case has been made out that the property contracted to be transferred was even a substantial part of the assests of the Wakf and that if the contract is enforced, it would be a case of extreme hardship. In the instant case the Wakf Estate, which has many other properties, contracted to transfer the suit property for the purpose of acquiring a more valuable property for the benefit of the Wakf Estate. The principle of law enunciated in the reported decision in 28 D.L.R. 238 is not attracted and we are unable to consider it to be a fit case in which we should exercise our discretion by refusing specific performance of the contract. It would evidently be unjust to the plaintiff if he is otherwise entitled to get a decree for specific performance. It may also be noted that in the case reported in 28 D.L.R. 238 the Administrator of Wakfs had revoked the earlier permission to transfer and the appeal was filed by the Administrator of the Wakf.</u>

22. In the result, the appeal is dismissed and the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court are confirmed. The date for execution and registration of the kabala in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the suit land after obtaining permission of pro-defendant No.5 C.D.A. as required by the C.D.A. Resolution dated 12-11-74 in accordance with the terms thereof and after obtaining Income Tax Clearance Certificate as required by law from the Income Tax Authority be extended upto 15-6-84. The plaintiff appellant has already deposited the balance amount of consideration money. Failing amicable execution and registration or the required kabala within the time allowed above the plaintiff will be at liberty to get such kabala executed and registered through the Court in execution.

The parties shall bear their own costs.

End.

lawyer:
A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, Advocate, with Mustafa Niaz Mohammad, Advocate ----- for the appellant in Appeal No. 16/83. 
C.R. Das, Advocate, with Mokbul Ahmed, Advocate ----- for the appellant in Appeal No. 17/83. Mozammel Hoque, Advocate, with Syed Moazzem Hossain, Fazlul Karim and Md. Ahsanul Kabir, Advocate ----- for the respondent No.1 in both the appeals.
parties:
(1) Burmah Eastern Ltd.
Vs.
M/s. Hazi Mohammad Ali & Ors.
(2) Idris Alam
Vs.
M/s. Haji Mohammad Ali & Ors
full_judgment:
Fazle Hussain, Mohammed Habibur Rahman, J.:- These Two appeals are taken up together as they arise out of the same judgment passed by Mr. Md. Alauddin Sarder, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong on 14-12-82 in Other Suit No. 125 of 1977. In First Appeal No. 16 of 1983 Idris Alam is the appellant (defendant No. 2) and in First Appeal No. 17 of 1983 Burmah Eastern Ltd. is the appellant (defendant No. 1).

2. The case for the plaintiff-respondent M/S. Haji Mohammad Ali & Sons, in brief, is that on the basis of dispensing pump and selling licence Ext.6 executed on 2-9-68 between defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. and the plaintiff-respondent the plaintiff firm was appointed as dealer for operating the filling station (known as petrol pump) at Askarabad, Dhaka Trunk Road, Chittagong. The plaintiff respondent under the said licence Ext.6 was granted permission to use the premises in question along with the pump storage tank and all other facilities provided by the defendant No. 1 Company for the purpose of selling the petroleum products supplied by the Company. The plaintiff respondent was to purchase the Company's products at the Company's market price at the time of delivery and sell the products supplied by the Company at the prices fixed by the Company from time to time. The plaintiff respondent was entitled to get a commission on the price of motor spirits and high speed diesel oil purchased from the Company. The licence could be terminated by either party upon giving to the other party not less than 30 days’ notice in writing with a proviso that notwithstanding anything contained to the contrary in the licence Ext. 6 the Company shall be at liberty to revoke the licence forthwith upon the happening of certain events contained in clause 12(b) of the licence, such as, commission of any breach of any of the covenants and stipulations contained in the licence etc. The plff. firm was required to maintain at their own expense an adequate and efficient staff upon the said premises for supplying petroleum products to the public as supplied by the defendant Company. Since the appointment of the plaintiff firm as dealer in respect of the filling station in question the plaintiff firm has been operating the filling station to the satisfaction of all concerned with the assistance of the 9 employees and even during turbulant period of war of liberation, the plaintiff firm regularly operated the filling station without any dislocation whatsoever. In the later part of November, 1971 the Managing Partner P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali of the plaintiff firm went on pilgrimage to Holy Mecca after making necessary arrangement for managing and operating the filling station in question and for the said purpose he executed before the Notary Public, Chittagong a Special Power of Attorney Ext. 4(a) dated 19-10-71 in favour of his daughter P.W. 5 Noor Begum. Previously Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing Partner had gone for performing the Hajj and for visiting the holy places and shrines in the Middle East and in his absence his employees managed the filling station efficiently. On this occasion the filling station was being managed smoothly and efficiently by the plaintiff firm's employees. While P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing partner was in Mecca in 1971 Bangladesh emerged as an independent State on 16-12-71. P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing Partner of the plaintiff firm was stranded in Saudi Arabia. He ultimately returned to Bangladesh on 24-6-72. P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing Partner then was shocked to learn from his employees of the filling station that on 18-1-72 the filling station in question was abruptly and illegally taken over by defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. at the instance of defendant No. 2 Idris Alam driving away the employees of the plaintiff firm. Defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. handed over the filling station on that very day to defendant No. 2 Idris Alam with the assistance of defendant No. 3 Mohammad Hossain, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development), Chittagong. Since then the filling station in question was being run by the defendant No. 2 Idris Alam. P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing Partner of the plaintiff firm approached the Officers of defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. and came to learn that they had to take over the filling station in question under political pressure from Awami League leaders and that they were unable to help the Managing Partner in any way in this matter. In 1972 there was a veritable reign of terror and nobody could pluck courage to seek or get any relief against any Awami League leader or worker without risking his life. The plaintiff firm therefore, could not seek any legal relief against the defendants immediately. Nevertheless the Managing Partner of the plaintiff firm ran from pillar to post with requests, prayers and entreaties to remedy the wrong, but he could not succeed. On 13-1-75 the plaintiff firm through their Advocate Mr. M. Fazlul Karim, Bar-at-Law wrote the letter Ext.8 to the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong as well as to the General Manager, Burmah Eastern Ltd. requesting them to return the filling station in question to the plaintiff firm within 7 days of the receipt of the notice. On 25-10-75 P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing Partner wrote another letter Ext.8(a) to the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong stating that on 15-1-72 the filling station in question was illegally and arbitrarily sealed by the O.C. Zone No. 2 Abandoned Properties Managing Committee at the instance of some interested persons in a most clandestine manner and that after holding an enquiry necessary arrangement should be made to restore the legal and legitimate possession of the petrol pump to P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali. The Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong got the matter enquired into by the two Deputy Magistrate, namely, P.W. 1 Mr. M.A. Kamal and P.W. 2 Mr. P.R. Chakma. In the report Ext.1 Mr. M.A. Kamal submitted his report concluding that the defendant petrolium company M/s. Burmah Eastern Ltd. acted arbitrarily in cancelling the agency of the plaintiff firm ant appointing the defendant No. 2 M/s. Idris Alam and Co. as agent in place of the plaintiff firm. P.W. Mr. P.R. Chakma submitted his report Ext.1 (a) on 17-12-75 stating that defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. did not comply with the stipulation of one month's notice for cancelling the dealership of the petrol pump granted in favour of the plaintiff firm, that the sealed filling station was released on 18-1-72, that on the same date defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. appointed defendant No. 2 M/S. Idris Alam and Co. as dealer in respect of the petrol pump in question, that thereafter defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. wrote to the Manager Partner Haji Mohammad Ali about taking over the petrol pump without giving him any opportunity to defend himself against any allegation and that there was apparently some wire pulling by some unseen hands in the matter of removal of the plaintiff from dealership and appointment of defendant No. 2 as the new dealer abruptly. During the enquiry of Mr. M.A. Kamal defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. produced three letters namely. Ext. L(III) dated 14-1-72, Ext. 3 dated 20-1-72 and Ext. B dated 20-1-72. In the letter Ext.B(III) dated 14-1-72 the defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. is said to have written a letter to the Enemy Property and Abandoned Property Sub-Committee stating that the filling station in question has been sealed on the ground that the plaintiff Haji Mohammad Ali who was defendant No. l's dealer was declared as an enemy of the State (Collaborator), that the filling station does not belong to the plaintiff Haji Mohammad Ali who was merely defendant no. 1's dealer and the filling station should be unsealed so that defendant No. 1 can make arrangement to operate the same again. The letter Ext.3 dated 20-1-72 is a letter addressed by defendant no. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. to plaintiff stating: "In view of the fact that Government of Bangladesh have declared you an enemy of the State and sealed all of your properties, we are arranging to take over our above filling station forthwith". In the letter Ext.B dated 20-1-72 the defendant No. 1 is said to have written to the plaintiff firm that as the plaintiff firm was not available to operate the filling station in question and as the whereabouts of none of the partners of the plaintiff firm were not known, defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. was, therefore, constrained to issue the notice terminating all their arrangements with plaintiff forth with in terms of clause 12 of the agreement dated 2-9-68 and that they would prepare and inventory of the properties entrusted to the plaintiff for the filling station in question. The said notice Ext.B dated 20-1-72 was not received by the plaintiff. The General Manager of the defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. wrote the letter Ext. B (II) dated 20-1-75 addressed to the plaintiff's Advocate Mr. M. Fazlul Karim with a copy to the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong stating,

Dear Sir,

Messrs Haji Mohammed Ali & Sons

We have for acknowledgment your letter dated 13-1-1975.

2. We write to advise that your client was not, available after liberation of Bangladesh to operate our filling station nor had be intimated to us in writing giving his whereabouts. We were, therefore, constrained in order to save our properties from destruction to terminate our all arrangements in connection to with his dealership business with us in tams of Clause to 12 of the Dealership Agreement dated 2-9-1968 executed by him with us. In this connection we enclose a copy of letter of termination dated 20-1-1972 issued by us to your client.

3. In the circumstances we regret we cannot in any way restore the filling station to your client.

Yours faithfully,

BURMAH EASTERN LIMITED

G. FARHAD.

FOR GENERAL MANAGER.

cc: Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong". Thereafter the plaintiff firm through their Advocate Syed Moazzem Hossain wrote to defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern. Ltd. by a notice dated 20-10-76 Est. B (IX) claiming restoration and possession of the filling station as well as compensation of Taka 3, 64, 241.56 for loss of business from January, 1972 to 30-11-76, outstanding dues from customers deposit with defendant No. 1, compensation for loss of reputation and mental agonies, stock of oil and lubricants etc. as well as for fittings and fixtures. Thereafter defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. through their Advocate Mr. C.R. Das by a letter dated 15-11-76 Ext. B (X) informed the plaintiffs Advocate re-writing the circumstances under which defendant No. 1 had to take over possession of the filling station in question revoking the plff's licence, further stating that the defendant No. 1 acted within their legal right in canceling the licence agreement, that nothing belonging to the plaintiff was taken over by defendant No. 1 at the time of taking over possession of the filling station in question and that therefore the plaintiff was not entitled to receive any compensation. Thereafter the plaintiff firm filed the present suit on 5-11-77 for declaration and consequential relief. In paragraph 24 of the plaint it was stated that the suit was valued at Taka 1,83,330.00 for the jurisdiction of the court and for court fees of which Taka 10,000/- is the value for declaration and consequential reliefs as prayed for in prayer "A" and "B" as there is no objective standard of valuation of the same and the balance of Taka 1,73,330/- was the value of the claim prayed for in prayer "C". The details of compensation calmed under clause "C" were given in the schedule as follows:-

I.	Loss of average monthly income from 18-1-72 to 20-5-77 @, Tk. 2,000.00 per month amounting to ----- Tk. 1,28,000.00

II.	Outstanding credit dues from customers ----- Tk. 7,000.00

III.	Deposit to defendant No.1 for lifting supplies of petrol oil and lubricant on 11-1-72 ----- Tk. 5,330.00

IV.	Stock of oil, lubricants, petrol, diesel oil, gear oil and brake oil illegally taken away by defendants Nos.1 and 2 on 18-1-72 ----- Tk. 35,000.00

V.	Fittings and fixtures illegally removed by defendant nos.1 and 2 on 18-1-72	 ----- Tk. 5,000.00

Total Tk. 1,80,330.00

3. Defendant No. 3 Mr. Mohammad Hossain, the then A.D.C. (Dev.), Chittagong and defendant No. 4 The People's Republic of Bangladesh as represented by the Deputy Commissioner, did not appear and contest the suit. Defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. contested the suit by filing written statement.

Their case is that the suit as framed and instituted is not maintainable according to Law. The suit is barred under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The declaration sought for not being for any legal right or for legal status is not legally sustainable. The whole claim of the plaintiff is false and frivolous. The filling station in question and all the assets there in including all the fittings and fixtures belong to defdt. No. 1 the licensor and the plaintiff is merely a licencee at will. The licence having been admittedly cancelled the question of declaration that the plaintiff is continuing as the lawful dealer and the licencee in respect of the defendant No. 1's filling station does not arise. Defendant No. 1 denied that there was any kind of political pressure for which the licence was cancelled. After duly revoking the licence under clause 12 of the Agreement Ext.6 defendant No. 1 allowed defendant No. 2 Idris Alam to operate the filling station from 18-1-72 under provisional licence Ext. A1 dated 18-1-72 and subsequently under regular licence Ext. B1 dated 26-12-72. The plaintiffs licence having been revoked and cancelled by defendant No. 1, defendant No. 2 having been put in possession to operate the filling station as licencee under defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff having no subsisting legal right either to the licence or to operate the filling station, the plaintiff is not entitled to the relief claimed in the suit. After the liberation of Bangladesh the District Authorities on physical survey neither could find any of the plaintiff firm's partners nor any of their employees. The filling station in question the war of liberation was left completely unprotected with all the valuable properties which were exposed to all risks and hazards Defendant No. 3 Additional Deputy Commissioner, (Dev.), Chittagong sealed the filling station. Thereafter defendant No. 1 explained the whole position to the District Authorities who handed over the filling station to defendant No. 1 on preparation of the joint inventory Ext. A. Thereafter, as already stated, defendant No. 2 was appointed to run the filling station from 18-1-72. There was no outstanding credit dues to any customer. There was no lubricants, stock of oil, petrol, diesel oil, gear oil and brake oil of the value of Taka 35, 000/- in the filling station in question when defendant No. 1 took over possession of the same. There was no deposit of Taka 5, 330/- with any appropriate authority of defendant No. 1 on 11-1-72. Defendant No. 1 did not remove any fittings and fixtures of the value of Taka 5,000/-. The plaintiff is also not entitled to recover any business loss @ Taka 2000/- per month as prayed for. There is no cause of action for the present suit against the defendants.

4. Defendant No. 2 Idris Alam contested the suit by filing a separate written statement. Defendant No. 2 also contended that the plaintiff's suit is barred under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and also by limitation. He also contended that the suit is barred by principles of waiver, estoppel and acquiesce. After revocation of the plaintiff’s dealership licence defendant No. 2 was duly appointed as licencee under defendant No.1 and since 18-1-72 defendant No. 2 is duly and legally operating the filling station as a licencee under defendant No. 1. Defendant No. 1 took over possession of the filling station after it was unsealed by the then District Authorities. Under clause 12 of the Agreement Ext.6 the licence was always revocable with or without notice. On 18-1-72 the defendant Nos.1, 2 and 3 did not take over possession of the filling station forcibly by driving away any of the employees of the plaintiff firm or with the help of any goonda. The plaintiff has no locus-standi and cause of action against the defendant No. 2 After provisional appointment of defendant No. 2 as licencee on 18-1-72 by defendant No. 1, the defendant No. 2 was regularly appointed as licencee on 26-12-72 after he had deposited Taka 15,000/- as security with defendant No. 1. Since 18-1-72 defendant No. 2 is running and managing the filling station as a bonafide licencee under defendant No.1. Defendant No. 2 has been wrongly dragged in to the suit out of malice and jealousy.

5. On behalf of the plaintiff 9 witnesses were examined and Exts.1 to 12 was filed. On behalf of the two contesting defendants 5 witnesses were examined and Exts. A, B to Ext. B (XIII) were filed. The learned Subordinate Judge found that there was no reliable evidence that the filling station was abandoned and sealed, that defendant No. 2 was appointed as a dealer by defendant No. 1 on 18-1-72 while defendant No. 1 revoked the licence of the plaintiff on 20-1-72 without admittedly giving any prior notice, that defendant no. 1 and defendant No. 2 collusively took over possession of the filling station forcibly from the employees of the plaintiff firm on 18-1-72 that in undue haste defendant No. 1 granted provisional licence to defendant No. 2 in to possession, that since all the previous employees of the plaintiff firm are now serving as employees under defendant No. 2, they have not come forward to depose in favour of the plaintiff, that thus wrongfully and unjustly defendant No. 1 revoked the licence of the plaintiff without giving prior notice and that it is a fact that defendant No. 1 has revoked the licence of the plaintiff and inducted defendant No. 2 into possession of the filling station as a licencee. Thereafter the learned Subordinate Judge held that the plaintiff was not entitled to any declaration that he is still continued to be the lawful licencee and to a permanent injunction restraining defendant No. 1 from supplying oil to defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 2 from running the filling station inasmuch as it was within the competent authority of defendant No. 1 to supply or not to supply oil to the plaintiff and inasmuch as defendant No. 2 has been already appointed dealer by defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 was entitled to run the filling station until the dealership of defendant No. 2 was cancelled. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the plaintiff was entitled to get Taka 2,000/- as business loss for 30 days, that as per receipt Ext. 2 dated 11-1-72 the plaintiff firm had deposited Taka 5,330/- with the defendant No. 1 but against the said deposit no oil appears to have been supplied and accordingly the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for the said amount of Taka 5,330/- and according to D.W. 4(Mohammad Rafique) there were chair, table, fan and telephone etc. belonging to the plaintiff in the filling station in question and the plaintiff therefore was entitled to a compensation of Taka 5000/- for the same, that on 18-1-72 there was according to the plaintiff oil, diesel, Mobil etc. valued at Taka 35.000/-, that admittedly the underground tank was not examined at the time of taking over possession on 18-1-72, that therefore the plaintiff was entitled to a decree for a further compensation of Taka 35, 000/- on that account and that the plaintiff in all was entitled to a decree for a compensation of Taka 47,330/-. The learned Subordinate Judge thereafter declared that the orders of revocation of the licence of the plaintiff and appointment of defendant No. 2 as dealer under defendant No. 1 are illegal, unjust and invalid and that the plaintiff would get Taka 47,330/- as compensation within 60 days from the date of the passing of a decree.

6. It is undisputed that the plaintiff respondent was the holder of the licence Ext.6 granted by defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. It is also undisputed that the plaintiff is partnership firm of which there are three partners namely, P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali and his two sons Md. Illias and Md. Idris. P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali admits that he along with his aforesaid two sons had left for Saudi Arabia in the later part of November 1971 for performing the Haji. It is also undisputed that P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali came back to Bangladesh on 24-6-72. P.W. 1 Mr. M.A. Kamal and P.W. 2 Mr. P.R. Chakma are two Magistrates who held inquiries in 1975. They have no personal knowledge about what happened in January, 1972. P.W. 3 Fazal Karim was the holder of the licence in respect of the disputed filling station previous to the plaintiff respondent. He has also no personal knowledge about what happened in January, 1972. P.W. 4 Nabidur Rahman, Notary Public is a formal witness who proved the power of attorney Ext. 4(a) executed by P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali on 19-10-71 in favour of his daughter P.W. 5 Noor Begum to manage, administer and supervise the affairs of all his firms and all allied business including transport business during his absence. P.W. 5 Noor Begum herself states in her cross examination that she observed parda very strictly. She admittedly never visited the filling station in question personally. She admits that the business affairs of the filling station used to be run by the employees of the plaintiff respondent. She stated that on 11-1-72 she had paid Taka 5, 330/- to the Manager Mr. Shafi (since dead) for depositing the same with defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. for the purpose of bringing petrol for the filling station in question. It appears that Ext.2 is the receipt by which Taka 5,330/- was received by defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. from the plaintiff firm on 11-1-72. She has no personal knowledge as to who the filling station was taken over in January, 1972; but she states that she received the letter Ext.3 dated 21-1-72 from defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. The said letter Ext.3 was addressed by defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff firm and it reads as follows:

Dear Sirs,

Our Filling Station at Dacca Trunk Road.

7. In view of the fact that Government of Bangladesh have declared you an enemy of the State and sealed all of your properties, we are arranging to take over our above filling station forthwith.

Yours faithfully;

BARMAH EASTERN LIMITED.

Sd/-Illegible.

For General Manager."

8. She handed over the said letter to her father P.W. 6 Haji Md. Ali when he returned from Hajj. In her cross examination she stated that while handing over Ext.3 plaintiff's Manager Shafi told her that the Government had taken over the filling station as there was none to operate the petrol pump. She stated in her cross examination that she does not know when defendant No. 2 Idris A lam took over possession of the petrol pump. She stated that neither she nor her husband had any enmity with defendant No. 2 Idris Alam. She also stated that her husband P.W. 9 Md. Shafiqul Hoque was an Awami League Leader.

9. P.W. 6 Haji Mohammad Ali, the Managing Partner of the plaintiff firm has no personal knowledge as to why and under what circumstances the filling station in question was taken over in January, 1972. He states that he used to get the filling station in question run by the employees and that defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. terminated his licence without any reason and without giving him the notice of 30 days as required under the Agreement Ext. 6 and that defendant No. 2 Idris Alam was given dealership licence in respect of the filling station in question on 18-1-72 which is 2 days prior to the termination of plaintiff's licence. He states that on behalf of his firm as per receipt Ext.3 dt. 11-1-72 Taka 5, 330/- was deposited with defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. but against that deposit no petrol was supplied to the plaintiff firm. He states that as defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. had no right to cancel his dealership licence without any notice and without reason, his dealership should be deemed to be still valid and binding on defendant No. 1 He claimed that he is entitled to receive compensation Tk. 2000/- as business loss per month from 18-1-72 to the date of the institution of the present suit on 20-5-77. He also claimed to be entitled to get Taka 5,330/- which was deposited under the receipt Ext.3 with defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. on 11-1-72 as against the said amount no petrol was supplied by defendant No.1. He states that when defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 took over possession of the filling station there was in the filling station diesel oil, petrol etc. worth Taka 35, 000/- which he is entitled to get as compensation. He also states that there was furniture, fan and telephone set worth Taka 5000/-. He states that he returned to Bangladesh on 24-6-72 from Hajj and that his two sons Idris and Illias had also gone with him to Holy Mecca for performing Hajj.

10. Through P.W. 7 Haji Md. Islam. P.W. 8 Haji Abdul Barik and P.W. 9 Md. Shafiqul Hoque (husband of P.W. 6's daughter P.W. 5 Noor Begum) the plaintiff introduced a new story which was not in the plaint. P.W. 7 Haji Md. Islam stated that in the middle of January, 1972 defendant No. 2 with the help of some people took over possession of the filling station forcibly. P.W.8 Haji Abdul Barik and P.W. 9 Md. Shafiqul Hoque state that on 18-1-72 defendant No. 2 along with some people forcibly took over possession of the filling station. P.W. 9 Md. Shafiqul Hoque stated that the previous employees of the plaintiff are now serving in the filling station as employees under defendant No. 2 Idris Alam.

11. D.W. 1 Manjur Ahmed Chowdhury who was the District Marketing Officer of defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. in January, 1972 states that in the middle of January, 1972 they came to know that the filling station in question had been seized by the Government as abandoned property, that they applied to the Deputy Commissioner. Chittagong for release of the filling station and that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Dev.) Chittagong gave the release order. He further states that on 18-1-72 he took over possession of the filling station in question on behalf of defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. by putting his signature in the inventory Ext. A which also contained the signature of the Officer who gave possession to him on behalf of the Government on 18-1-72. He denied that he took over possession of the filling station in question on 18-1-72 in collusion with defendant No. 2 Idris Alam forcibly. It appears from the inventory list Ext.A that no quantity of diesel oil, petrol or any other lubricants was found in any tank or pump. He states that after taking over possession of the filling station on 18-1-72 defendant No. 2 Idris Alam was appointed as licencee to operate the said filling station. He further states that by two letters issued on 20-1-72 they terminated the licence of the plaintiff firm. The letter Ext.3 dated 20-1-72 has already been reproduced earlier. Ext. B is the letter dated 20-1-72 which has already been reproduced by us while stating the plaintiff’s case. The plaintiff states that neither he nor his employees nor his daughter received this letter Ext.B. Ext.B is said to be an office copy of the original letter which is said to have been sent by defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff firm terminating the licence Ext.6 in terms of clause 12 of the Agreement on the ground that there was no one available on January, 1972 to operate the filling station in question. From the side of the, Government, i.e. defendant No. 3 and defendant No. no one has come forward to say that the filling station in question was sealed by them. As it was a very disturbed period, nothing is clear as to what happened between 11-1-72 i.e. the date on which the plaintiff firm deposited Taka 5,330/- under the receipt Ext.3 with defendant no. 1 and the date 18-1-72 which is undisputedly the date when defendant No. 1 took over possession of the filling station and allowed defendant No. 2 Idris Alam to operate their pump as their provisional licencee under provisional licence Ext. A(1) dated 18-1-72. Letter Ext.B (XIII) dated 14-1-71 alleged to have been sent by the defendant Burmah Eastern Ltd. to the Enemy property and Abandoned Property Sub Committee, Ispahani Mansion, Tiger Pass, Chittagong and the application Ext. A (1) dated 14-1-72 sent by the defendant No. 2 Idris Alam to the General Manager of defendant No. 1 Burmah Eastern Ltd. praying for dealership licence for the filling station in question have been produced by the defendants. But since there is nothing concrete and reliable to show as to whether any one on behalf of the Government during the disturbed period had sealed the filling station in question, it can only be held in the facts and circumstances of the case that defendant No. 1 through D.W. 1 Mr. Manjur Ahmed Chowdhury, District Marketing Officer of defendant No. 1 took over possession of the filling station on 18-1-72 and allowed defendant No. 2 Idris Alam to operate the filling station as their licencee under provisional licence Ext.A(1). Ext.3 and B both dated 20-1-72 have been filed before the Court. Ext.3 was admittedly received by the plaintiff's employees and P.W. 6's daughter P.W. 5 Noor Begum. But the fact remains that on 18-1-72 the defendant No. 1 impliedly revoked plaintiff's licence Ext. 6 without prior notice. Section 61 of the Easements Act enacts the judicial principle that the revocation of a licence may be express or implied. From the facts of eviction of the plaintiff firm from the filling station in question on that date and induction of defendant No. 2 Idris Alam for operating the filling station as a new licencee under the defendant No. 1 on that date it clearly appears that the earlier licence Ext.6 granted to the plaintiff by defendant No. 1 stood impliedly revoked on 18-1-72 without any prior notice of 30 days as required under clause 12(a) the said Agreement Ext.6. The action of defendant No. 1 can therefore be said to be wrongful termination of the plaintiff's licence Ext.6.

He states that he applied for dealership to defendant No. 1 on 14-1-72 and that defendant No. 1 granted him dealership licence in respect of the filling station in question on 18-1-72. He stated that D.W. 1 Mr. Manzur Ahmed Chowdhury. District Marketing Officer of defendant No. 1 on behalf of the defendant No. 1 handed over possession of the filling station to him. In his cross examination he stated that he was the Publicity Secretary of the Awami League and that he used to work for the Awami League since 1966. He denied the defence suggestion that no employee of the Government sealed the filling station in question. He also denied the defence suggestion that on 18-1-72 he forcibly took over possession of the filling station in question. This in short is the entire oral evidence on record.

17. Mr. Mozammel Hoque, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff respondent referred to the decision in the case of Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distributing Co. Ltd. of India.
