case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 23.3.73 passed by the High Court Division in F.M.A. No. 28 of 1972 with C.O. 645/72.)
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J. This appeal by Special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division setting aside an order of dismissal of an execution case respecting a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale of certain properties and caution case respecting a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale of certain directing the said execution case to proceed after the construction of the records Of Title Suit No. 50 of 1957 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca in which the said decree was passed.

2. The chequered career of this litigation underlines the proverbial trouble of a decree-holder for which, more than anything else, as appears to us; abuse of the process of the Court' is responsible. A resume of the various phases of the proceeding for execution of 'a decree, which .was affirmed by the High Court and the Supreme Court of the country is necessary for the proper appreciation of the procedural vagaries which have .thwarted its progress during the course of about twelve years,

3. Respondent before us obtained a decree for specific performance of a contract for 'sale of certain land in the City of Dacca on 22-5-58 in Title Suit. No. 50 of 1957 of the 5th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca and appear being F.A. No. 164 of 1958 which was preferred against the said decree, was dismissed by the High Court on 4-7-61. Title Execution Case No. 19 of 1961 was initiated thereafter on 19-8-61 but further proceeding of the said execution case was stayed, as the judgment debtors preferred an appeal against the decree passed by the Dacca High Court to the Supreme Court of Pakistan, which was, however, dismissed on 27-2-64. The proceeding of the execution case was, thereafter restarted on 21-1-65, and it appears from an order of the Executing Court dated 16-4-65 that the notices upon the judgment debtors were duly served and that the decree holder was directed to file certified copies of the judgment and decree of the' trial court in the execution proceeding. The decree-holder filed a certified copy of the, decree on 7-9-65 and that of the judgment on 2-12-65. Balance of the consideration money as decreed by the Court was deposited by the decree-holder on 24-12-65 and a draft of the proposed kabala was, thereafter, served on the judgment-debtors under the order of the executing court. After the deposit of the balance of the consideration by the decree-holder in the Court, an application was made by the decree-holder on 22-2-66 for attachment of a sum of Rs. 4906.62 out of the said money deposited by the decree-holder towards the decretal cost of the, suit as well as the appeals and fresh notice was directed by the Executing Court to be issued upon the judgment-debtors. Notice appears to have been served upon the judgment-debtors for the second time as shown in the order dated 12-8-66, and the judgment-debtors as a matter of fact, entered appearance by filing a vakalatnama on 15-8-66. Decree-holder renewed his prayer for attachment of a sum of money out of the balance of the consideration money on 8.11.66 and an order of attachment of the said sum of money was made on 1-12-66 after a copy of the application for attachment had been served upon the judgment debtors. It appears that another certified copy of the decree was filed by the decree-holder on 13-12-66, and an application for a certificate of clearance of the judgment-debtors income tax, as required under Transfer of Property Ordinance, 1947, was forwarded to the Income Tax Officer concerned under the order of the Executing Court. No such certificate of Income Tax clearance having been forth-coming the execution proceeding was, being adjourned from date to date and about 2 years after i.e. in October, 1968, a letter was received from the Income Tax Officer Dacca in which it was stated that no action could be taken as the original letter of the Court was missing. Full particulars were, thereafter, supplied to the Income Tax Officer in pursuance of the direction of the Court but no action seems to have been taken by the Income Tax Department until 12-7-69, on which date the Income Tax Officer sent a letter requesting the Court to furnish a fresh Transfer of Property application for taking necessary action.

4. It appears that the Execution case was dismissed for default on 24-11-69 for the failure of the decree-holder to take steps in regard to furnishing a fresh Transfer of Property application to the Income Tax Department, but the said order of dismissal was subsequently set aside, and the Execution case, was restored to file. The Executing Court being, however, of the view that fresh notice should be served upon the judgment-debtors after the restoration of the Execution case directed notices to be issued to the judgment-debtors, whereupon steps were taken for service of notices upon the judgment-debtors. But as no notice could be served upon the judgment-debtors, the Executing Court, being of the' opinion that the judgment  debtors were avoiding service of notice, directed, by an order dated 12-6-70, to effect substituted service of notice under Order 5, Rule 20 of the Code of Civil procedure, Judgment-debtors thereafter appeared in the case on 20-8-70 after the substituted service of notice but took repeated adjournments for filing written objection. The decree-holder was, ill the meantime, asked by the Court on 28-1-71 to file, another certified copy of the decree to be sent to the Income-Tax Officer for the purpose of the judgment income-tax clearance certificate and the execution case was dismissed for default on 15-5-71 for decree-holders failure to file a certified copy of the decree. The Execution case was, however, subsequently restored to file and the decree-holder thereafter filed an application on 13-10-71 for reconstruction of the records of the Title Suit stating that the, certified copies of the judgment and decree of the Trial Court had not been supplied to him by the office of the Court on the ground that the records of the suit were missing and that as such the records of the suit should be reconstructed on the basis of the Paper Book printed in the High Court in F.A. No. 167 of 1958 On 6-12-11 Surat Ali, one of the judgment-debtors, filed a petition of objection purporting to be under section 47, C.P.C. contending, inter alia, that the Execution case was not maintainable in the absence of certified copies of the judgment and decree, that the description of the property as given in the execution petition, was wrong, that there could not be any reconstruction of the records on the basis of the printed paper book in, the High Court in the absence Of sufficient proof and that there ought to have been fresh service of notice under Order 21, Rule 22 C.P. Code after the restoration of  the Execution case. This petition of objection was registered as Misc. Case No. 48 of 1972. Subsequently another point was taken by the objecting judgment-debtor to the effect that the decree which was passed by a Court of Pakistan was not executable in a Court of Bangladesh in the absence of a specific legislation enabling such execution.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 29-4-72 gave effect to almost all the contentions of the objecting judgment-debtor and dismissed the Execution case holding that the Execution case was not maintainable in the absence of a certified copy of the decree that it could not proceed without serving notice under Order 21, Rule 22 C.P. Code and that the reconstruction of the records could not be made on the basis of the paper book prepared in the First Appeal before the High Court. The learned Subordinate Judge refrained from making any comment on the objection taken, in the case relating to the executability the decree passed by Court of Pakistan in a Court of Bangladesh.

6. An appeal against the said order at the instance of the decree-holder was heard by a Bench of the High Court Division, who, by their judgment dated 23-3-73, have allowed the appeal, set aside the order of dismissal of the Execution case and have directed the Execution case to proceed on the basis of the decree reconstructed in accordance with the direction given in the judgment.

7. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have come to the findings; in course of the judgment, that there was no necessity of fresh service of notice under Order 21, Rule 22 C.P: Code, that it was the duty of the Court, from whose custody the records were missing to reconstruct the records on the basis of the available materials, that the paper book of the First Appeal prepared at the: instance of the judgment-debtors and the judgment and decree passed by the High Court in the said First Appeal are the proper materials on the basis of which the reconstruction of records may be made and that .there is no substance in the objection as to executability of the decree in a Court of Bangladesh. A new point was argued before the High Court Division as to the authority of the Executing Court to ask for an Income Tax Clearance Certificate from the Income Tax Officer, but the High Court Division overruled the said contention on the view that the Executing Court was competent to do whatever was necessary under the-law for the execution of the decree. It was also contended before the High Court Division that the copy of the decree as printed in the Paper Book was obviously not a correct and dependable copy inasmuch as there was no schedule of the properties in the copy, of the decree contained in the Paper-Book. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have observed that the schedule to the plaint being the same as the schedule to the decree, the Court may reconstruct the schedule to the decree on the basis of the schedule to the plaint.

8. Leave has been granted to the appellant judgment debtors for considering the following points

(1) That the paper book being a copy of copy is not admissible as secondary evidence and as such it cannot be used for the purpose of reconstruction of the missing records.

(2) That the direction to the executing Court to insert the schedule of the property in the decree from the plaint amounts to a direction to the said Court to amend the decree.

(3) That in the absence of any direction in the decree itself requiring the Court to take	steps for obtaining income tax clearance on behalf Of the judgment-debtors for the purpose of registration of the document, the Executing Court is not competent to take such steps.

9. It should be made clear at the outset that the filing of a certified copy of the decree in the execution case is not necessary for the purpose of the execution of the said decree, particularly when the Court executing the decree was the very court which passed the decree because, if any reference to the decree was needed the original records could easily have been examined: Under sub-rule (3) of Rule 11 of Order 21 C.P. Code, which has been subsequently added by an amendment of the rule, an executing-Court may, of course, require the application to produce a certified copy of the decree but that is obviously for the satisfaction of the. Court in case the original decree is not available for reference for the time being. Rule 195 of the Civil Rules and Orders prepared under the authority of the High Court for the guidance of the Civil Court has accordingly provided The filing of a copy of the decree along with the execution petition is not compulsory but if it is not possible to verify the correctness of the particulars in the application for execution from the Court register etc. the Court may require the applicant to produce a certified copy (Or. 21, r 11(3)

10. In this case the order of stay of the execution proceeding due to the pendency of the appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan having been vacated, the notice of the execution case was duly served upon the judgment debtors but no objection was taken on their behalf to the execution proceeding. The Executing Court however for its own satisfaction, directed the decree-holder to file certified copies of the Judgment and the decree and the said certified copies were duly filed by the decree-holder and, thereafter, the balance of the consideration money was deposited by the decree-holder under an order of the Court. Whatever doubt the Executing Court might have entertained as to the terms of the decree under execution must have been dispelled by the production of the said copy of the decree, and therefore, ordinarily, there should not have arisen under the rule of procedure any more occasion necessitating the prod action of another certified copy of the decree for the purpose of the execution of the decree. As a matter of fact, no further copy of the decree was required by the Executing Court for such purpose, but the decree-holder appears to have been directed by the said Court to furnish further copies of the decree in connection with the judgment-debtors  income-tax clearance certificate.

11. A draft kabala was prepared after the deposit of the balance of the consideration on the basis of the decree and a copy of the same was served upon the judgment-debtors under Order 21, rule 34(2) C. P. Code but neither any objection was taken on behalf of the judgment- debtors to the said draft nor did they appear before the Court to execute and register the document as directed in the decree. The decree-holder, thereafter, in order to realised the costs awarded by the decree, prayed for attachment of a certain amount of money, belonging to the judgment-debtors, as deposited in the Court, for recovery of the decretal costs and ail attachment was effected of the said money by an order of the Executing Court dated 1. 12. 66. No objection was taken, by the judgment-debtors to the said order of attachment as well. The execution of the decree in the instant case meant apart from the a ward of costs, only the execution and registration of the kabala a draft of which was served upon the judgment-debtors, by the Executing Court on behalf of the judgment-debtors, under sub-rules (5) and (6) of Order 21, rule 34 of the C. P Code.

12. On being directed by the Court, a second copy of the decree was filed by the decree holder on 31-12-66 for transmitting the same to the Income-tax Department along with the decree holder's application for the judgment-debtors income tax clearance certificate. It is, however, found from the records that the decree-holder was again asked to produce a copy of the decree for sending the same to the Income-tax Department on the ground that the earlier application along with the copy of the decree had been missing from the office of the Income-Tax Department. On the failure of the decree-holder to produce any such copy due to the missing of the original records from the office of the Court the Execution case was held by the Executing Court to be not maintainable.

13. It should, however, be noticed that the filing of a certified copy of the decree Was not an essential requirements under the procedural law for the purpose of the execution of the decree and that it was for an auxiliary purpose that the decree-holder was directed by the Court to furnish the same. In the circumstances, it was not for the judgment-debtors to plead the absence of such a copy of the decree as a bar to the execution of the decree Moreover even if such a plea was available to them they having failed to take it at the appropriate stage were estopped from taking it at the subsequent stage by the principle of constructive res-judicata as applicable to execution proceeding.

14. The judgment-debtors having failed to appear before the Court to take any objection to the execution, after being served with notice, as shown in the order dated 16-5-65, and the Executing Court having taken positive steps towards execution of the decree, the judgment-debtors are hit by the principle of constructive res-judicata and are precluded from taking any objection to the further execution of the said decree. Notice of a draft kabala as required under Order 21, Rule 34(1) of the Civil Procedure Code was served upon the judgment-debtors under Order 21, Rule 34(2) of the C.P.C. as shown in the order dated 12-8-66, and the judgment-debtors again appear to have failed to take any objection to the said draft. The Executing Court having thereafter taken further steps for execution of the decree, namely, attachment of a sum of money and asking for production of income tax clearance certificate from the Income-Tax  Department, the judgment-debtors are once more faced with the bar of constructive res-judicata as to any objection relating to the contents or any particulars contained in the said draft. In the premises, the judgment-debtors should not have been allowed to obstruct the proceedings of the Execution case on the ground of the absence of a certified copy of the decree in the file of the execution case, which the decree-holder had filed in Court more than once. It is not a case of the judgment-debtors that there was no decree for specific performance of contract for sale in favour of the decree-holder, as stated in the application for execution. The only objection which was taken in the application of the judgment-debtors under section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code respecting the decree was with regard to the description of the decretal property and the said objection was extremely indefinite and vague. To permit the judgment-debtors to urge such objection more than 6 years after the due date and to give effect to it was a patent abuse of the process of the Court and it has rendered the order of the Executing Court dismissing the Execution case on such objection extremely infirmed and untenable.

15. The Executing Court having required the decree-holder to file a certified copy of the decree, the decree-holder was constrained to pray for reconstruction of the records of the Title Suit including the judgment and the decree passed therein; which were found missing from the said Court and under the circumstances, it was undoubtedly obligatory on the part of the said Court which was the Court which passed the decree, to take steps to reconstruct the said records.

<u>16. The substantial question which has been raised in connection with the reconstruction of the records is with regard to the nature of the documents which may be used for the purpose of such reconstruction. It is in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction to do justice that steps are taken by a Court to reconstruct its own records on the basis of the available materials which may be lawfully taken notice of it. It can hardly be disputed that such a proceeding is a judicial proceeding and the proof of the contents of the documents which are, to be reconstructed must be in conformity to the law of evidence. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have directed the Court of the Subordinate Judge to reconstruct the required documents on the basis of the Paper Book of the First Appeal which was preferred to the High Court against the decree under execution, as well as certified copies of the judgment and decree passed by the High Court in the said appeal.</u>

17. Learned Counsel for the appellants has contended that the Paper Book printed for the purpose of the. High Court appeal cannot be the valid basis of such reconstruction as the manner of preparation of such paper book as prescribed by the Appellate Side Rules of the High Court clearly shows, according to the learned Counsel, that the printed papers of the Paper Book are merely copies of copies, and as such are not admissible in evidence.

18. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel for the appellants has placed his reliance upon the decisions in the cases of Rammanuj Roy Vs Dakshineswar Roy, 30 CWN 259, Santokori, Mandar and others Vs Rameswar Singh Bahadur A.I.R. 1929 Pat.41, Alapati Narasimham Vs Aibori Ram Rao A.I.R. 1939 Mad.40, and Maung Chi Vs Maung tha Ku A.I.R. 1923 Rang. 113.

19. Of these, the Rangoon case deals with the question of admissibility of oral account of the contents of a lost judgment, but the other three cases respectively of the Calcutta, Patna and. Madras High Courts deal directly with the question of admissibility of the Paper Book printed by the High Court in connection with the appeal preferred to it and have laid down that having regard to the practice prevailing in the said High Courts for preparation of such paper books, they do not prove themselves, but some oral evidence is necessary to show that the printed papers were compared with the original papers, as required under section 63(3) of the Evidence Act,

20. The Patna High Court, in the case of Chandreswar Vs Biswaswar, A.I.R. 1927 Pat. 61, and the Madras High court, in the case of Ganapathl Ayar Vs Sakharayappa, A.I.R. 1929 Mad. 187, admitted printed copies of High Court printed papers in evidence as secondary evidence of certain depositions, but in the later Patna and Madras cases, the earlier cases have been distinguished and have not been followed.

21. In a case of Indian Jurisdiction, namely, the case of Subrahmaniya Shastri Vs. Laksminarasamtna, A.I.R. 1958 Andhra Pradesh 22, the High Court of Andhra Pradesh followed the view taken by the Madras High Court in A.I.R. 1939 Md. 40 and held that according to the procedure for printing of paper books followed in Madras High Court as well as in the High court of Andhra Pradesh, a paper book printed in the said High Court is not a copy made from or compared with the original, but only a copy of a copy, and in the absence of the evidence as to its comparison with the original papers, it could not be treated as secondary evidence.

22. The preposition of law that for the admissibility of a copy of a document as secondary evidence of the contents of the said document as there must be evidence to show that the said copy was compared with the original, as contemplated in section 63(3) of the Evidence Act, admits of no controversy. But for the applicability of the said decisions in the instant case it is necessary to examine the rules of the Dacca High Court for the preparation of paper books in order to see whether the paper book printed under the said rules are mere copies of copies and as such cannot be treated as secondary evidence of the missing judgment and decree.

23. According to the rules as contained in chapter IX of Rules of the High Court of Judicature for East Pakistan, the preparation of a paper book comprises seven main stages, namely, (a) settlement of the list of. papers to be printed, (b) making transcript of the said papers, (c) translation of the vernacular papers, (d) examination of the translations, (e)editing, (f) printing and (g) taxing.

24. After the settlement of the list of papers, an Advocate who is duly authorised to prepare a. paper book shall have to prepare a transcript of the papers to be printed and also translation of the vernacular determents from the original records. The translations so prepared are thereafter examined by an Examiner of Translations. Then the "Editing" of the paper book commences, which according to rule 2(a) of Chapter IX includes:

(i) Collecting and/arranging the paper required for inclusion in the paper book;

(ii) Examining and comparing proof, or when several Copies of a typed paper book are prepared, examining and comparing such copies, with the originals or authenticated copies of English papers or translations where the rules provide for translations ;

(iii) The preparation of title pages and indexes;

(iv) The General supervision necessary to ensure the accuracy of the record and compliance with the provisions of the Appellate Side Rules with regard to the preparation of paper books."

25. The main function of the Editor is thus to supervise the preparation of the paper book to ensure accuracy of the record and one of his tasks, in case of printed paper books, is to examine and compare proofs with the originals or authenticated copies of English papers or translation where rules provide for such translations.

26. After the papers have been edited they are printed and after the printed paper books have been prepared they are taxed by a Taxing Officer, whose function also is very important. His duty is, according to rule 39(c) of Chapter IX, to see that the paper books have been prepared in accordance with the Rules, and under clause (d) of the said rule, he is to give a certificate that the paper books have been so prepared, after being satisfied to the said effect. It is pertinent to notice the relevant portion of rule 41 in this connection, which is to the following effect : "It shall be the duty of the Examiners of Translations to report through the Taxing Officer to the Registrar any case in which the translations have been carelessly, negligently or imperfectly done, and it shall be the duty of the Taxing Officer to report to the Registrar any case in which the preparation of any other portion of the paper book has been carelessly, negligently or imperfectly done. The main object of all these rules seems to be the preparation of a paper book which will be a correct copy of the record.

27. This paper book is used, at the time of the hearing of the appeal by the High Court itself as well as by the Advocates of the two parties, instead of the original records, to which reference may be made in case of any doubt as to its accuracy and with which the paper book or any part of may be compared. The Advocates of the parties also used those paper books at the hearing for the purpose of conducting the case on behalf of their respective clients.

28. In accordance with the Rules of Chapter XIV made for preservation and destruction of certain records the paper book of the appeal is retained as a part of Part I of the Civil Records of the High Court Appeal and preserved as a permanent record along with certain other papers. The copies of the judgment and decree filed with the memorandum of appeal are also to be preserved as permanent re-records but if the paper book which is preserved contain the said documents; the said copies are not to be preserved. The copies of the judgment and decree which are filed with the memorandum of appeal are certified copies, and the fact that the preservation of the said copies are dispensed with, in case the said documents are included in the paper book, shows that the printed copies of the documents as contained in the paper book are treated, at least, on the same level as the certified co-pies of the said documents.

<u>29. The meticulous rules for the preparation of paper book have been framed with the sole purpose of preparing correct and true copies of the records, which are to be used by the lawyers as well as by the Court, instead of original records, for the hearing and disposal of the appeal. It may also be noticed that this paper book is to constitute, ultimately, after disposal, a part of the permanent records of the High Court, which is a Court of record.</u>

<u>30. In Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition Vol. 9 the following statement has been made in paragraph 816 at page 348 respecting a Court' of record. The proceedings of a Court of record are called records, and are conclusive evidence of that which is recorded therein."</u>

<u>31. Having regard to the common course of public business and regularity of official acts, there may be presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act that the printed paper book, used in an appeal before the High Court, and made a part of the permanent record of the said High Court was duly prepared and is a correct copy of the records of the case. Elaborate procedure for preparation of paper books on the basis of the original records of the case and use of such paper books at the hearing by the High Court, which had, during such hearing the original records in its possession, may very well lead to the presumption that the printed copies contained in the paper book were compared with the original documents of the records and as such are correct and true copies of the same. In view of the rules referred to above, the paper books printed by the Dacca High Court cannot, in our opinion, be said to be mere copies of copies and inadmissible as secondary evidence. We therefore held that learned Judges of the Dacca High Court were not wrong in directing reconstruction of the records on the basis of such paper books.</u>

32. The second point urged by the appellants is based upon some misconception. The learned Counsel for the appellants has contended that the copy of the decree as included in the paper book does not contain any schedule of properties and that the direction of High Court Division to insert the schedule of properties to the plaint as the schedule to the decree is nothing but a direction to amend the decree, which is beyond the jurisdiction of the High Court Division setting as a Court of appeal.

33. It will appear from the High Court Rules that rule. 11A of Chapter IX of the said rules enumerates the list of the documents which are to be printed in a paper book as compulsory papers and includes in item (v) of the said Rule: "The judgment and the decree from which the appeal is preferred, exclusive of schedules; but including annexures.

34. We thus see that the Rule itself provides that the schedule to the decree shall be omitted, presumably because the plaint which is also a compulsory paper contains the same schedule. The absence of the schedule in the printed copy of the decree as contained in the paper book does not therefore mean that the original decree itself did not contain the schedule and so the direction of the Court to insert the plaint schedule in the decree did not amount to an order of amendment of the decree.

<u>35. Learned Counsel for the appellants has tried to build up a point on the basis of the absence of the schedule in the printed copy of the decree that no presumption of accuracy or correctness does attach to such a copy. But as has been already pointed out, the omission of the schedule in the copy of the decree was in accordance with the High Court Rules and cannot be read in rebuttal of the presumption raised under section 114 of the Evidence Act.</u>

36. The third point which has been urged on behalf of the appellants is that in the absence of any direction in the decree the executing court exceeded its power in taking stem to obtain income tax clearance certificate from the Income-tax Department. This objection to the execution of a decree for Specific Performance of a Contract for sale has little force. When an owner of a certain property agrees to transfer the said property to another person for a consideration, the said agreement involves, by necessary implication, a further agreement to do everything which May be necessary to give effect to his primary agreement. In the panic way when a Court has passed a decree for specific enforcement of such an agreement the Court may require the judgment-debtor to do everything which may be necessary for the purpose of performance of the said agreement. Order 21, rule 32(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure which authorises the Court to take appropriate action in this regard is to the following effect: "Where a decree for the specific performance . bf the contract has not been obeyed the court may, in lieu of or in addition to all or any of the processes aforesaid, direct that the act required to be done, may be done, so far as practicable by the decree-holder or some other person appointed by the Court at the costs of the judgment-debtor and upon the act being done the expresses incurred may be ascertained in such manner as the Court may direct and may be, recovered as if they were included in the decree."

<u>37. As was observed by Sir Lancelet Sanderson in delivering the judgment on behalf of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Martial and others Vs. Nanhelal and another, reported in L.R. 57 I.A. 333 same case A.I.R. 1930 P.C. 287 same case 35 C.W.N. 93 that when the defendant "agreed to transfer the cultivating right in 'Sir lands, there was, in their Lordship's opinion, an implied covenant on his part to do all things necessary to effect such transfer, which would include an application to the Revenue Officer to sanction the transfer". It is no doubt true that the said. case was for incorporation of certain implied terms of contract as the specific terms in the decree, while we are concerned in the instant case with giving effect, by way of Execution of the decree, to the said implied terms of the contract which have not been specifically stated in the said decree. The distinction between the two cases does not, in our opinion, present any material difference. The proposition of law is that when a person agrees to transfer a property to another he must be deemed to have agreed to do everything which he is capable of doing according to law, in order to give effect to his primary agreement of transferring the said property and if the Court requires the said person to carry out his primary agreement by a decree made by the Court, he has the obligation, by necessary implication, under the said decree to do everything for the purpose of carrying out the specific direction in the decree of the Court because a decree made by a Court directing a contracting party to implement the agreement, contains by necessary implication, a direction requiring such person to carry out all of his implied terms of the agreement.</u>

<u>38. It may be mentioned that the same principle has been followed by a preponderance of judicial opinion in this subcontinent in holding that even if in a decree for specific performance of contract for sale of a certain property there is no specific direction for delivery of possession of the said property, the said decree may be executed for the purpose of enforcing, delivery of possession of the said property to the decree-holder under the above quoted Rule 32(5) of Order 21, C.P.C., on the basis that delivery of possession of the property was an implied term of the contract and also an implied term of the decree for specific performance of the said contract. Reference may be made to the cases of Atal Behary Vs. Barada Prasad, A.I.R. 1931 Patna 179, Kartic Chandra Vs. Dibakar, A.I.R. 1952 Cal. 363, Arkin Vs. Sahu A.I.R. 1950 Allahabad 415, Janardhan Vs. Girtlhari A.I.R. 1957 Patna 701, Warn. Vs. Chaudhury A.I.R. 1949 Lahore 72, Dudulal Vs. De Khmer A.I.R. 1963 M.P. 86 and Birgis Jahau Vs. Muhammad Hasan (1963) 15 DLR 298 PLD 1964 Dacca 202, in which it has been held that the executing Court has abundant authority to execute a decree for specific performance of contract for sale of a property for enforcing delivery of possession of the said property, even though the decree under execution is silent as to the relief of delivery of possession. In our view a decree for specific performance of a contract for, sale of a property has been correctly interpreted in the said decisions.</u>

<u>39. We are therefore of the opinion that the executing Court was perfectly within its power to direct the decree-holder to apply to the Income-Tax Officer concerned for necessary certificate of income-tax clearance on behalf of the judgment-debtor.</u>

40. The learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that as there was no decree requiring the Income-tax Officer to do anything, the Executing Court exceeded its jurisdiction to direct the Income Tax Officer, who was not a party to the proceeding, to comply with its order. The various orders which were passed in the Execution case were placed before us and does not appear that there was any judicial order of the .Court which required he Income Tax Officer to comply with any specific direction. It was, however, made clear to the Income Tax Officer concerned that the application for Income Tax Clearance Certificate was forwarded under the order of the Court as the judgment-debtors were not carrying out their obligation under the-decree. If there were procedural or other kinds of, difficulty in providing the necessary certificate under the provision of any law it was the duty of the Officer concerned to inform the Court with the utmost dispatch. In a country which is to be governed under the rule of law, it is the duty of all the administrative functionaries of the State to act in aid of the Judicial organ of the State and to see that all the judicial orders are duly carried into effect. The manner in which the Executing Court has dealt with this case and the Income Tax Department has treated the various communications of the Court has left many things to be desired for. It is expected that both the Civil Court as well as the other functionaries of the State should be more conscious about their respective, responsibilities for carrying a solemn decree of a Court into effect. We do not find any substance in any of the contentions raised on behalf of the appellants.

The appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

case_source: Form the judgment and order dated 22.3.82 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1255 of 1979.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order in Civil Revision No. 1255 of 1979 passed by the High Court Division.

2. The respondents Nos. 1 and 2 filed Title Suit No. 200 of 1974 in the Court of Munsif, Natore for a declaration that the 4 kabalas alleged to have been executed by them on 24.5.73 in favour of the defendants appellants were hit by section 23 of the Contract Act and also for possession of the land.

3. Plaintiff's case was that the land described in schedule Ka of the plaint belonged to Haji Mohan Ali and Abdul Hoque who out of this land sold Ka schedule land to some other party in 1970 and sold the Kha schedule land to the plaintiff by executing kabala on 18.9.70 but the kabala was not presented for registration and the vendors refused to register the same when the plaintiffs presented it to the Sub-Registrar Office and got the same registered The defendant Abdul Hannan and others filed Criminal case against the plaintiff under section 144 Cr.P.C. and subsequently the proceeding was drawn up under section 145 Cr.P.C. and a receiver was appointed. The defendant Joynal Abedin brought a Criminal case against plaintiff No. 1 and his relation under section 385/148/448 and warrants were issued. Another case brought against the plaintiff under section 143 and 379 B.P.O Plaintiff's further case was that a salish was held by the relations of defendants and the plaintiffs and in pursuance of the salish the plaintiff was directed to execute kabala in favour of the defendant who in turn withdrew the criminal cases. Accordingly the kabala was executed and defendants withdrew the Criminal case. The plaintiff contended that the kabalas concerned in Kha schedule land were without consideration and the plaintiffs executed them in the face of pressure of the Criminal cases and they were of no effect.

4. The defendants contested the suit by filing a joint written statement and contended that at the intervention of the local head-men and the villagers the parties were advised to settle their dispute and in terms of the Salishnama both parties agreed to compromise by exchange of lands and accordingly litigations were withdrawn. The suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial court noticed that there were litigation between the parties "over the property which admittedly belonged to Haji Mohah Ali and Abdul Hoque. Both sides placed before the Court certain registered documents though "in spite of having registered documents the defendant did not state "their case" is the written statement which warranted a comment by the learned Munsif "Perhaps the defendants' lawyer failed to do his duty honestly". The learned Munsif the considered the contention of the plaintiffs that the consideration of ‘Gha' schedule kabalas were the compromise of a non-compoundable criminal case. The trial court noticed that the Criminal cases had ended in compromise and then considered the salishnama Ext. F which shows:

"that a compromise between the parties was made on the condition that the defendants would give some lands to the plaintiffs and the plaintiffs in consideration of that will also give the lands of the disputed kabala".

The trial court noticed that the plaintiffs have not examined any witness to give evidence that the consideration of the disputed kabala was the compounding a of non-compoundable case. Its view was that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the consideration of the suit kabala was unlawful. Accordingly the suit was dismissed.

6. On appeal the learned Additional District Judge took the view that the impugned kabalas were executed by the plaintiff at a time when non-compoundable criminal case was pending against him and found that the execution of the kabala were made for the purpose of stifling a criminal case and as such it is hit by section 23 of the Contract Act because the transaction is unlawful and against the public policy. The appellate Court below noticed the Criminal proceeding under sections 380 and 148 pending against the plaintiff started by the defendants and its view was that the trial court was not justified in dismissing the suit, and accordingly the appeal was allowed and the suit was decreed declaring that the impugned kabalas dated 24.5.73 executed by the plaintiff in favour of the defendants as void. Reliance was placed on 21 DLR 918 and 5 DLR 114 and 338

7. On revision the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division noticed the material portion of Salishnama Ext. which runs as follows:

১ম পক্ষ সাহাজ উদ্দিন দিং ২য় পক্ষকে রোস্তম আলীকে বাড়ী সংলগ্ন জমি মৌজা মৃচাপিলা মধ্যে ৩৪৮ নং দাগ হইতে ৩৫/১ বিঘা ২ কাঠা জমি বিনামুল্যে রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দিবে। রেজিষ্ট্রি খরচ রোস্তম আলী বহন করিবে। ২য় পক্ষ রোস্তম আলী দিং কবলা মূলে হাজী মহন ও আব্দুল হক সাহেবের কাছে যে ৭ বিঘা জমি রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়াছিল তাহা হইতে ১ বিঘা ২ কাঠা বাদ রাখিয়া যাবতীয় জমি ১ম পক্ষ সাহাজ উদ্দিনদিগকে বিনামূল্যে রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দিবে। রেজিষ্ট্রি খরচ সাহাবুদ্দিন বহন করিবে।

প্রকাশ থাকে আমরা উভয়ে উভয়ের বিরুদ্ধে যে সব মামলা কোর্টে বা থানায় দায়ের করা হইয়াছে তাহা উভয় পক্ষ একত্রিত হইয়া আপোষ নামা দরখাস্ত দিয়া উক্ত মামলা উঠাইয়া লইব। খরচ উভয় পক্ষ বহন করিব।

তাঃ১২-৫-৭৩ইং

The learned Judge noticed in all there were three cases pending namely (1) Criminal case No. 40C of 1973 under sections 145/379 (2) Criminal Case No. 207 of 1973 uncle' sections 148/448/380 P.C. (3) Proceeding under section 145 bearing case No. 149M of 1972 It was further noticed that on 24.5.73 the plaintiff executed 4 kabalas in favour of the defendants and on the same date defendants withdrew the Criminal cases as a result the accused were discharged under section 2531 2) Cr.P.C. and proceeding under sections 145 were dropped and the attached properties were released. The learned Judge posed the question:

"Whether the disputed kabalas were executed in exchange of the properties of the defendants or in consideration of the compounding of some non-compoundable criminal cases".

The learned Judge kept in view the well-settled principle that it is against the public policy to make a trade of felony or compromise an offence which is not compoundable in law and that an agreement to that effect is wholly void. He further noticed a decision of the West Pakistan High Court wherein it was held that in order to settle the dispute between the parties concerning their title to the land but to finish criminal cases as well. The compromise that was arrived as was not hit by section 23 of the Contract Act. The matter went before the Supreme Court and leave was granted to consider the question being of public importance but the decision of the Supreme Court could not be traced in the subsequent volume of P.L.D. though the leave order in that case was published in 1968 SC M.R. 1313 tin the case of Md. Isha Khan Vs. Md. Jahan Khan).

8. The learned Judge then observed that there was no evidence of dispute and repelled the contention that the compromise was in fact for exchange of property between the parties. It was concluded:

It appears that the plaintiffs had to pay a price for withdrawal of some non-compoundable criminal case hanging over then heads and that the suit lands, the which they were the undisputed owned; were brought in the bargain agreements, without there being previous history of bonafide civil disputes, cannot be hit by section 23 of the Contract Act".

9. Notwithstanding the above observation the learned Judge noticed that a kabala was also executed by the defendants in favour of the plaintiffs and observed that the defendant themselves will be within their right to cancel the document obtained by the plaintiff No. 1 and his brother for the same reason. In this view of matter the rule was discharged and the judgment and decree of the learned Additional District Judge were affirmed.

10. Leave was granted to consider the question whether the Salishnama Ext. F was correctly construed by the High Court Division to show that the kabala in question were hit by the provision of section 23 of the Contract Act.

11. It will be noticed that the plaintiff executed 4 kabalas in favour of the defendants and the defendant executed one kabala in favour of the plaintiff and his brother. The terms of the kabala have been mentioned above whereby the plaintiff had to execute the kabala for 5 bighas and odd land out of the 7 bighas land purchased from Haji Mohan and Abdul Hoque whereas the defendants had to execute a kabala for 1 bigha 2 kathas in favour of the plaintiff which is a part of their homestead land. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan, learned Counsel argued that the teams show that this was mere exchange of properties between the parties and in consideration of the dispute over the land which originally belonged to Haji Mohan and Abdul Hoque. It is true that a Criminal proceeding under section 145. Cr.P.C. was pending being Criminal Case No. 259M of 1972 wherein proceedings were started and receiver was appointed by the Magistrate. That was a case of 1972 whereas the kabalas were executed on 24.5.73. It is argued that the court of appeal below and the High Court Division have overlooked these aspects of the case and concentrated mere on a point namely whether any compound able offence was compounded which was never agitated before a Criminal Court.

12. This contention has substance. In the Criminal Court there were two cases pending namely (1) Criminal Case No. 207 of 1973 wherein the defendant Joynal Abedin filed a Criminal case against the plaintiff under sections 38/148/448/ and the second case being Criminal case No. 40C of 1973 under Sections 143/379 B P. C. against the plaintiff. It is true that both the cases were withdrawn by the prosecutor namely the defendant on the very day when the kabalas were executed and in both the cases the plaintiff accused were discharged by the learned Magistrate under section 253 (2) Cr. P. C. Having secured this discharge order the plaintiff now come round to say that the kabala executed by him were hit by section 23 of the Contract Act as void. Nothing was said as to the effect of the kabala that was executed by the defendant in favour of the plaintiff surrendering 1 bigha 2 kathas of his homestead land.

13 Section 23 of the Contract Act is in the following terms:

"23. What considerations and objects are lawful and what not The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless-

it is forbidden by law; of; or

is of such a nature that, it' permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or

is fraudulent; or

involves or implies injury to the person or

property of another; or

the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy In each of these cases the consideration to object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful void.

The appellate Court below or the High Court Division did not specify how the kabalas are hit and by which of the provision. Presumably the view was taken that such agreement is forbidden by law or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provision of any law. The trial court noticed that no evidence was given nor any witness was examined to show that the consideration of the disputed kabala was a compounding of a non-compoundable case.

14. Section 345 Cr. P.C. lays down which of the offences should be compounded and again it is divided into two parts. Some offences can be compounded by the parties themselves and some offence can be compounded with permission of the Court before which any prosecution for such offence is pending. The courts below did not specify which of the offence was non-compounding. Again in the Criminal Court this question was not raised because the plaintiffs are the accused persons and it was to their advantage not to raise the point, inasmuch as they secured their discharge from the Criminal Court. Had there been any non-compoundable offence that would have attracted the attention of the Criminal Court but since the Criminal Court passed the order of discharge obviously took the view that there was no non-compounding offence. Because sub-section (7) says that no offence can be compounded except as provided by this section.

15. Next if there be any offence which can be compounded only with permission of the court then the legitimate inference can be drawn that the Court had permitted for the compounding of such offence.

16. Our Criminal Administration of Justice encourages the compromise of certain disputes and even carat’s offence can be compound as provided by section 345 Cr. P.C. Shalish or compromise had been although a mode of settlement of dispute in this sub-continent from time immemorial. In the Conciliation Court Ordinance, 1961, section 3 provides for the certain offences referable to the Conciliation Court and no Civil or Criminal Court shall have jurisdiction to try any such case and even cases falling under Part II of the Schedule may be so referred if all the parties thereto agree to such a reference. Sub-section (2) provides for that in some matters Conciliation Court will have no jurisdiction such as the case in which interest of minor is involved or in case of arbitration or the case against the Government or Public Organisation and clause (d) adds:

"cases which according to the customary law of a community are referable to a community panchayat."

This is a legislative recognition of a settlement of a dispute by a community panchayet and sub section (3) further provides that the Government may add to the Schedule any class of cases elating to such dispute between private parties as are of "a local nature and are capable of settlement of compromise". The whole emphasis is on settlement of dispute either by Panchayet or by compromise. The same trend was maintained after repeal of the Conciliation Court by the village Court Ordinance. 1976 and in the Schedule section 143 figures Part I and Sections 379, 380 and 381 were also added to the list under certain circumstances to be decided by the Village Court. The decision of the Village Court either by the unanimous or by majority opinion shall be enforceable and section 14 bars the appearance of a legal practitioner. The composition of the Village Court provides that two members to he nominated by each of the parties to the dispute. Thus the legislative Scheme seems to be that those offences are to be tried by Village Court and compensation can be awarded by such Court.

<u>17. The pattern is clear, namely that the law encourages settlement of dispute. either by Panchayet or by Arbitration or by way of compromise and if it is a Criminal offence, the offence can be compounded within the limit of section 345 Cr.P.0 The category of offence compoundable have been enlarged by the Law Reforms Ordinance and at the moment all the offences which are subject matter g Criminal Case No. 207 of 1073, 400 of 1973 e.g. offence under sections. 380/148/448/143 and 379 of the Penal Code are compoundable. The main ground of the judgment of the appellate Court and the High Court Division is that some of the offences are non-compoundable offence although unfortunately none of the Courts below have specified which of the offences is non-compoundable. Insofar as the case under section 145 Cr.P C. is concerned that was not a case involving any Criminal charge. In Jugadish Vs. Kausilluh Devi, Alk 1947 All 317 this point was considered and it was observed:</u>

<u>"In could, in no sense be contrary to public policy that persons concerned in a dispute about land should settle their dispute so as to avoid any future danger of a breach of the peace. The provisions of section 145 deal with an inquiry primarily into possession over property in dispute and they are of judicial nature. Them is nothing in them which should cause any apprehension which would vitiate an agreement to settle the disputes between the parties.</u>

<u>"In the present case the case under section 145 Cr.P.C. was started in 1972 and admittedly the dispute was concerning the land which originally belonged to Hajs and Abdul Hoque. Such dispute is compoundable and as a matter of fact the learned Magistrate dropped the proceeding because he was satisfied that there was no apprehension of breach of peace.</u>

18. The defendant took the stand that the village headmen and the elders persuaded them to have compromise settling all the disputes which resulted in the Salishnama Ext. F. Accordingly the Criminal Cases were withdrawn.

19. In one of the oldest cases reported in 10. Cr.L.J. page 228 (Emperor Vs. Lilaram and others) a petition was filed in Court "that s reconciliation bad been effected by the intervention of some respectable persons, and the matter had been compromised". The Magistrate refused to accept the compromise and referred to Sadar Court Building in Criminal Report No. 15 of 1894 whereupon the Court of Judicial Commissioner observed:

'‘We are of the opinion however, the Court is not concerned to inquire into the nature or value of the consideration, and if, as in the present case, the complainant considers that his grievance is redressed, by the mere fact of respectable persons intervening, though he has received no money payment or even a direct apology from accused, he is, nevertheless, at full liberty to compound the prosecution".

The High Court Division noticed 21 D.L.R. (Dhaka) 918. Purnendu Kumar Das Vs. Hiran Kumar Das. Mr. Shaukat Ali Khan does not contest the proposition laid in this decision. He submits that the facts of that case and the present case are completely different because here by the Salishnama parties exchanged their properties with each other. The High Court Division noticed that it is well settled that it is against the public policy to make a trade or felony or compromise of an offence which is not compoundable in law and that an agreement to that effect is void. As proposition of law it is not disputed but the Supreme Court of India 1965 (SC) page 166 in the case of Ouseph Poulo Vs Catholic Union Bank observed:

"Where the validity of an agreement is impeached on the ground that it is opposed to public policy under section 23 of the Act, the party setting up the plea must be called upon to prove that plea by clear and satisfactory evidence."

It was observed:

"Reliance on a mere sequence of events may tend to obliterate the real difference between the motive for the agreement and the consideration for it. Did the parties offer to give security and execute the documents in consideration for the withdrawal of the Criminal complaint by the Bank? That is the question which has to be decided in the present appeals, and in proving their case, the plaintiffs are expected to lead satisfactory evidences: and in our opinion, the High Court is, on the whole, right when it came to the conclusion, that the evidences led by the plaintiffs is far from satisfactory. Therefore, we are satisfied that the view taken by the High Court is right and cannot be reversed".

In the present case the trial court noticed as under:

"The plaintiffs have not examined any witness to give evidence that the consideration of the disputed kabalas was the compounding of a non compoundable case".

<u>20. In the absence of such evidence it does not appear clearly as to how the appellate Court below and the High Court Division took the view that the kabalas were hit by section 23 of the Contract Act. As has been noticed already in the Criminal Court this issue was not made and the Criminal Court did not take any exception to the petition for withdrawal of the complaint case. Understandably the accused plaintiff would not take any exception because by the withdrawal of the prosecution he had secured his discharge Now in the second round he has assailed the kabalas by which he had to forgo his claim over 5 bighas and odd quantity of land which originally belonged to Haji Md. Mohan and Abdul Hoque. He wanted to enrich himself by assailing these kabalas without, however, saying a word as to the kabala given by the defendant wherein 1 bigha 2 kathas was surrendered in favour. A person in pari delicto cannot seek any relief before any Court of law. The complainant having secured his discharge in pursuance of the Salish which was accepted by both the parties had thought it fit to disown the Salishnama. Law does not encourage a person to take advantage of his own wrong. The Trial Court rightly dismissed the suit.</u>

<u>21. Withdrawal and composition are two distinct concepts. Withdrawal is the act of the complainant whereas the composition of an offence requires the co-operation of both parties. Whether a petition is one for withdrawal or compromise, is to be judged from the fact of each case. In AIR 1923 All 474 inc complainant wrote out: "This is to say that Mr. John came to me and offered and additional apology [beg to withdraw the case against him", the document was held to that the offence was compounded. Though the compounding of an offence signified the person against whom the offence has been has received some gratification to act as an inducement for his desiring to abstain from persecution, even an apology may be sufficient consideration for a compromise. Here, the parties exchanged their land at the intervention of the village elders and they have settled up all their differences. Such compromises are allowed by Courts and the Court is not concerned with the nature of value of the consideration. (AIR 1950 All 86).</u>

<u>22. The present case is on all fours with the case of Moulvi Mohammad Ismail vs. Amad Ali, 20 CWN 948 where the plaintiff sued for a declaration that certain documents executed by him in favour of the defendants were invalid and void for want of consideration. The trial Court found that there was no coercion exercised upon the plaintiff and the suit was dismissed. On appeal, the plain- tiff appellant contended that the contracts were opposed to public policy as they were entered into for compounding a Criminal Case. The learned Subordinate Judge noticed that the plaintiff had been summoned under section 325 of the Penal Code and such offence is compoundable with the permission of the Court and the Magistrate gave permission to compound the case. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed. In Second Appeal the Calcutta High Court dismissed the appeal by observing "the parties entered into a compromise for settling their long standing disputes by executing the documents and payment of money in cash", and the matter was compounded with the leave of the Court. Precisely that is the position here and therefore the plaintiff cannot make a grievance to invalidate the documents executed by him in pursuance of a compromise.</u>

<u>In the result, therefore this appeal is allowed. Judgment of the High Court Division and appellate Court below arc set aside and that of the trial Court dismissing the suit is restored. There will be no order as to costs.</u>

End.

case_source: From the judgment and decree dated 18-11-82 passed by the High Court Division. Jessore Bench in S.A. No.213 of 1973
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—In this appeal by the plaintiffs the question is whether the decree obtained by them in their suit for setting aside the decree of a previous partition suit, namely, T.S. No.21 of 1965, has been reversed on correct appreciation of facts and proper application of law. The plaintiffs suit, namely T.S. No. 93 of 1966, was decreed by the trial Court namely, the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal, on 8 July 1967. But on appeal the decree was reversed by the Additional District Judge on 28 April 1973 in Title Appeal No.203 of 1967; this decision of the appellate Court has been upheld by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division on 18 November 1982 in Second Appeal No.213 of 1976; both these Courts took the concurrent view that plaintiffs' suit is not maintainable as five of them were not parties to the partition suit but one of them was a party.

2. The suit property, as the appellants' case in T.S. No. 93 of 1966 shows, belonged to proforma-defendants Nos. 4 to 55 and plaintiffs Nos. 5 and 6, and this property has been described in 'ka' schedule of the plaint. Respondent, defendant No.1, Shamsuddin (died since then and has been duly substituted) had filed the previous suit, T.S. No.21 of 1965, claiming partition of his 8-annas share in the suit land against defend-ant Nos. 2 and 4 of the present suit who were principal defendants, Nos.1 to 3, in the previous suit alleging that those three defendants had also acquired, along with him, the remaining 8 annas share. The basis of their shares was stated to be a settlement In the year 1354 B.S., corresponding to 1948 A.D., from the ex-landlords, namely proforma defendants Nos.4 to 55 and others as stated above. In the said partition suit which was filed on 29 March 1965 defend-ant Nos. 1 to 3 (principal defendants), and proforma-defendants Nos. 4, 10, 19, 22 and 39 filed a compromise petition within 9 days, that is on 7 April 1965, admitting the plaintiffs claim and on that compromise petition the suit was decreed that very day in terms of the compromise petition.

3. The appellants filed the present suit for a declaration that the compromise decree in the partition suit is void, fraudulent and collusive and not binding upon them. In support of their claim they set forth a number of grounds, such as ; they (appellants-plaintiffs 1 to 5) were not parties to the said partition suit but their lands were included in the suit property which was sought to be partitioned, that the respondent (plaintiff of that suit) got no title or possession at all but his claim as to title by settlement was totally false, that he acted in collusion with the principal defendants of that suit who also claimed 8-annas share by a similar false claim to, settlement, that the said suit was filed as a partition suit to establish title by circumventing Ordinance No.1 of 1964 which put restriction on the filing of any declaratory suit in respect of landed property of a member of minority-community, that summons of that suit was fraudulently suppressed in that three of the defendants were already dead and most of the other defendants had left Pakistan for India long before the filing of the suit.

4. The allegations contained in these grounds were denied by the respondent, plaintiff of that partition suit. The trial Court on evidence decreed the appellants' suit setting aside the decree of the partition suit, among other things, on the following grounds ; that plaintiff of the partition suit totally failed to prove his prima facie title to the suit land by any settlement, that three of the defendants having died and others having left the country before the filing of the suit, the purported service of notice upon them was a clear fraud, that the plaintiffs of the present suit who got shares in the suit land having not been made parties to the partition suit, not only the decree passed in that suit is not binding upon them, but the partition suit itself was not maintainable for want of necessary parties.

5. The lower Appellate Court as well as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division concurrently held that since the plaintiffs Nos. 1 to 5 were not parties to the partition suit, the decree passed in that suit is not binding upon them, and as such, they need not worry about it, and in case they feel that their title has been clouded by the decree, they may file a suit for declaration of their title. As to plaintiff No. 6, who was a party to the partition suit, these courts held that he is debarred from filing the present suit for setting aside the decree.

<u>6. Judgment of the High Court Division shows that the suit of the appellants was held to be not maintainable for two opposing reasons, and this has also been pointed out by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the appellants. One reason is that so far as plaintiffs 1-5 (appellants Nos, 1-5) are concerned, the suit is not maintainable as they were not parties and their interest was not affected by the decree; and the other reason is that so far as plaintiff No. 6 (appellant No. 6) is concerned, as he was a party thereto he cannot challenge the decree. We find it very difficult to get to the logic of this argument set forth by these courts, particularly, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, in holding that the appellant's suit far setting aside the decree passed in the partition suit is not maintainable. The trial Court in an elaborate judgment arrived at a number of findings including the finding that three of the defendants having been dead and most of the other defendants having left the country before the filing of the suit, the decree was obtained by fraudulent suppression of summons and that by resorting to a partition suit the respondent (plaintiff in that suit) got his title established by avoiding the provisions of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 which barred the filing of any declaratory suit in respect of property belonging to a member of the minority community. For the purpose of disposal of this appeal we need not refer to all these findings, but we shall concentrate on the finding as to defect of party. In the partition suit five of the appellants, namely, plaintiff’s Nos. 1-5 were not impleaded. In a partition suit, the established principle of law is that all co-sharers shall be impleaded and that failure to implead any co-sharer shall render the suit liable for dismissal on the ground of maintainability. This principle of law was also accepted by the learned Single Judge a High Court Division, but the learned Judge fell into an utter confusion as to which of the two suits before him this principle is to be applied in. The learned Single Judge, after agreeing with the appellants that defect of party is fatal to a partition suit, observed "But in the present case it is not a partition suit but is a suit for declaration that the sule-decree passed in the partition suit is not binding upon the plaintiff; moreover the plaintiffs could not show that in the present suit there is any defect of party." It should be kept in mind that it is not the Title Suit No. 93 of 1966, filed by the appellants themselves which they are challenging on the ground of defect of parties; but it is the partition suit, T.S. No. 21 of 1965, whose decree has been challenged by them on the ground of defect of party Admittedly T.S. No. 21 of 1965 was a partition suit in which five of the six appellants were not parties. As such the partition suit was liable to be dismissed on this ground alone the appellants filed their suit challenging the decree of the respondent's partition suit; to challenge the decree of partition suit, it is not necessary that another partition suit is to be filed</u>

<u>7. Mr. Md. Ayub, learned Advocate for the respondent-defendant No. 1, has made strenuous efforts to defend the impugned Judgment of the High Court Division taking resort to a novel argument. It is that in e very suit it is for the plaintiff to decide whom he will implead and against whom he will seek relief; and according to the plaintiff of the Partition suit these appellants were not his co-sharers in the suit property and as such he is not required to implead in his suit the appellants who were mere strangers to him. So far as a stranger is concerned, the learned Advocate is perfectly correct in his argument, for a stranger need not be impleaded in a partition suit or for that matter in any suit But when the stranger's property is included in a suit the "stranger" must be impleaded as a party, for a person having any interest or share in the disputed property cannot be avoided by simply branding him a stranger. Facts proved before the trial court are that Tarak Saha was a recorded co-sharer in the holding comprising R.S. Khatians Nos. 60, 61 and 61 (3) of Monza Takshar (vide Exts. 5 to 5 (b)) on whose death his son, Chittaranjan Shaba, inherited his share, and that it is this Chittaranjan from whom the appellants purchased his share by a registered kabala and, further, that at is this share which has been included in the suit land which was sought to be partitioned in T.S. No. 21 of 1965. On the face of record the plaintiff appellants were necessary parties to the partition suit but were left out. Contention of the learned Advocate is therefore devoid of any substance. The learned Advocate has made a last minute effort to salvage the impugned judgment of the High Court Division arguing that the appellants' suit for setting aside the decree of the partition suit is not maintainable without a prayer for establishment of their title. Evidence shows that they have got title as well as possession in their share of the suit holding. In these circumstances their suit for declaration of nullity of the decree of the partition suit to which they were not party is quite maintainable. On the ground of defect of party alone that suit fell through as a whole.</u>

8. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division confirming that of the lower Appellate Court is set aside and that of the trial court is restored. No order as to costs.

End.
